name: Ensure reads of union fields produce valid values for the field's type
description: Reading a union field whose stored bytes are not a valid representation of the selected field type can trigger undefined behaviour.
extended_description: Similar to C, unions allow multiple fields to occupy the same memory. Unlike enumeration types, unions do not track which field is currently active. You must ensure that when a field is read that the underlying bytes are valid for that field's type . Every type has a *validity invariant* — a set of constraints that all values of that type must satisfy . Reading a union field performs a *typed read*, which asserts that the bytes are valid for the target type. Examples of validity requirements for common types: * **bool**: Must be 0 (false) or 1 (true). Any other value (e.g., 3) is invalid. * **char**: Must be a valid Unicode scalar value (0x0 to 0xD7FF or 0xE000 to 0x10FFFF). * **References**: Must be non-null and properly aligned. * **Enums**: Must hold a valid discriminant value. * **Floating point**: All bit patterns are valid for the f32 or f64 types. * **Integers**: All bit patterns are valid for integer types. Reading an invalid value is undefined behavior.
detection_methods: Search for union field reads and trace the most recent field write
Review unsafe union accesses for explicit validity checks
Run Miri and targeted tests over invalid discriminants, booleans, characters, references and pointers
potential_mitigations: Track the active representation explicitly
Validate raw bytes before typed interpretation
Replace unions with enums or strongly typed wrappers where practical

name: Use strong types to differentiate between logically distinct values
description: Primitive or structurally identical values are reused for different domain concepts, allowing validly typed but semantically incorrect values to be mixed.
extended_description: This rule ensures that parameters and variables convey intent directly through the type system to avoid accidental misuse of values with identical primitives but different semantics. In particular: * Prevents mixing logically distinct values. Primitive types like u32 or u64 can represent lengths, counters, timestamps, durations, IDs, or other values. Different semantic domains can be confused, leading to incorrect computations. The Rust type system prevents such mistakes when semantics are encoded into distinct types. * Improves static safety. Statically distinct types allow the compiler to enforce domain distinctions. Accidental swapping of parameters or returning the wrong quantity becomes a compile-time error. * Improves readability and discoverability. Intent-revealing names (Meters, Seconds, UserId) make code self-documenting. Type signatures become easier to read and understand. * Enables domain-specific trait implementations. Statically distinct types allow you to implement Add, Mul, or custom traits in ways that match the domain logic. Aliases cannot do this, because they are not distinct types. * Supports API evolution. Statically distinct types act as strong API contracts that can evolve independently from their underlying representations.
detection_methods: Look for multiple parameters or fields of the same primitive type with different units or meanings
Search for aliases that do not create distinct types
Review call sites where argument order can be confused
potential_mitigations: Introduce newtype wrappers for units and domain concepts
Encode valid ranges and invariants in constructors
Use distinct enums for closed domain states

name: The 'as' operator should not be used with numeric operands
description: Numeric conversion with as may silently truncate, wrap, change sign, or lose precision.
extended_description: Although the conversions performed by as between numeric types are all well-defined, as coerces the value to fit in the destination type, which may result in unexpected data loss if the value needs to be truncated, rounded, or produce a nearest possible non-equal value. Although some conversions are lossless, others are not symmetrical. Instead of relying on either a defined lossy behaviour or risking loss of precision, the code can communicate intent by using Into or From and TryInto or TryFrom to signal which conversions are intended to perfectly preserve the original value, and which are intended to be fallible. The latter cannot be used from const functions, indicating that these should avoid using fallible conversions. A pointer-to-address cast does not lose value, but will be truncated unless the destination type is large enough to hold the address value. The usize type is guaranteed to be wide enough for this purpose. A pointer-to-address cast is not symmetrical because the resulting pointer may not point to a valid object, may not point to an object of the right type, or may not be properly aligned. If a conversion in this direction is needed, will communicate the intent to perform an unsafe operation.
detection_methods: Search for `as` casts between numeric types
Flag narrowing, signedness-changing and integer-to-float casts
Test boundary values at every conversion
potential_mitigations: Use TryFrom or TryInto for fallible conversions
Use From or Into for lossless conversions
Check ranges explicitly before conversion

name: Avoid as underscore pointer casts
description: An `as _` pointer cast hides the destination pointer type and can conceal an incorrect representation, mutability, provenance or alignment assumption.
extended_description: var as Type casts and \s between raw pointer types are generally valid and unchecked by the compiler as long the target pointer type is a thin pointer. Not specifying the concrete target pointer type allows the compiler to infer it from the surroundings context which may result in the cast accidentally changing due to surrounding type changes resulting in semantically invalid pointer casts. Raw pointers have a variety of invariants to manually keep track of. Specifying the concrete types in these scenarios allows the compiler to catch some of these potential issues for the user.
detection_methods: Search for `as _` in pointer-related expressions
Inspect inferred target types at each cast
Review casts that cross mutability or pointee types
potential_mitigations: Spell out the complete destination pointer type
Use typed conversion helpers
Document and verify provenance and alignment assumptions

potential_mitigations: Use checked_shl or checked_shr and handle failure

name: An integer shall not be converted to a pointer
description: An integer is converted directly to a pointer, losing or fabricating pointer provenance and risking invalid or unauthorised memory access.
extended_description: A pointer created from an arbitrary arithmetic expression may designate an invalid address, including an address that does not point to a valid object, an address that points to an object of the wrong type, or an address that is not properly aligned. Use of such a pointer to access memory will result in undefined behavior. The as operator also does not check that the size of the source operand is the same as the size of a pointer, which may lead to unexpected results if the address computation was originally performed in a differently-sized address space. While as can notionally be used to create a null pointer, the functions and are the more idiomatic way to do this.
detection_methods: Search for integer-to-pointer casts
Review address arithmetic and memory-mapped I/O abstractions
Run provenance-aware dynamic analysis where supported
potential_mitigations: Derive pointers from valid pointers rather than integers
Isolate unavoidable hardware-address construction behind a reviewed abstraction
Document target-specific provenance and validity requirements

name: Recursive function are not allowed
description: Direct or indirect recursion creates an execution depth that may be difficult to bound, risking stack exhaustion and non-deterministic timing.
extended_description: Recursive functions can easily cause stack overflows, which may result in exceptions or, in some cases, undefined behavior (typically some embedded systems). Although the Rust compiler supports tail call optimization , this optimization is not guaranteed and depends on the specific implementation and function structure. There is an open RFC to guarantee tail call optimization in the Rust compiler , but this feature has not yet been stabilized. Until tail call optimization is guaranteed and stabilized, developers should avoid using recursive functions to prevent potential stack overflows and ensure program reliability.
detection_methods: Build a call graph and detect cycles
Search for functions that call themselves directly or through traits and callbacks
Measure stack use and execution depth under worst-case inputs
potential_mitigations: Replace recursion with bounded iteration
Use an explicit fixed-capacity work stack where traversal is required
Prove and enforce a strict depth bound if deviation is unavoidable

name: Assure visibility of unsafe keyword in unsafe code
description: Unsafe operations or unsafe linkage attributes are not visibly marked, weakening auditability and allowing safety obligations to be missed during review.
extended_description: * Auditability and review * unsafe blocks create clear audit boundaries where reviewers can focus on code that may violate Rust's safety guarantees * Safety-critical standards like ISO 26262 and DO-178C require traceability of hazardous operations * Helps enumerate and document all places where safety requirements must be manually upheld * Satisfies ISO 26262 Part 6, Table 1, objective 1c (use of language subsets) * Satisfies DO-178C Section 6.3.4.f (source code traceability) * Explicit acknowledgment of responsibility * The unsafe keyword signals that the programmer is taking responsibility for upholding invariants the compiler cannot verify * Prevents accidental use of unsafe operations without conscious decision * Aligns with the principle of defense in depth in safety-critical systems * Static analysis and tooling * Tools like cargo-geiger , unsafe-inspect, and custom linters can automatically locate and count unsafe blocks * Enables metrics like "unsafe density" for safety assessments * Supports qualification evidence required by certification standards * Traceability for certification * Safety-critical certifications require demonstrating that hazardous operations are identified and controlled * Visible unsafe tokens provide direct linkage to safety cases and hazard analyses * Facilitates the required documentation that each unsafe operation has been reviewed and justified

Search for extern blocks and unsafe attributes lacking explicit unsafe markers
Audit macro expansions for hidden unsafe constructs

name: A macro should not be used in place of a function
description: A macro is used where a function would provide clearer typing, evaluation and control-flow semantics.
extended_description: Although the compiler reports both the macro expansion and its invocation site, diagnostics originating within macros can be more difficult to interpret than those from ordinary function or type definitions. Complex or deeply nested macros may obscure intent and hinder static analysis, increasing the risk of misinterpretation or overlooked errors during code review. **Debugging Complexity** - Errors point to expanded code rather than source locations, making it difficult to trace compile-time errors back to the original macro invocation. **Optimization** - Macros may inhibit compiler optimizations that work better with functions. - Macros act like #[inline(always)] functions, which can lead to code bloat. - They don't benefit from the compiler's inlining heuristics, missing out on selective inlining where the compiler decides when inlining is beneficial. **Functions provide** - Clear type signatures. - Predictable behavior. - Proper stack traces. - Consistent optimization opportunities.
detection_methods: Find macros whose expansion behaves like an ordinary function
Inspect repeated argument evaluation and control-flow effects
Compare whether a generic or const function can express the same behaviour
potential_mitigations: Replace function-like macros with functions
Use generics, traits or const functions for reusable typed behaviour
Retain macros only where syntax generation is essential and justified

name: Shall not write code that expands macros
description: Source code depends on macro expansion, so the reviewed form differs from the compiled form and traceability can be lost.
extended_description: Explanation of why this guideline is important.
detection_methods: Generate fully expanded source in CI
Compare compiled artefacts to reviewed expanded code
Identify nested and transitive expansions
potential_mitigations: Avoid macro-generating source in safety-critical components
Check in generated code where permitted
Control and verify the expansion toolchain and output

name: Missing Run-Time Guards Before Hazardous Operations
description: The code performs operations that can fail at run time, such as division, pointer dereference, array indexing or narrowing arithmetic, without first checking that the operands are in a safe range, so a bad value causes a crash or silently corrupt results.
extended_description: C performs almost no checking of its own at run time, so a divisor of zero, an out-of-range index, a NULL or stale pointer, or a signed result that exceeds its type produces undefined behaviour or a wrapped value rather than a clean error. In source this shows up as / and % with a divisor taken from input, a calculation or a function parameter; buf[i] or ptr + n where the index comes from a message, loop counter or length field; dereferences of pointers returned by lookup functions that may return NULL; shift counts not bounded by the operand width; and malloc or similar results used without a NULL test. Hotspots include message parsers, protocol handlers, sensor scaling code and interrupt handlers that consume hardware values. Code where the operand range is proven locally, for example a divisor that is a non-zero constant or an index masked to the array size, does not count. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Dir 4.1 (Required).
detection_methods: Find / and % expressions whose right operand is not a non-zero constant and confirm a zero check dominates each one
Find array subscripts and pointer offsets derived from external data, length fields or parameters and check for a bound test against the array size before use
Find dereferences of pointers returned by functions that can return NULL and check for a NULL test on every path
Review arithmetic on values from sensors, messages or configuration for overflow of the result type, especially multiplications and left shifts
Run a static analyser with run-time error detection, then confirm findings manually because the property is undecidable
potential_mitigations: Validate divisors, indices, shift counts and pointer arguments against their safe ranges immediately before the operation
Return or propagate an error, or substitute a documented safe value, when a guard fails instead of continuing
Where a guard is omitted because the range is proven, record the reasoning in a comment next to the operation
Treat any remaining unchecked cases as a documented deviation with the supporting analysis
common_consequences: Availability; DoS: Crash, Exit, or Restart
Integrity, Confidentiality; Read Memory, Modify Memory

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Guard operations that can fail during execution

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Dir 4.1 (Required; directive). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Undocumented Assembly Language in C Sources
description: The code contains assembly language, inline or in separate files, with no explanation of why it is needed or how it exchanges data with the surrounding C, so maintainers cannot safely change or port it.
extended_description: Assembly is tied to one processor and one compiler's calling convention, so its meaning is implementation-defined and it silently breaks when the toolchain, optimisation level or target changes. In source it appears as asm, __asm, __asm__ or _asm blocks, #pragma asm or #pragma inline regions, and .s, .S or .asm files linked into the build, often in startup code, context switch routines, interrupt entry and exit, cache or MMU control, and critical section macros. The weakness is the absence of a nearby comment or header documentation explaining the purpose, the registers used or clobbered, and how arguments and results pass between C and assembly. Assembly that is accompanied by such an explanation, or compiler intrinsics with standard names, does not count. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Dir 4.2 (Advisory).
detection_methods: Search for asm, __asm, __asm__, _asm, #pragma asm and #pragma inline in .c and .h files
List .s, .S and .asm files in the source tree and check whether the C code that calls into them documents the interface
At each hit, check for a comment giving the reason for using assembly and describing register use, arguments and return values
potential_mitigations: Add a comment or header block to each assembly section stating why C cannot be used and how parameters, results and clobbered registers are handled
Prefer compiler intrinsics or standard library facilities where they provide the same effect
Record any accepted undocumented legacy assembly as a documented deviation

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Explain the purpose and interface of any assembly code

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Dir 4.2 (Advisory; directive). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Inline Assembly Mixed Into Ordinary C Logic
description: The code embeds assembly instructions directly inside general C functions rather than wrapping them in a dedicated macro, inline function or assembly routine, so target-specific code is scattered and hard to review, replace or analyse.
extended_description: When asm statements sit in the middle of application logic, every function containing them becomes non-portable, static analysers cannot reason about the surrounding code, and porting to another core means editing many places. Typical examples are an asm("cpsid i") or __asm__ volatile("nop") placed inline within a driver routine, a state machine or an interrupt handler alongside ordinary C statements, or the same instruction sequence repeated across several files. The concern is placement: a small function or macro whose sole job is to issue the instruction, with a descriptive name such as DISABLE_INTERRUPTS() or cpu_barrier(), is acceptable, as are separate assembly source files called through a declared C prototype. Compiler intrinsics like __disable_irq() do not count. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Dir 4.3 (Required).
detection_methods: Search .c files for asm, __asm, __asm__ and _asm and inspect the enclosing function
Flag functions where asm statements are interleaved with other C statements rather than forming the whole body of a small wrapper
Look for the same asm instruction string duplicated across files, which indicates missing encapsulation
Run a MISRA C checker that reports inline assembly outside wrapper functions or macros
potential_mitigations: Move each assembly sequence into a dedicated inline function, macro or assembly routine with a name that states its purpose
Group target-specific wrappers in a single port or HAL header so they can be swapped for another target or a stub during analysis
Replace inline assembly with vendor intrinsics where available
Record any unavoidable inline placement as a documented deviation

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Keep assembly behind dedicated wrappers

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Dir 4.3 (Required; directive). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Disabled Code Left Inside Comments
description: The code disables statements or declarations by placing them inside /* */ or // comments instead of removing them or excluding them with the preprocessor, so the source is misleading and nested comment markers can silently change what compiles.
extended_description: Commented-out code obscures what actually runs, tends to rot as surrounding code changes, and is dangerous with block comments because C does not nest them: an inner */ ends the outer comment early and the remainder becomes live code. In source it looks like comments containing statement-like text such as semicolon-terminated lines, function calls, assignments, braces, if or for headers, or #include lines, frequently left behind after debugging, for example a commented-out printf, a disabled safety check, or an old version of an algorithm. Ordinary prose comments, pseudo-code that is clearly explanatory, and code examples in documentation comments for an API are not violations, nor is code excluded with #if 0 or #ifdef. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Dir 4.4 (Advisory).
detection_methods: Scan comments for lines that end in ; or { or } or that start with if, for, while, return, #include or #define
Look for commented-out calls to logging, printf, assert, watchdog or safety check functions in particular
Check block comments that contain an embedded /* sequence, which indicates nesting problems
Run a MISRA C checker or a commented-out code detector and review each hit
potential_mitigations: Delete code that is no longer needed and rely on version control for history
Where code must be retained but not built, wrap it in #if 0 or a named #ifdef with a comment explaining why
Rewrite explanatory comments in prose so they are not mistaken for disabled code

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Do not disable code by commenting it out

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Dir 4.4 (Advisory; directive). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Visually Confusable Identifiers in Shared Scope
description: The code declares two identifiers that are visible at the same time and look almost identical, differing only in case, underscores or look-alike characters, so a developer can easily use the wrong one without the compiler noticing.
extended_description: Because both names are valid and in scope, a mix-up compiles cleanly and produces a logic error that review struggles to spot. Typical pairs differ only by upper versus lower case (rxCount and RxCount), by an underscore (msg_len and msglen), or by characters that look alike in many fonts such as O and 0, I, l and 1, S and 5, Z and 2, B and 8, or rn and m (for example buf0 and bufO, or val1 and vall). Hotspots are module-level globals and macros in shared headers, register definitions, and long functions with many similarly named locals. Names that are similar but live in separate scopes that never overlap, such as two unrelated functions' locals or a struct member and an unrelated variable, are not a problem. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Dir 4.5 (Advisory).
detection_methods: Normalise identifiers in each scope by lower-casing, removing underscores and mapping look-alike characters (O/0, I/l/1, S/5, Z/2, B/8, rn/m, n/h) and report collisions
Pay particular attention to globals, macros and enumerators in headers that are included together
Run a MISRA C checker or identifier similarity lint and review each reported pair
potential_mitigations: Rename one identifier of each confusable pair so the names differ in meaningful words rather than single characters
Adopt a naming convention that fixes case and underscore usage for each kind of identifier
Record any retained pair, for example names fixed by an external interface, as a documented deviation

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Avoid look-alike names that are visible together

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Dir 4.5 (Advisory; directive). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Use of Basic Numeric Types With Platform-Dependent Width
description: The code declares objects, parameters and return values with plain int, short, long, char, float or double instead of fixed-width typedefs, so the storage size and range change from one compiler or target to another.
extended_description: The width of int and long varies between 16, 32 and 64 bits across embedded targets, and plain char may be signed or unsigned, so values that fit on one build can overflow or truncate on another and structures shared with hardware or over a link change layout. In source this means declarations such as int count, unsigned long timestamp or short adc_value, struct members describing register maps or message frames, and function signatures in driver and protocol code, rather than uint8_t, int16_t, uint32_t, float32_t or project equivalents from <stdint.h>. A related defect is a home-made typedef that claims a width it does not have, such as typedef int int16_t on a 32-bit target. The following do not count: int main and its argc and argv parameters, typedef lines that define the fixed-width types themselves, bit-field declarations, abstract typedefs built on fixed-width types, and calls that must match a standard library prototype. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Dir 4.6 (Advisory).
detection_methods: Search declarations for the keywords int, short, long, char, float and double outside typedef lines and outside main
Prioritise struct members used for hardware registers, file formats or communication frames, and globals shared between modules
Check project typedef headers to confirm that each fixed-width name maps to a type of that exact size on the target
Run a MISRA C checker configured with the project's fixed-width type names
potential_mitigations: Include <stdint.h> or a project types header and declare objects with fixed-width types such as uint16_t or int32_t
Use float32_t and float64_t style typedefs for floating values
Add static assertions on sizeof for any project-defined fixed-width typedef
Record retained basic types at external library boundaries as a documented deviation

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Prefer explicitly sized numeric typedefs

name: Ignored Error Indication From Called Function
description: The code calls a function that reports failure through its return value, an out-parameter or errno, and then carries on without examining that indication, so a failed operation is treated as a success.
extended_description: When an error is not checked straight after the call, the program continues with unset buffers, partial writes, unopened handles or stale data, and the fault surfaces later far from its cause. In source this looks like library calls used as statements or with results discarded, such as fopen, fread, fwrite, fclose, fprintf, snprintf, strtol without an errno or end-pointer check, malloc, pthread_mutex_lock, read, write, send or ioctl, and project or HAL functions returning a status code (for example HAL_StatusTypeDef, an E_OK style enum or a negative errno value) whose result is never compared. Casting a call to (void) does not resolve the problem when the function can actually fail; it only marks the omission. Calls proven unable to fail for the given arguments, and functions whose return value carries no error meaning, do not count. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Dir 4.7 (Required).
detection_methods: Find call statements whose return value is discarded or cast to (void) where the callee returns a status, pointer or count that signals failure
Check each call to fopen, malloc, read, write, fread, fwrite, strtol, snprintf and similar for a comparison against the documented failure value
Find project functions returning a status type or enum and check every caller tests it before relying on the operation's effects
Check out-parameter error flags and errno are read right after the call that sets them
Run a MISRA C checker or -Wunused-result with warn_unused_result attributes, then review results across translation units
potential_mitigations: Test the return value or error indicator of each fallible call immediately and handle the failure path explicitly
Mark status-returning project functions with a warn_unused_result attribute where the compiler supports it
Validate inputs before the call so that, where possible, the function cannot fail, and document that reasoning where the check is omitted
Record any deliberately unchecked call as a documented deviation
common_consequences: Availability; DoS: Crash, Exit, or Restart

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Act on failure indications returned by calls

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Dir 4.7 (Required; directive). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Exposed Structure Layout Where Opaque Handle Suffices
description: The code makes the full definition of a struct or union visible to source files that only pass pointers to it around, so those files can reach into and alter its members without going through the owning module.
extended_description: If a module's internals are published in a shared header, any client can read or write fields directly, coupling the client to the layout and allowing unintended changes that bypass the module's invariants. In source this appears as a header that contains the complete struct body for a driver, queue, context or handle type, while the .c files that include it only declare pointers to it, pass them to API functions and never use -> or . on them. The preferred form is a forward declaration such as struct uart_ctx; or typedef struct uart_ctx *uart_handle_t; in the header, with the body confined to the implementing .c file. Structures whose members clients genuinely need to access, such as configuration structs filled in by the caller or plain data records, are not violations. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Dir 4.8 (Advisory).
detection_methods: List struct and union types fully defined in headers and, for each translation unit that includes the header, check whether members are ever accessed with . or ->
Flag types where only the implementing .c file accesses members while other files only hold pointers
Check handle or context types in driver and middleware APIs for full definitions in public headers
Analyse across translation units, since the property depends on all includers
potential_mitigations: Move the struct body into the implementing source file and leave only a forward declaration or pointer typedef in the header
Provide accessor functions for any fields clients legitimately need
Record any type that must stay visible, for example for static allocation by clients, as a documented deviation

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Hide layouts of types only handled by pointer

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Dir 4.8 (Advisory; directive). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Function-Like Macro Used Where a Function Would Work
description: The code defines a function-like macro to perform a computation that an ordinary or inline function could do, so arguments escape type checking and may be evaluated more than once.
extended_description: Macro arguments are substituted as text, so an argument with a side effect such as i++ or a function call can run twice, operator precedence can go wrong if parameters are not parenthesised, and no type checking happens on inputs or outputs. In source look for #define NAME(a, b) bodies that compute a value or run statements, such as MAX(a,b), MIN, ABS, SQUARE, CLAMP, SWAP, BIT_SET or do { ... } while (0) blocks, especially in shared headers, and for call sites that pass expressions with side effects. Macros that cannot be functions are fine: those taking operators, types or token-pasting (##) or stringising (#) arguments, those used in contexts requiring a constant expression such as static initialisers, case labels or array sizes, and those wrapping __FILE__ or __LINE__. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Dir 4.9 (Advisory).
detection_methods: List #define directives with a parameter list and check whether the body is an expression or statement block that a function could implement
Exclude macros using #, ##, type or operator parameters, or used where a constant expression is required
Find call sites of these macros that pass arguments with side effects such as ++, --, assignments or function calls
Run a MISRA C checker and review each reported macro
potential_mitigations: Replace the macro with a static inline function with typed parameters and return value
Where a macro must remain, parenthesise each parameter and the whole body and avoid evaluating any parameter more than once
Record any macro kept for performance or compile-time evaluation reasons as a documented deviation

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Prefer functions to interchangeable parameterised macros

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Dir 4.9 (Advisory; directive). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Header File Without Effective Include Guard
description: The code provides a header file whose contents are not protected against being processed twice in one translation unit, so repeated inclusion can produce duplicate or conflicting definitions.
extended_description: With nested includes it is common for the same header to be reached by several paths; without a guard, typedefs, struct and enum definitions, inline functions or object definitions appear twice and cause compile errors or, in worse cases, inconsistent definitions. In source the defect is a .h file that lacks a wrapping #ifndef X / #define X ... #endif (or #if !defined(X)) around its whole content, or has a broken guard: the #define is missing or spelt differently from the #ifndef test, the #endif closes before the end of the content, declarations sit outside the guard, or two headers use the same guard macro so one silently hides the other. Files intentionally designed for repeated inclusion, such as X-macro tables, and generated files documented as such, need individual review rather than automatic flagging. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Dir 4.10 (Required).
detection_methods: For each .h file, check that the first non-comment directive is #ifndef X or #if !defined(X), followed by #define X, and that the matching #endif is the last directive
Check that the macro name in the #define exactly matches the one tested
Collect all guard macro names across the project and report duplicates
Note that #pragma once is a compiler extension and check whether the project accepts it
Run a MISRA C checker that verifies include guards
potential_mitigations: Wrap the entire header content in an #ifndef/#define/#endif guard using a unique name derived from the file path
Fix mismatched guard names and move stray declarations inside the guard
Record headers intentionally included multiple times, such as X-macro lists, as a documented deviation

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Guard headers against repeated inclusion

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Dir 4.10 (Required; directive). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Unvalidated Arguments to Library Functions With Restricted Domains
description: The code passes values to standard, third-party or in-house library functions that only accept a limited input range, without first confirming the values are inside that range, so the call can produce undefined behaviour or meaningless results.
extended_description: Many library routines do not check their inputs and simply misbehave when given out-of-domain values. Typical cases are sqrt, log, log10, pow, asin, acos or fmod with negative, zero or out-of-range arguments; isalpha, isdigit, toupper and the rest of <ctype.h> given a plain char that may be negative rather than a value representable as unsigned char or EOF; abs or labs on the most negative integer; memcpy, memset or strncpy with lengths or NULL pointers taken from input; and in-house or vendor HAL calls given channel numbers, buffer sizes or handles from untrusted sources. The weakness is the missing pre-check or wrapper at the call site. Calls where the argument is a constant or has already been range-checked on every path, or library functions that document and perform their own validation, do not count. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Dir 4.11 (Required).
detection_methods: Find calls to <math.h> functions such as sqrt, log, pow, fmod, asin and acos and check the argument is proven to be in domain before the call
Find calls to <ctype.h> functions and check the argument is cast to unsigned char or is EOF
Find memcpy, memmove, memset, strncpy and similar calls whose pointer or length arguments come from parameters or input and check for prior validation
Review calls into project or vendor library APIs with documented parameter ranges and check guards at each caller
Use static analysis for value ranges, then confirm across translation units manually
potential_mitigations: Check each argument against the function's valid domain immediately before the call and handle out-of-range values explicitly
Provide checked wrapper functions for commonly used restricted-domain library calls and use them throughout
Cast plain char to unsigned char before passing it to <ctype.h> functions
Where checks are omitted because inputs are proven safe, document the reasoning or record a documented deviation
common_consequences: Availability; DoS: Crash, Exit, or Restart

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Check inputs before calling domain-limited library routines

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Dir 4.11 (Required; directive). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Use of Heap Allocation in Embedded Code
description: The code obtains memory at run time from a heap allocator, so it is exposed to allocation failure, fragmentation, unpredictable timing and lifetime errors such as leaks, double frees and use after free.
extended_description: Heap allocation makes memory use and timing depend on the history of requests, so a long-running embedded system can fail long after start-up when the heap fragments or is exhausted, and errors in freeing memory lead to undefined behaviour. In source this means calls to malloc, calloc, realloc, free and aligned_alloc, and equivalents in RTOS and third-party libraries such as pvPortMalloc, vPortFree, k_malloc, rt_malloc, OSMemGet or custom pool allocators that behave like a heap, as well as library functions that allocate internally, for example strdup or some printf and stdio implementations. Fixed-size statically declared buffers and pools sized at build time do not count, nor do allocations made exclusively during a documented initialisation phase if the project has accepted that as a deviation. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Dir 4.12 (Required).
detection_methods: Search for malloc, calloc, realloc, free, aligned_alloc and strdup, and for RTOS allocators such as pvPortMalloc, vPortFree, k_malloc and rt_malloc
Search for project allocator wrappers and custom memory pool APIs that hand out variable-sized blocks
Check third-party libraries linked into the build for internal heap use, for example via the linker map or symbol references to malloc
Where allocation is present, check each result for NULL and each block for a single matching free on every path
potential_mitigations: Replace dynamic allocation with statically sized arrays, fixed-block pools or objects allocated at build time
Configure third-party libraries and the C runtime to avoid internal heap use, or link a stub allocator that fails the build
Where allocation is unavoidable, restrict it to start-up, check every result and record it as a documented deviation
common_consequences: Availability; DoS: Crash, Exit, or Restart
Integrity, Confidentiality; Read Memory, Modify Memory

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Avoid run-time heap allocation

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Dir 4.12 (Required; directive). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Resource Operations Called Out of Order
description: The code uses a resource API in an invalid sequence, for example acquiring without a matching release on some path, operating on a resource that is not yet opened or already closed, or releasing it twice, so the resource leaks, deadlocks or is misused.
extended_description: Paired operations such as open and close, lock and unlock, enable and disable, or init and deinit only work if every path through the code follows the expected order. In source the defect shows up as early return, break, goto or error branches that skip fclose, close, pthread_mutex_unlock, xSemaphoreGive, irq restore or a driver's release call after the matching acquire; calls to read, write or ioctl on a handle before its open succeeded or after it was closed; and double calls to the release function. Interrupt enable and disable pairs in critical sections and RTOS mutex take and give pairs are common hotspots. Acquire and release split deliberately across functions with a documented ownership hand-over, such as a constructor and destructor pair, are not violations by themselves but should be checked as a whole. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Dir 4.13 (Advisory).
detection_methods: Find acquire calls such as fopen, open, pthread_mutex_lock, xSemaphoreTake, taskENTER_CRITICAL and __disable_irq, and check every exit path of the function reaches the matching release
Inspect early returns, goto targets and error branches between an acquire and its release
Check handles are not used after their close or free call and are not closed twice
Run a static analyser with resource-pairing or lock checks, configuring project-specific acquire and release functions
potential_mitigations: Structure functions with a single cleanup point, for example a common exit label, that releases every acquired resource
Set handles to an invalid value after release and test that value before further use
Declare project-specific paired functions to the static analyser so path checks cover them
Record intentional cross-function ownership patterns as a documented deviation
common_consequences: Availability; DoS: Crash, Exit, or Restart

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Keep acquire, use and release calls correctly ordered

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Dir 4.13 (Advisory; directive). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Non-Conforming C Syntax or Constraint Violations
description: The code contains constructs that break the syntax or constraints of the chosen ISO C standard, or exceeds the compiler's translation limits, so the compiler may accept it with only a warning and generate code whose behaviour is not defined.
extended_description: Compilers often downgrade constraint violations to warnings and still emit object code, and they need not report exceeded translation limits at all, so the resulting program can behave unpredictably. Examples observable in source include assigning directly to a const-qualified object when the compiler only warns, implicit int or implicit function declarations in C99 code, incompatible pointer assignments without a cast, C99 or later features such as // comments, designated initialisers, variable-length arrays or mixed declarations used in a project built as C90, C11 features such as _Static_assert or _Generic in a C99 build, and excessive nesting of blocks, includes or macro expansion. Deliberate use of extensions the compiler documents, such as __near, __far, __interrupt or __inline, is not a violation of this rule, though it falls under the separate concern of language extensions. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 1.1 (Required).
detection_methods: Build with the project's selected standard enforced, for example -std=c99 -pedantic-errors, and review every diagnostic
Check build logs and makefiles for suppressed warnings such as -w or disabled pedantic diagnostics that could hide constraint violations
Search for features newer than the selected standard, such as // comments in C90 code or _Generic and _Static_assert in C99 code
Look for implicit function declarations and incompatible pointer conversions reported as warnings rather than errors
Run a MISRA C checker configured for the project's C version
potential_mitigations: Compile with strict conformance flags for the chosen C standard and treat warnings as errors
Rewrite constructs that are not valid in the selected standard, or formally move the project to a newer standard
Reduce deeply nested blocks, includes and macro expansions to stay within documented translation limits
Record any required non-standard construct as a documented deviation

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Stay within standard C syntax, constraints and limits

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 1.1 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.
view_names: MISRA C:2012 - A Standard C Environment

name: Reliance on Compiler-Specific Language Extensions
description: The code uses keywords, attributes, pragmas or syntax that a particular compiler adds beyond ISO C, so its meaning depends on that toolchain and may be incompletely documented or change between versions.
extended_description: Extensions tie the code to a single compiler, may be ignored silently by another, and their exact semantics in corner cases are often poorly specified. In source look for GNU constructs such as __attribute__, typeof, statement expressions ({ ... }), zero-length arrays, case ranges (case 1 ... 5), nested functions, labels as values and the ?: shorthand; embedded keywords such as __interrupt, __irq, __near, __far, __packed, __at, @ address placement, __no_init and __ramfunc; #pragma directives that change packing, section placement or optimisation; #pragma once; and inline asm. Hotspots are startup files, vector tables, linker-placement code, register definition headers and RTOS ports. Standard C features and standard library calls do not count, and an extension isolated in a single documented port header is lower risk than one spread across application code. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 1.2 (Advisory).
detection_methods: Search for double-underscore keywords such as __attribute__, __interrupt, __packed, __near, __far, __at and __asm
Search for #pragma and _Pragma and identify which ones alter semantics such as packing, sections or optimisation
Search for GNU syntax such as typeof, ({ statement expressions, case a ... b ranges and the a ?: b form
Compile with -pedantic or the compiler's strict ISO mode and review extension warnings
Run a MISRA C checker, accepting that some extensions require manual identification
potential_mitigations: Replace extensions with standard C equivalents where one exists
Confine unavoidable extensions to a small port or compiler abstraction header behind portable macro names
Document each extension that is kept, including how its correct use is verified, as a documented deviation

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Avoid toolchain-specific additions to C

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 1.2 (Advisory; Undecidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.
view_names: MISRA C:2012 - A Standard C Environment

name: Code Exhibiting Undefined or Critical Unspecified Behaviour
description: The code performs an operation whose result the C standard leaves undefined, or relies on an unspecified choice that matters to the outcome, so the compiled program may do anything from working by chance to corrupting memory or being optimised away.
extended_description: Optimising compilers assume undefined behaviour never happens, so code that triggers it can be removed or transformed in surprising ways, and results can differ between compilers, versions and optimisation levels. This entry is a catch-all for cases not covered by more specific guidelines, for example signed integer overflow in a loop counter or timestamp, shifting by a negative amount or by at least the operand width, modifying a string literal, accessing an object through an incompatible pointer type, reading a union member other than the one last written when relying on it, returning without a value from a non-void function whose result is used, calling a function through a pointer of incompatible type, using the value of a pointer after the object it pointed to has ended its lifetime, and depending on argument evaluation order. Code where a documented compiler guarantee is deliberately relied on, such as -fwrapv, should be recorded as a deviation rather than silently accepted. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 1.3 (Required).
detection_methods: Check signed arithmetic on counters, timestamps and accumulated values for possible overflow
Check shift expressions for counts that can be negative or not less than the width of the promoted left operand
Look for writes through pointers to string literals, casts between unrelated pointer types followed by dereference, and calls through cast function pointers
Check non-void functions for paths that fall off the end without return and for callers that use the result
Run a static analyser with undefined behaviour checks and sanitisers such as -fsanitize=undefined in testing, then review across translation units
potential_mitigations: Rewrite each construct so its behaviour is fully defined by the standard, for example using unsigned arithmetic with explicit range checks or memcpy for type punning
Make evaluation order explicit by splitting expressions with side effects into separate statements
Ensure every non-void function returns a value on all paths
Where the project relies on a compiler-defined behaviour, record it as a documented deviation with the compiler option that guarantees it
common_consequences: Integrity, Confidentiality; Read Memory, Modify Memory
Availability; DoS: Crash, Exit, or Restart

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Never trigger behaviour the standard leaves undefined or critically unspecified

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 1.3 (Required; Undecidable; System). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.
view_names: MISRA C:2012 - A Standard C Environment

name: Statements That Can Never Be Executed
description: The code contains statements that no execution path can reach, so the logic the author intended never runs and the dead statements mislead reviewers and testers.
extended_description: Unreachable code usually signals a logic error: a guard condition that is always false, a return, break, continue or goto that ends a block too early, or a call to a function that never returns placed before cleanup code. Typical sites in C are statements after an unconditional return or break inside a switch case, code following a call to exit, abort, longjmp or a project-specific panic or reset routine, statements after an infinite for(;;) or while(1) loop with no break, and else branches of conditions on constants or values whose range excludes them. It also wastes memory in constrained targets and can hide that a safety check is never applied. Code removed by the preprocessor through #if 0 or disabled configuration macros is not part of this weakness, and neither is defensive default handling that is reachable in principle when data are corrupted. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 2.1 (Required).
detection_methods: Search for statements that follow return, break, continue or goto in the same block and are not the target of a label
Find calls to exit, abort, _Exit, longjmp, assert(0) style helpers and functions marked noreturn, and check for code placed after them in the same path
Inspect for(;;) and while(1) loops without break or return and check for statements after the loop
Check if, while and switch conditions built from constants, enum ranges or previously tested values that make a branch impossible
Run a MISRA C checker or compiler warnings such as -Wunreachable-code, then confirm manually because reachability is undecidable
potential_mitigations: Delete statements that cannot be reached, or fix the control flow so the intended path reaches them
Move cleanup and status reporting before any non-returning call or early return
Replace conditions that are always true or false with the intended test
Record a documented deviation where unreachable defensive code is deliberately retained for robustness

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: No statements that no path can reach

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 2.1 (Required; Undecidable; System). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Executed Operations With No Observable Effect
description: The code executes operations whose results are never used and which change nothing observable, so the program does not do what the author apparently meant and real defects are masked.
extended_description: An operation that runs but can be removed without changing program behaviour often reveals a typing mistake or a missing assignment, for example a comparison written where an assignment was intended, or a computed value that was meant to be stored or returned. In C source this appears as expression statements such as x == 0; or p + 1; or a + b; on their own, values assigned to a local that is overwritten or goes out of scope before being read, shifts or masks whose result is discarded, and casts of an expression to a type followed by nothing. Calls to functions that have no side effects and whose return value is dropped also fall in this group. Operations involving volatile objects, hardware register reads that clear status bits, explicit (void) casts used to document a deliberately ignored return value, and statements that are reachable only conditionally are not covered here; unreachable code is a separate weakness. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 2.2 (Required).
detection_methods: Search for expression statements consisting only of a comparison, arithmetic or bitwise operator, such as a lone == or + expression terminated by a semicolon
Find local variables that are assigned and then reassigned or leave scope without an intervening read
Check calls to pure helper functions whose return value is discarded without a (void) cast
Exclude reads and writes of volatile objects and memory-mapped registers, which have effects outside the abstract machine
Run a MISRA C checker or compiler warnings such as -Wunused-value and -Wunused-but-set-variable, then review each hit because the property is undecidable
potential_mitigations: Remove operations whose results are not needed, or correct them so the result is stored, returned or tested as intended
Replace mistaken comparisons used as statements with the intended assignment
Cast deliberately ignored function results to (void) so intent is explicit
Record a documented deviation where an apparently redundant operation is required for timing or hardware reasons

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Executed code whose removal changes nothing

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 2.2 (Required; Undecidable; System). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Type Alias Declared but Never Referenced
description: The code declares a typedef name that nothing uses, so readers cannot tell whether the type was meant to be applied somewhere and the declaration adds clutter.
extended_description: An unused typedef suggests that code was partly refactored or that a declaration meant to use the alias uses a raw type instead, which can matter when the alias encodes a width or signedness. It appears as typedef statements in headers or at file scope, or inside functions, for example a typedef of an unsigned integer or a struct that no variable, parameter, cast, sizeof or other declaration ever names. Look at project-specific type headers, driver headers and local typedefs in .c files. Typedefs that are used anywhere in the project, including only in other translation units, are not affected, and widely shared library headers that intentionally offer a complete set of types are usually excluded by deviation. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 2.3 (Advisory).
detection_methods: List every typedef name declared in the project and search all source and header files for later uses of that name
Pay attention to typedefs declared inside function bodies or in .c files, where no other translation unit can use them
Check structures and enumerations declared together with a typedef where the alias is never used and the tag is used instead
Run a MISRA C checker with whole-project analysis, since use may occur in another translation unit
potential_mitigations: Delete typedef declarations that no code uses
Use the alias where the raw type was written by mistake, so width and signedness stay consistent
Record a documented deviation for shared type headers that intentionally define a complete set of aliases

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Typedef names that are never used

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 2.3 (Advisory; Decidable; System). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Struct, Union or Enum Tag Declared but Never Referenced
description: The code declares a struct, union or enum tag that is never used, so it is unclear whether the tag is leftover code or a sign that a related declaration was written incorrectly.
extended_description: Tags that nothing refers to add noise and can hide mismatches, for example where a typedef was intended to use a tagged struct but a different, anonymous definition is used instead. In source this looks like struct sensor_cfg { ... }; or enum mode { ... }; definitions, or forward declarations such as struct foo; whose tag never appears again in a variable, parameter, pointer, cast or sizeof. A common pattern is typedef struct tag { ... } alias_t; where only alias_t is ever used, leaving the tag redundant. Tags referenced anywhere in the project, including other translation units, are not affected, and enumeration constants being used does not count as use of the enum tag itself. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 2.4 (Advisory).
detection_methods: List every struct, union and enum tag and search the whole project for the keyword followed by that tag name outside its own declaration
Check typedef struct tag { ... } alias; patterns where only the alias is used
Look for orphan forward declarations of the form struct name; in headers
Run a MISRA C checker with whole-project analysis, since use may occur in another translation unit
potential_mitigations: Remove unused tags, for example by declaring the typedef over an anonymous struct when the tag is never needed
Delete forward declarations that nothing relies on
Record a documented deviation for public headers that deliberately expose tags for external users

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Tags that are never used

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 2.4 (Advisory; Decidable; System). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Macro Defined but Never Expanded or Tested
description: The code defines a preprocessor macro that is never expanded, tested or undefined anywhere, so stale constants and configuration switches accumulate and may be mistaken for active settings.
extended_description: Unused macros make it hard to tell which configuration values and limits actually affect the build, and an unused macro next to a hard-coded literal often shows that the literal should have used the macro. In C projects these are #define lines for buffer sizes, register addresses, bit masks, timeouts, feature flags and function-like helper macros that no later expansion, #if, #ifdef, defined() test or #undef ever names. Configuration headers, board support headers and protocol definition headers are the usual places. Include guard macros are used by their own #ifndef and do not count, and neither do macros consumed only in other translation units or by the build system on the command line. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 2.5 (Advisory).
detection_methods: List every #define name in the project and search all source and header files for any expansion, #ifdef, #ifndef, #if defined() or #undef of that name
Compare unused size, mask and timeout macros with nearby numeric literals that may have been intended to use them
Exclude include guards and macros referenced from build scripts, makefiles or compiler -D options
Run a MISRA C checker with whole-project analysis, since use may occur in another translation unit
potential_mitigations: Delete macro definitions that nothing uses
Replace hard-coded literals with the matching macro where it was meant to be used
Record a documented deviation for shared headers that intentionally provide complete register or protocol definitions

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Macros that are never used

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 2.5 (Advisory; Decidable; System). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Statement Label With No Goto Referring to It
description: A function contains a statement label that no goto targets, so the label is leftover or the jump meant to use it was written to a different label or omitted.
extended_description: An orphan label may indicate that an error-handling goto was removed or points at the wrong place, so a cleanup or recovery path is skipped. In C source labels look like an identifier followed by a colon at the start of a statement, such as cleanup: or retry:, typically near the end of functions with error handling. A label is used only when a goto with the same name appears in the same function, since labels have function scope. Case and default labels inside a switch, bit-field widths and the ternary operator are not statement labels and are not covered; neither is a label whose only goto is inside conditionally compiled code that is active in some build configuration. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 2.6 (Advisory).
detection_methods: Search each function for identifier-colon statement labels, excluding case and default labels
For each label, search the same function for a goto naming it
Check labels near error handling or cleanup blocks to see whether an expected goto from a failure path is missing
Run a MISRA C checker or compiler warning such as -Wunused-label
potential_mitigations: Delete labels that no goto uses
Restore or correct the goto in failure paths that were intended to jump to a cleanup label
Record a documented deviation where labels are used only under some build configurations

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Labels that are never jumped to

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 2.6 (Advisory; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Function Parameter Never Read in Function Body
description: A function accepts a parameter that its body never uses, which suggests the implementation does not match its interface and callers may rely on an argument that is silently ignored.
extended_description: When a parameter such as a length, timeout, channel number or flags value is ignored, the function may operate on a fixed value instead of the caller's request, for example copying a hard-coded number of bytes or always addressing the first device. In C source look at function definitions in .c files and compare the parameter list with identifiers referenced in the body. Typical cases are callback and interrupt handler signatures imposed by a framework, stub implementations, and functions whose logic was simplified without updating the prototype. Parameters in prototypes without a body, unnamed parameters, and parameters that are referenced only through a (void)param; statement to document deliberate non-use are not considered unused by most tools, but each such case should still be justified. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 2.7 (Advisory).
detection_methods: For each function definition, check every named parameter for at least one read in the body
Focus on size, length, count, index and flags parameters, since ignoring these often means the function uses a fixed value instead
Review callback, ISR and driver operation-table functions where the signature is fixed but some arguments must still be honoured
Run a MISRA C checker or compiler warning such as -Wunused-parameter
potential_mitigations: Use the parameter as the specification requires, or remove it from the prototype and all callers
Where a fixed signature forces an unused parameter, mark it with a (void) cast and a comment explaining why
Record a documented deviation for framework callback signatures that deliberately carry unused arguments

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Parameters the function never uses

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 2.7 (Advisory; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Comment Opening Sequence Inside an Existing Comment
description: The code places /* or // inside a comment, so a missing comment terminator can silently turn live code into comment text or the reader misjudges where a comment ends.
extended_description: C block comments do not nest: the first */ closes the comment regardless of how many /* sequences appear inside it. If a closing */ is accidentally omitted, every line up to the next */ becomes comment, so assignments, checks or calls disappear from the build without any error. Look for a /* that appears inside a block comment already opened by an earlier /*, for a // inside a /* ... */ block, and for /* or // inside a // comment, which often comes from commenting out code that already contained comments. Text such as URLs written as http:// inside a comment also matches literally and is a common, usually harmless, hit that may need a documented deviation. Sequences inside string literals or character constants are not comments and are not affected. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 3.1 (Required).
detection_methods: Scan block comments for an inner /* before the closing */ and check whether a terminator was lost
Scan both block and line comments for // or /* sequences, such as commented-out code that itself contained comments
Inspect large commented-out regions and compare with surrounding code for lines that were unintentionally swallowed
Run a MISRA C checker or compiler warning such as -Wcomment
potential_mitigations: Remove nested comment openers and ensure every block comment has its own terminator
Use #if 0 ... #endif rather than comments to disable code temporarily, and remove it before release
Record a documented deviation for comment text such as URLs that legitimately contain //

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Comment start sequences inside comments

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 3.1 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Line Comment Ending in Backslash Continuation
description: A // comment ends with a backslash immediately before the newline, so the following source line is spliced into the comment and its code is silently not compiled.
extended_description: Line splicing happens in an early translation phase, before comments are recognised, so a backslash at the very end of a line joins the next physical line onto it. When that line holds a // comment, the next line, which may be a condition, assignment or function call, becomes part of the comment and vanishes from the program without a compiler error. This often comes from ASCII art, Windows paths such as C:\dir\ or trailing backslashes copied from a multi-line macro into a comment. Look for any line containing // whose last character before the line ending is \, including when trailing spaces are absent but a carriage return is present. Backslash continuations in #define macros and in /* */ comments are not covered here. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 3.2 (Required).
detection_methods: Search for lines that contain // and end with a backslash immediately before the newline, for example with a regular expression such as //.*\\$
Check the line after each hit to see which code has been absorbed into the comment
Inspect comments containing Windows paths, diagrams or text copied from multi-line macros
Run a MISRA C checker or compiler warning such as -Wcomment
potential_mitigations: Remove the trailing backslash from the comment or add a non-backslash character after it
Use /* */ comments for diagrams and paths that need backslashes at line ends
Rebuild and retest after the fix, since previously ignored code will now be compiled

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Backslash continuation of line comments

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 3.2 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Unterminated Numeric Escape Followed by Literal Characters
description: A string literal or character constant contains an octal or hexadecimal escape sequence directly followed by ordinary characters, so the escape may absorb or stop at different characters than the author expected and the resulting bytes are wrong.
extended_description: Hex escapes consume every following hexadecimal digit and octal escapes consume up to three octal digits, so a literal such as "\x1BABC" or "\0123" may encode a different value from the one intended, and a following letter like g in "\x41g" is easily misread. In character constants this can also create a multi-character constant whose integer value is implementation-defined. Search string literals and character constants for \x or \ followed by digits, and check what character comes immediately after the escape; protocol frames, terminal control sequences such as ANSI escapes, and binary command tables are typical locations. An escape is safe when it is followed by another escape sequence or by the end of the literal, for example "\x41" "g" using adjacent string concatenation. Simple escapes such as \n, \t and \0 at the end of a literal are not affected. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 4.1 (Required).
detection_methods: Search string literals and character constants for \x escapes and check whether the next character is anything other than another backslash escape or the closing quote
Search for octal escapes (a backslash followed by 0 to 7) followed by further plain characters, especially digits
Review protocol message strings, ANSI terminal sequences and binary lookup tables built from string literals
Run a MISRA C checker, which can decide this property from the tokens alone
potential_mitigations: Split the literal so the escape ends at a string boundary, for example "\x1B" "ABC"
Write the following characters as escapes too so every numeric escape is terminated by another escape
Use byte arrays with explicit hexadecimal initialisers for binary data instead of string literals

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Numeric escapes not explicitly ended

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 4.1 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.
view_names: MISRA C:2012 - Character Sets and Lexical Conventions

name: Trigraph Sequence in Source Text
description: The source contains a ??x trigraph sequence, so the compiler may replace it with a different character inside strings, comments or code and change the program's meaning.
extended_description: Trigraphs are three-character sequences beginning with two question marks, such as ??= ??( ??) ??/ ??' ??< ??> ??! and ??-, which a conforming compiler replaces before any other processing, including inside string literals and comments. A user message like "Ready??!" or a date mask such as "??-??-??" can therefore be silently changed into different characters, and ??/ becomes a backslash that can splice lines or create escape sequences. Look for two consecutive question marks followed by one of = ( ) / ' < > ! - in .c and .h files, particularly in format strings, user-facing text and comments. Digraphs such as <: and %> are ordinary tokens and are not covered, and question marks that are separated, for example "?\?-" or "?" "?-", do not form trigraphs. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 4.2 (Advisory).
detection_methods: Search all source and header files for the regular expression \?\?[=()/'<>!-]
Review hits in string literals and comments for text that would be altered by trigraph replacement
Check whether the build enables trigraph processing, for example -trigraphs or strict ISO modes, to judge impact
Run a MISRA C checker or compiler warning such as -Wtrigraphs
potential_mitigations: Break the sequence using an escaped question mark, for example ?\?-, or adjacent string literal concatenation
Rewrite comments and messages to avoid doubled question marks
Record a documented deviation if trigraphs are genuinely required by the target character set

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Use of trigraph sequences

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 4.2 (Advisory; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.
view_names: MISRA C:2012 - Character Sets and Lexical Conventions

name: External Identifiers Indistinguishable Within Linker Significance Limit
description: Two identifiers with external linkage differ only beyond the number of characters the implementation is guaranteed to treat as significant, so the linker may merge them into one symbol and calls or data accesses reach the wrong object.
extended_description: C only guarantees that the first 31 characters of an external identifier are significant in C99, and only 6 characters ignoring case in C90, so longer global names that share a long common prefix may collide at link time, which is undefined behaviour. In code this appears as global functions or variables declared without static, often with long module prefixes such as sensor_calibration_offset_channel_a and sensor_calibration_offset_channel_b, or names that differ only in letter case on a toolchain that folds case. Compare names of non-static functions and file-scope variables across all translation units, as well as extern declarations in headers. Identifiers with internal linkage (static) or block scope are covered by other weaknesses, and collisions only matter relative to the significance limit of the actual toolchain in use. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 5.1 (Required).
detection_methods: Collect all non-static function names and file-scope object names across the project and compare them truncated to 31 characters, or 6 case-insensitive characters for C90 toolchains
Look for long shared prefixes from module naming schemes, where only the tail of the name distinguishes symbols
Check the linker map file for unexpectedly merged or missing symbols
Run a MISRA C checker with whole-program analysis configured with the toolchain's significance limits
potential_mitigations: Rename external identifiers so they differ within the guaranteed number of significant characters
Give file-local functions and variables internal linkage with static to remove them from the external namespace
Record a documented deviation stating the toolchain's actual significance limit if it exceeds the language minimum
common_consequences: Integrity, Confidentiality; Read Memory, Modify Memory

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: External names must differ within significant length

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 5.1 (Required; Decidable; System). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Same-Scope Identifiers Differing Only Beyond Significant Characters
description: Two identifiers declared in the same scope and name space differ only after the compiler's guaranteed number of significant characters, so the compiler may treat them as the same name and bind uses to the wrong declaration.
extended_description: For internal identifiers C99 guarantees 63 significant characters and C90 only 31, so two very long names in the same scope can be considered identical, leading to undefined behaviour or a silent redeclaration. In code this happens with long, generated or prefix-heavy names such as static functions, file-scope static variables, local variables, struct members within the same struct, or enumeration constants that share a long common stem. Look in generated code, register definition files and state machine tables where names are formed by concatenating long prefixes. Identifiers in different scopes or different name spaces (for example a tag and an ordinary identifier) are not covered here, and nor are external identifiers, which have their own weakness. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 5.2 (Required).
detection_methods: Within each scope, compare identifiers in the same name space truncated to 63 characters for C99 or 31 for C90
Review generated sources, autogenerated register maps and long enumerations whose names share long prefixes
Check struct and union member lists for members that differ only near the end of long names
Run a MISRA C checker configured with the toolchain's significance limits
potential_mitigations: Shorten or restructure names so they differ within the first significant characters
Adjust code generators to emit shorter, distinctive identifiers
Record a documented deviation stating the compiler's actual significance limit if it is longer

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Same-scope names must differ within significant length

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 5.2 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Inner Declaration Shadowing an Outer Identifier
description: A declaration in an inner scope reuses the name of an identifier visible from an outer scope, so code in the inner scope silently reads or writes the inner object when the outer one was intended.
extended_description: Shadowing makes it easy to update a local copy while believing the global state, an outer loop counter or a function parameter is being changed, for example a local int status inside an if block that hides the function's status variable, or a nested for loop that redeclares i. Look for block-scope declarations inside functions, nested blocks and for loop initialisers whose names match a parameter, an enclosing local, a file-scope variable, a global declared in an included header, or a function name.
