Common names such as status, err, ret, i, len, buf and count are frequent offenders. Identifiers in different name spaces, such as a struct member or tag with the same spelling as a variable, do not hide each other and are not covered. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 5.3 (Required).
detection_methods: For each block-scope declaration, check whether the same name is already visible from an enclosing block, the parameter list, file scope or an included header
Inspect nested loops for counters redeclared with the same name
Check locals named like global configuration or state variables declared in shared headers
Run a MISRA C checker or compiler warning such as -Wshadow
potential_mitigations: Rename the inner identifier so it is distinct from every name visible in enclosing scopes
Remove redundant inner declarations and use the outer variable where that was intended
Adopt naming prefixes for globals and module-level statics to avoid accidental reuse

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Names reused in nested scopes

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 5.3 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Macro Names or Parameters Not Distinct Within Significant Length
description: Two macro names, or the parameters of one function-like macro, differ only beyond the preprocessor's significant character limit, so one definition may replace another or a parameter may substitute in the wrong place.
extended_description: The preprocessor is only guaranteed to distinguish the first 63 characters of a macro name in C99 (31 in C90); two long macro names that share that prefix may be treated as one, so a later #define silently redefines an earlier one or an #ifdef tests the wrong switch. The same applies to the parameter names of a function-like macro, where two indistinguishable parameters make the expansion ambiguous. Typical sites are configuration headers with long feature switches like ENABLE_CHANNEL_CALIBRATION_FOR_SENSOR_GROUP_A, register map headers with long bit field macros, and generated headers. Look at every #define in the project, comparing the leading characters of names, and at the parameter lists of function-like macros. Macros with clearly different leading characters and ordinary C identifiers are not affected here. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 5.4 (Required).
detection_methods: Collect all #define names and compare them truncated to 63 characters for C99 or 31 for C90
Check the parameter list of each function-like macro for names that are identical within the significant length
Review configuration and generated headers with long, prefix-heavy macro names
Enable compiler warnings for macro redefinition and run a MISRA C checker configured with the preprocessor's limits
potential_mitigations: Rename macros so they differ within the guaranteed number of significant characters
Use short, distinct parameter names in function-like macros
Record a documented deviation stating the preprocessor's actual significance limit if it is longer

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Macro names must be distinguishable

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 5.4 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Ordinary Identifier Sharing a Name With a Macro
description: A variable, function, type, member or other identifier has the same name as a preprocessor macro, so the preprocessor may rewrite the identifier and the compiled code differs from what the source appears to say.
extended_description: Macros are expanded before the compiler sees declarations, so if a macro named BUFFER_SIZE or max is defined and code later declares a variable or function of the same name, the declaration is rewritten, either producing confusing errors or, worse, compiling into something unexpected. Even where a macro is #undef'd before the identifier is used, readers cannot tell which meaning applies at any given line. Look for #define names, particularly lowercase or function-like macros such as min, max, abs, swap or errno-style names, that also appear as variable, parameter, function, typedef, struct member or enumeration constant names in any included file. Library headers that provide both a macro and a function with the same name, as permitted by the C standard, are a known source of hits and are usually accepted. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 5.5 (Required).
detection_methods: Collect all macro names visible in each translation unit and check whether any declared identifier uses the same spelling
Focus on lowercase and function-like macros with common names such as min, max, abs, check or swap
Check for #undef followed by a declaration of the same name, which indicates deliberate reuse
Run a MISRA C checker, which can decide this property per translation unit
potential_mitigations: Rename the macro or the identifier so the two names are distinct
Write macro names in upper case and keep ordinary identifiers in mixed or lower case
Replace function-like macros with static inline functions where possible

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Identifiers reusing macro names

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 5.5 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Typedef Name Reused for Another Declaration
description: A typedef name is also used for another typedef or for some other identifier elsewhere in the program, so readers and tools can confuse which type or object a name denotes.
extended_description: When the same spelling is a type in one file and a variable, function, member or different type in another, code that looks equivalent can operate on different widths or layouts, for example a module-local typedef of uint8_t named counter_t while another module defines counter_t as uint32_t. Look across all headers and .c files for typedef declarations whose name appears again as another typedef, a variable, a parameter, a function, a struct member or an enumeration constant. A common accepted pattern is typedef struct name { ... } name;, where the tag and typedef share a spelling and refer to the same type, and re-including the same header that declares the typedef only once is also fine. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 5.6 (Required).
detection_methods: List all typedef names in the project and search for any other declaration using the same identifier in any translation unit
Check for conflicting typedefs of the same name in different modules or in vendor and project headers
Exclude typedef struct tag { ... } tag; where tag and alias denote the same type
Run a MISRA C checker with whole-project analysis
potential_mitigations: Give every typedef a unique name across the whole project, for example with a module prefix and _t suffix
Consolidate duplicated typedefs into one shared header
Rename variables, members or functions that reuse a typedef name

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Typedef names reused elsewhere

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 5.6 (Required; Decidable; System). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Struct, Union or Enum Tag Reused for Another Declaration
description: A struct, union or enum tag name is reused for a different tagged type or another identifier somewhere in the program, so the same spelling can denote different layouts in different files.
extended_description: Because each translation unit can define its own struct with a given tag, two modules can end up with different layouts under the same name, and passing pointers between them corrupts memory without a compiler diagnostic. Look for struct, union or enum definitions with the same tag in different .c files or headers, for a tag defined inside a function that matches a file-scope tag, and for tags whose spelling is also used as a variable, function, member or typedef for a different type. Generic tags such as config, state, msg, buffer or node are frequent collisions. Including one header with the tag definition into several files is a single declaration and is fine, and the pattern typedef struct name { ... } name; is generally accepted. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 5.7 (Required).
detection_methods: List all struct, union and enum tags in the project and search for second definitions or other declarations with the same name
Compare member lists of same-named structs defined in different translation units
Check tags declared inside function bodies for clashes with file-scope tags
Run a MISRA C checker with whole-project analysis
potential_mitigations: Give each tag a unique, module-prefixed name
Define shared structures once in a common header and include it wherever needed
Rename other identifiers that reuse a tag spelling
common_consequences: Integrity, Confidentiality; Read Memory, Modify Memory

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Tag names reused elsewhere

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 5.7 (Required; Decidable; System). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Global Symbol Name Reused for Another Identifier
description: The name of a function or object with external linkage is also used for a local variable, a static object or another declaration elsewhere, so code in some files silently refers to a different entity than the global one.
extended_description: A global such as g_error_count or a function such as init declared extern in one module can be hidden by a static variable or local of the same name in another, so updates go to the local copy and the shared state is never changed. Duplicate definitions of the same external name in two files can also cause link errors or, with common symbols and weak linkage, silently merge storage. Look for non-static functions and file-scope objects, then search the whole project for the same spelling declared as a static object, static function, local variable, parameter, member, or a second external definition. Generic names like init, process, reset, buffer, status and count are typical clashes. A single external definition with matching extern declarations in a header is the intended pattern and is not affected. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 5.8 (Required).
detection_methods: List every identifier with external linkage (non-static functions and file-scope objects) and search all translation units for any other declaration with the same name
Check for static functions or variables in one module that share names with global symbols from another
Look for duplicate global definitions, including tentative definitions without extern in headers
Inspect the linker map file and run a MISRA C checker with whole-project analysis
potential_mitigations: Use unique, module-prefixed names for every external identifier
Rename locals and statics that clash with global symbols
Define each external object once in a .c file and declare it extern in a single header

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Externally linked names reused elsewhere

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 5.8 (Required; Decidable; System). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: File-Local Static Name Reused Across the Program
description: A static function or file-scope static object shares its name with another identifier elsewhere in the program, so readers and debuggers can confuse the module-private entity with a different one.
extended_description: Static identifiers have internal linkage, so the compiler keeps them separate, but identical names in different modules make code review, debugging by symbol name and refactoring error-prone; changing one static buffer or helper may be assumed to affect another module that only has a look-alike. Look for static functions such as static void init(void) or static int helper(...) and static file-scope variables such as static uint8_t buffer[], then search other files for the same spelling used as another static, a global, a local, a parameter or a member. Static helpers defined in a header and included in several files create such duplicates by design, and inline functions declared static in headers are the main accepted exception. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 5.9 (Advisory).
detection_methods: List every static function and file-scope static object and search all translation units for other declarations with the same name
Check generic helper names such as init, update, buf, state and count defined static in several modules
Review static definitions placed in headers, which create one copy per including file
Run a MISRA C checker with whole-project analysis
potential_mitigations: Prefix static identifiers with a module-specific name so each is unique in the program
Move shared helpers into one module with external linkage instead of duplicating static copies
Record a documented deviation for static inline functions deliberately provided in headers

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Internally linked names reused elsewhere

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 5.9 (Advisory; Decidable; System). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Bit-Field Declared with Non-Portable Base Type
description: The code declares a structure or union bit-field using a base type other than an explicitly signed or unsigned int or _Bool, so its signedness, width and layout depend on the compiler.
extended_description: C only guarantees bit-field behaviour for a small set of base types; whether a plain int bit-field is signed is implementation-defined, and bit-fields of char, short, long, enum or fixed-width typedefs are compiler extensions whose packing and sign handling differ between toolchains. This typically appears in headers that model hardware registers, protocol frames or packed status words, as members such as 'int mode : 3;', 'uint8_t flag : 1;', 'unsigned short id : 10;' or 'enum state s : 2;'. A typedef that resolves to signed int or unsigned int is acceptable, as are explicitly signed int, unsigned int and _Bool bit-fields. Ordinary (non bit-field) structure members are not affected. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 6.1 (Required).
detection_methods: Search struct and union definitions, mostly in headers and register map files, for member declarators containing ' : ' followed by a width
At each bit-field, resolve the base type through typedefs and flag plain int, char, short, long, enum and 8 or 16 bit fixed-width types
Check vendor-generated peripheral headers and protocol packing headers, where non-standard bit-field types are common
Run a MISRA C checker, which can decide this rule within a single translation unit
potential_mitigations: Declare bit-fields as unsigned int, signed int or _Bool, or through a typedef that resolves to one of these
Replace register or wire-format bit-fields with explicit masks and shifts on a fixed-width unsigned integer
Where a compiler extension type is unavoidable for vendor headers, record a documented deviation naming the toolchain behaviour relied upon

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Restrict bit-field base types to portable choices

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 6.1 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Named One-Bit Bit-Field of Signed Type
description: The code declares a named bit-field of width one with a signed type, so the field can only hold 0 and a negative value and comparisons with 1 never succeed.
extended_description: A signed bit-field one bit wide has room only for the sign bit, so on two's complement targets it stores 0 or -1, and assigning 1 to it gives an implementation-defined result. Code that then tests 'if (s.flag == 1)' or sums such flags silently misbehaves. It appears in flag and status structures in headers, written as 'int ready : 1;', 'signed int err : 1;' or through a signed typedef such as 'int32_t valid : 1;'. Plain int is included because many compilers treat it as signed. Unnamed padding bit-fields of width 1, unsigned or _Bool one-bit fields and wider signed fields are not affected. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 6.2 (Required).
detection_methods: Search struct and union definitions for member declarators ending in ': 1' and check whether the field is named
For each named one-bit field, resolve the declared type and flag signed int, plain int and signed typedefs such as int32_t or int16_t
Look for comparisons or assignments of such fields against the constant 1 to confirm functional impact
Run a MISRA C checker or compiler warnings such as -Wsingle-bit-bitfield-constant-conversion
potential_mitigations: Declare single-bit flags as unsigned int or _Bool
Test flags for non-zero rather than equality with 1 where the type cannot be changed immediately
Record a documented deviation only where a fixed external layout forces a signed one-bit field

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: One-bit named fields need an unsigned type

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 6.2 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Integer Constant Written in Octal Notation
description: The code writes an integer constant or escape sequence in octal form with a leading zero, so a value intended as decimal is silently interpreted in base 8.
extended_description: In C any integer literal starting with 0 followed by further digits is octal, so 010 means eight and 0755 is not seven hundred and fifty-five; a reader or maintainer padding numbers for alignment can change values without noticing. Typical places are tables of codes or identifiers padded to equal width (for example 052, 071), date and time constants, file permission values passed to open or chmod, and octal escapes inside character or string literals such as '\012'. The literal 0 on its own is permitted, as are hexadecimal constants beginning 0x and the escape '\0'. Decimal values inside comments or string text are not affected. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 7.1 (Required).
detection_methods: Search source and header files for numeric tokens matching a leading 0 followed by one or more digits, excluding 0x and 0b prefixes and floating constants
Check lookup tables, enum initialisers and #define values where numbers have been zero-padded for alignment
Search character and string literals for backslash followed by octal digits other than a lone \0
Run a MISRA C checker, which can decide this rule within a single translation unit
potential_mitigations: Write the intended value in decimal or hexadecimal instead of octal
Use hexadecimal escapes in character and string literals rather than octal escapes
Where octal is natural, such as POSIX permission bits, use named symbolic constants from the system headers or record a documented deviation

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Avoid base-8 literals

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 7.1 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Unsigned Integer Constant Lacking U Suffix
description: The code uses an integer constant whose value only fits an unsigned type but omits the U suffix, so its signedness depends on the target's integer sizes and is easily misread.
extended_description: C chooses the type of an unsuffixed constant from the first type that can hold it, and for hexadecimal and octal constants that list includes unsigned types, so a literal such as 0x80000000 is unsigned int on a 32-bit int target but signed long on another. Comparisons, shifts and arithmetic involving such constants can then change between platforms, and readers assume a signed value. These constants typically appear as register masks and addresses in hardware headers, as large bit masks in #define macros, and in comparisons against limits like 0xFFFFFFFF. Constants that fit in a signed type, and constants already carrying u or U (including UL or ULL), are not affected. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 7.2 (Required).
detection_methods: Search headers and source files for hexadecimal and octal constants with the top bit set for the target int or long width, such as 0x8000 to 0xFFFF on 16-bit int or 0x80000000 and above on 32-bit int
Search for large decimal constants beyond LONG_MAX without a suffix
Check #define masks, register address macros and comparison limits for a missing U or u suffix
Run a MISRA C checker configured with the target integer sizes, since the result depends on them
potential_mitigations: Append U, UL or ULL to every integer constant intended to be unsigned
Define register masks and addresses with explicit suffixes or casts to a fixed-width unsigned type
Record a documented deviation only where a generated header cannot be edited

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Mark unsigned-typed integer literals with U

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 7.2 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Lowercase L Used in Numeric Literal Suffix
description: The code writes a long or long long literal with a lowercase l suffix, which is easily mistaken for the digit 1 and so misread as a different value.
extended_description: A literal such as 10l or 3ul looks almost identical to 101 or 31 in many fonts, so reviewers can misjudge both the value and the type of the constant. This is a readability and maintenance hazard rather than a language defect, but in timing constants, buffer sizes and scaling factors a misread value can lead to wrong fixes. Look for integer or floating constants ending in l, ul, lu, ll, ull or llu in source files, headers and macro definitions. Suffixes written in uppercase, such as 10L or 3UL, and the lowercase u on its own are not affected. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 7.3 (Required).
detection_methods: Search numeric tokens with a regular expression for a digit or hex digit followed by a suffix containing a lowercase l, such as [0-9]+[uU]?l, ll, lu and llu, including floating constants
Check #define constants and initialisers in headers, where long constants are most often declared
Run a MISRA C checker or a formatter rule that normalises literal suffixes
potential_mitigations: Write all long and long long suffixes with uppercase L, for example 100UL or 1LL
Apply an automated formatter or lint rule that rewrites lowercase l suffixes

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Use uppercase L in literal suffixes

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 7.3 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: String Literal Bound to Non-Const Char Pointer
description: The code assigns or passes a string literal to a pointer to non-const char, so a later write through that pointer modifies a literal and has undefined behaviour.
extended_description: String literals usually live in read-only memory, and modifying one is undefined behaviour that may fault, corrupt shared literal storage or appear to work on one target only. Because C gives literals the type char array rather than const char array, the compiler accepts 'char *msg = "OK";', returning a literal from a function declared to return char *, storing literals in a 'char *names[]' table, or passing a literal as an argument whose parameter is char * rather than const char *. Common locations are message and command tables, logging and UART output helpers, and APIs ported from older code. Initialising a char array with a literal (char buf[] = "OK";) makes a writable copy and is not affected, nor is binding a literal to const char *. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 7.4 (Required).
detection_methods: Search for declarations and assignments of the form 'char *' or 'char * name[]' initialised or assigned with a double-quoted literal
Find functions whose return type is char * and inspect return statements that yield literals
Check function prototypes taking char * parameters, especially print, log and send helpers, and find call sites passing literals
Enable -Wwrite-strings or run a MISRA C checker to list each binding
potential_mitigations: Declare pointers, table elements, parameters and return types that refer to string literals as const char *
Copy the literal into a char array when the text must be modified
Fix the const-correctness of library wrappers rather than casting away const at call sites
common_consequences: Availability; DoS: Crash, Exit, or Restart

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Literals may only be referenced through const char pointers

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 7.4 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Declaration Relying on Implicit Int Type
description: The code declares an object, parameter or function without stating a type specifier, so the compiler silently assumes int and the intended type is hidden.
extended_description: C90 allowed a missing type to default to int, and many compilers still accept it with only a warning, so declarations such as 'static x;', 'const limit = 10;', 'extern counter;', a function definition written as 'handler(void) { ... }' or an old-style parameter list with undeclared parameters all quietly become int. The reader cannot tell whether int was intended, and if the real object is a pointer, long or float the mismatch causes truncation or wrong calling conventions. Such code is typical of legacy modules, K&R-style function definitions and hastily written globals in source files. Declarations that name a type, including through a typedef, are not affected; note that 'unsigned', 'signed', 'short' and 'long' alone are explicit types. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 8.1 (Required).
detection_methods: Search for declarations that consist only of storage class or qualifier keywords (static, extern, const, volatile, register) followed directly by an identifier
Search for function definitions and prototypes at file scope with no return type before the function name
Inspect K&R-style function definitions for parameters missing from the declaration list
Compile with -Wimplicit-int or -std=c99 -pedantic-errors and run a MISRA C checker
potential_mitigations: Give every object, function return and parameter an explicit type specifier
Convert K&R-style definitions to prototype form with typed parameters
Treat implicit int diagnostics as errors in the build configuration

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Never rely on a default int type

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 8.1 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Function Declared Without Full Prototype
description: The code declares or defines a function, or a function pointer type, without a prototype listing named, typed parameters, so calls are not checked and arguments can be passed with the wrong number or type.
extended_description: An empty parameter list such as 'int read_sensor();' or a K&R-style definition tells the compiler nothing about the parameters, so callers can pass too many, too few or wrongly typed arguments, and default argument promotions apply; the resulting mismatch is undefined behaviour. Omitting parameter names in a prototype, as in 'void set(uint8_t, uint16_t);', is also discouraged because the meaning of each argument is lost and swapped arguments go unnoticed. Look in headers for prototypes and function pointer typedefs or callback members with empty parentheses or unnamed parameters, and in source files for old-style definitions with a separate parameter declaration list. A list written as (void) is a correct prototype for a function with no parameters. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 8.2 (Required).
detection_methods: Search headers and source files for function declarations, typedefs and struct members of function pointer type with empty parentheses '()' rather than '(void)'
Search for old-style definitions where the closing parenthesis of the parameter list is followed by type declarations before the opening brace
Check prototypes for parameters that have a type but no name
Compile with -Wstrict-prototypes and -Wold-style-definition and run a MISRA C checker
potential_mitigations: Write every function declaration, definition and function pointer type in prototype form with a type and a name for each parameter
Use (void) for functions that take no arguments
Make strict prototype warnings fatal in the build
common_consequences: Integrity, Confidentiality; Read Memory, Modify Memory

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Declare functions with typed, named parameter lists

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 8.2 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Inconsistent Declarations of the Same Object or Function
description: The code declares the same object or function more than once with differing parameter names, type qualifiers or type spellings, so readers and tools see conflicting interfaces and mismatches can hide real type errors.
extended_description: When a header prototype says 'void copy(uint8_t *dst, const uint8_t *src)' but the definition in the source file uses 'void copy(uint8_t *src, uint8_t *dst)', a maintainer reading either one misunderstands the argument order, and dropped const or volatile qualifiers remove protections the caller relies on. Differences in typedef choice for the same underlying type (for example int16_t in one place and short in another) are fragile because they only match on some targets. Look for function prototypes in headers paired with definitions in .c files, extern object declarations versus their definitions, and duplicate local re-declarations of the same function. Purely cosmetic whitespace differences do not count; a mismatch in the underlying type is a more serious defect also covered by checks for incompatible declarations. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 8.3 (Required).
detection_methods: For each function definition in a .c file, locate its prototype in headers and compare parameter names, order, typedef names and const or volatile qualifiers
Compare extern object declarations in headers with the defining declaration for qualifier and type differences
Search for functions declared in more than one header or re-declared locally in source files and compare each copy
Run a MISRA C checker with whole-program analysis, since matching declarations requires looking across translation units
potential_mitigations: Copy the definition's parameter list exactly into the header prototype, keeping names, typedefs and qualifiers identical
Declare each external function and object in a single header that the defining source file also includes
Record a documented deviation only for generated or third-party interfaces that cannot be aligned

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Keep every declaration of an entity identical

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 8.3 (Required; Decidable; System). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: External Definition Without Visible Prior Declaration
description: The code defines a function or object with external linkage in a source file that has no compatible declaration of it in scope, so the compiler cannot check the definition against the interface other files use.
extended_description: If a .c file defines 'uint32_t g_ticks;' or 'int init_bus(int speed)' without including the header that declares it, the definition and the declaration seen by callers can drift apart, for example in a parameter type or array size, and the program then has undefined behaviour that no compiler diagnoses. The usual cause is a source file that forgets to include its own header, a function meant to be private that lacks static, or a global defined in one file and declared by hand with extern in another. Definitions of static functions and objects are not affected, and main is normally exempt. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 8.4 (Required).
detection_methods: For each non-static function and file-scope object defined in a .c file, check that an earlier declaration appears in that file or in a header it includes
Check that each module's .c file includes its own .h file
Look for extern declarations written by hand inside other .c files instead of in a shared header
Compile with -Wmissing-prototypes and -Wmissing-variable-declarations and run a MISRA C checker
potential_mitigations: Declare every externally visible function and object in a header and include that header in the defining source file
Make functions and objects that are only used locally static so that no external declaration is needed
Enable missing-declaration warnings as errors in the build

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Define external entities only where their declaration is in scope

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 8.4 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: External Identifier Declared in Multiple Files
description: The code declares the same external function or object in more than one header or source file, so the copies can drift apart and different modules end up using incompatible views of one entity.
extended_description: Each extra 'extern uint16_t g_mode;' or hand-written prototype placed in a consumer .c file is a separate copy of the interface; when the real type changes, the copies are not updated and calls or accesses become undefined behaviour that the linker does not report. The pattern shows up as extern declarations inside .c files, prototypes repeated in several headers, and local function declarations inside function bodies. A single declaration in one header, included wherever it is needed, is the intended arrangement and is not affected; multiple inclusion of that one header is fine. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 8.5 (Required).
detection_methods: Search .c files for 'extern' declarations and for function prototypes at file or block scope that are not in a header
Collect all external declarations across headers and flag identifiers declared in more than one file
Check block-scope function declarations inside function bodies
Run a MISRA C checker with system-wide analysis because the rule spans translation units
potential_mitigations: Move each external declaration into exactly one header owned by the defining module and include it everywhere it is used
Delete hand-written extern declarations and prototypes from consumer source files
Record a documented deviation only for third-party headers that duplicate declarations

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Keep one shared declaration per external entity

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 8.5 (Required; Decidable; System). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: External Identifier With Missing or Duplicate Definition
description: The program defines an identifier with external linkage in more than one place, or uses it without defining it anywhere, so the link result is undefined or depends on toolchain-specific merging.
extended_description: C requires exactly one external definition for each externally linked identifier that is used. A common trap is placing a definition such as 'int g_count;' or 'uint8_t buf[64] = {0};' in a header without extern, so every including .c file creates its own definition; some linkers merge these tentative definitions as common symbols and others report an error, and GCC 10 and later changed the default. Other cases are the same function defined in two modules, weak or duplicate stubs in test and production files, and a declared function that is never defined but whose call is optimised or linked against a different symbol. Inline functions and static definitions are outside this concern. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 8.6 (Required).
detection_methods: Search header files for file-scope object declarations without 'extern' and for function bodies not marked static inline
Compare symbol definitions across object files or the linker map for identifiers defined more than once
Look for extern declarations and prototypes that have no matching definition in any source file
Build with -fno-common and run a MISRA C checker with system-wide analysis
potential_mitigations: Put only extern declarations in headers and place the single definition in one .c file
Build with -fno-common or the equivalent so that duplicate tentative definitions are reported
Remove or isolate duplicate stub implementations so that each build links exactly one definition
common_consequences: Integrity, Confidentiality; Read Memory, Modify Memory

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Each external identifier needs one and only one definition

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 8.6 (Required; Decidable; System). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Externally Visible Definition Used in Only One File
description: The code gives a function or file-scope object external linkage even though it is referenced only within its own translation unit, so it is exposed to accidental use and name clashes across the program.
extended_description: Leaving out static on helper functions and module-level state makes them global symbols, which widens their visibility, lets other modules modify state they should not touch, and risks collisions with identically named symbols elsewhere, possibly silently with common or weak linkage. It also prevents some optimisation and makes reasoning about who writes a variable harder. Look in .c files for non-static file-scope variables such as 'uint8_t rx_state;' and non-static helper functions that are not declared in any header and are not referenced from other files. Functions that form a module's public interface, interrupt handlers and entry points that the linker or startup code refers to by name are not affected. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 8.7 (Advisory).
detection_methods: List non-static functions and file-scope objects defined in each .c file
For each one, search the rest of the repository for references outside the defining file, and check whether it is declared in a public header
Treat interrupt vectors, startup symbols and functions referenced from assembly or linker scripts as legitimate external uses
Run a MISRA C checker or link-time analysis with system-wide scope
potential_mitigations: Declare functions and file-scope objects static when they are only used within their own source file
Move module state behind accessor functions instead of exporting the variable
Record a documented deviation where external linkage is required for test hooks or toolchain reasons

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Limit linkage to the file that actually uses the entity

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 8.7 (Advisory; Decidable; System). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Internal Linkage Implied Without Static Keyword
description: The code redeclares a function or object that already has internal linkage without repeating the static keyword, so the linkage is inherited silently and readers may assume it is externally visible.
extended_description: In C, if a function or object is first declared static and later declared or defined without a storage class (or with extern), the later declaration quietly keeps internal linkage. A reader looking only at the definition, for example 'void filter_step(void) { ... }' lower in the file after a forward declaration 'static void filter_step(void);', will believe it is global, and moving or reordering declarations can change linkage or produce undefined behaviour. This occurs in .c files that forward-declare static helpers at the top and define them later, and in files with extern redeclarations of file-local variables. Declarations that consistently use static, and genuinely external entities, are not affected. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 8.8 (Required).
detection_methods: In each .c file, collect identifiers first declared with static and check every later declaration and the definition for the static keyword
Look for forward declarations of static functions whose definitions omit static
Look for 'extern' declarations referring to identifiers already declared static in the same file
Run a MISRA C checker, which can decide this within a single translation unit
potential_mitigations: Write static on every declaration and the definition of each internally linked function and object
Place static forward declarations and definitions together or order the file so that forward declarations are not needed

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Repeat static on each internal-linkage declaration

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 8.8 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: File-Scope Object Used by a Single Function
description: The code defines an object at file scope although only one function refers to it, so its scope is wider than needed and other code can read or modify it unintentionally.
extended_description: A file-scope variable such as 'static uint16_t last_sample;' that is touched only inside one function can be changed by any later code in the file, and its role is harder to understand. Defining it inside the function, using static at block scope if its value must persist between calls, documents ownership and narrows the set of code that can corrupt it. Look in .c files for file-scope variables, including static ones, and count the functions that reference each. Objects shared by several functions, objects accessed by interrupt service routines and main code, and large buffers deliberately placed at file scope to control memory placement are not affected. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 8.9 (Advisory).
detection_methods: List file-scope object definitions in each .c file and find every function that references each one
Flag objects referenced from exactly one function, then confirm whether persistence, placement or ISR sharing justifies file scope
Check linker section attributes or pragmas on the object, which may explain a deliberate file-scope placement
Run a MISRA C checker with system-wide analysis, as external objects require checking all translation units
potential_mitigations: Move the object into the only function that uses it, adding static at block scope if it must keep its value between calls
Record a documented deviation where file scope is needed for memory placement or debugging access

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Scope single-function objects inside that function

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 8.9 (Advisory; Decidable; System). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Inline Function With External Linkage
description: The code declares an inline function without static, giving it external linkage, so whether calls use the inline body or a separate external definition is unspecified and may lead to link errors or inconsistent behaviour.
extended_description: Under C99 rules an inline function with external linkage needs exactly one external definition somewhere in the program, and the compiler may call either the inline version or that external one at each call site; if they differ or the external one is missing, the result is unpredictable or the link fails. Compilers also disagree in practice, with older GNU89 semantics treating 'inline' and 'extern inline' the opposite way to C99. This appears mostly in headers as 'inline uint32_t swap32(uint32_t v) { ... }' or 'extern inline' helper functions, and in .c files that use inline without static. Functions declared 'static inline' are not affected. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 8.10 (Required).
detection_methods: Search headers and source files for the 'inline' keyword, including __inline and __inline__ spellings and macros that expand to them
Flag each inline function declaration or definition that does not also include 'static'
Check build flags such as -std=gnu89 or -fgnu89-inline that alter inline semantics
Run a MISRA C checker, which can decide this within a single translation unit
potential_mitigations: Declare all inline functions as static inline, usually in a header
Replace externally shared inline functions with ordinary external functions when a single definition is required
Check compatibility macros that wrap inline so they also add static

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Inline functions must have internal linkage

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 8.10 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: External Array Declared Without Explicit Size
description: The code declares an array with external linkage using empty brackets, so users in other files cannot check indexes against its length and size mismatches with the definition go undetected.
extended_description: A header declaration such as 'extern uint8_t cal_table[];' is legal but gives every including file an incomplete type, so sizeof cannot be used, static analysers cannot check bounds and a change to the real array length in the defining file is invisible to callers that loop to a hard-coded limit. This is common for lookup tables, calibration data, message buffers and string tables shared between modules. Arrays whose size is given in the declaration (ideally via a shared macro or constant), and definitions whose size is fixed by an initialiser in the defining file, are not affected; the concern is the externally visible declaration. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 8.11 (Advisory).
detection_methods: Search headers and source files for 'extern' declarations of arrays with empty brackets '[]'
Check file-scope non-static array definitions with '[]' that rely only on their initialiser for size and are referenced from other files
At uses of such arrays in other files, look for loops or indexes bounded by literal numbers rather than a shared size constant
Run a MISRA C checker, which can decide this within a single translation unit
potential_mitigations: Give external array declarations an explicit size using a macro or constant shared with the definition
Export the element count alongside the array, or provide accessor functions that perform bounds checks
Record a documented deviation where an array's length is genuinely unknown at the declaration point
common_consequences: Integrity, Confidentiality; Read Memory, Modify Memory

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Give shared arrays a stated length

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 8.11 (Advisory; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Implicitly Numbered Enumerator Duplicating Another Value
description: The code mixes explicit and implicit values in an enumeration so that an implicitly numbered constant ends up with the same value as another constant, causing distinct states or codes to compare equal.
extended_description: An enumerator without an initialiser takes the previous value plus one, so a list such as 'enum { RED, GREEN, BLUE = 1, YELLOW };' gives GREEN and BLUE the same value by accident; switch statements then hit duplicate case errors or, worse, state machines and error-code checks treat different conditions as the same. This tends to appear in state, command, error and register-field enums in headers that have been edited over time, where someone inserted an explicit value part way through the list. Deliberate aliases where both constants are given explicit values are not affected, and nor are enums that are fully implicit or fully explicit with unique values. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 8.12 (Required).
detection_methods: Search headers and source files for enum definitions that contain both enumerators with '=' initialisers and enumerators without them
For each such enum, compute the value of every enumerator and flag any implicitly valued one that equals another enumerator's value
Check switch statements over these enums for duplicate case diagnostics or unreachable branches
Run a MISRA C checker, which can decide this within a single translation unit
potential_mitigations: Give every enumerator an explicit value when any enumerator in the list is explicitly valued, or none at all
Make intended aliases explicit by initialising the alias with the name of the original constant
Add compile-time assertions on critical enumerator values

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Auto-numbered enum constants must not collide

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 8.12 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Read-Only Pointer Target Lacking Const Qualification
description: The code declares a pointer to a non-const type even though nothing is ever written through it, so the compiler cannot catch accidental modification of data that should be read-only.
extended_description: Marking the pointed-to type const documents that a function only reads a buffer, lets the compiler reject unintended writes, and allows const data such as flash tables and string literals to be passed without casts. Missing const is most visible in function parameters such as 'uint16_t crc16(uint8_t *data, size_t len)' or 'int parse(char *msg)' that only read their input, and in local or struct member pointers used only for iteration over lookup tables. It also forces callers to cast away const, which hides real errors. Pointers whose targets are modified, passed to functions that modify them, or stored where modification later occurs are not affected; const on the pointer itself is a separate matter. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 8.13 (Advisory).
detection_methods: Examine function prototypes in headers for pointer parameters to non-const types and check the definition for any write through the pointer, including via callees
Look for casts that remove const at call sites, which often indicate a callee missing const on a read-only parameter
Check local and member pointers used only to read tables, buffers or strings
Run a MISRA C checker or a const-correctness analysis, then confirm manually because the property is undecidable and crosses translation units
potential_mitigations: Add const to the pointed-to type of every pointer that is only used for reading, starting with function parameters in public headers
Remove casts that discard const once callees are const-correct
Record a documented deviation where a third-party API forces a non-const parameter

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Prefer const targets for read-only pointers

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 8.13 (Advisory; Undecidable; System). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Use of the Restrict Type Qualifier
description: The code qualifies a pointer with restrict, promising the compiler that it is the only access path to its object, so any aliasing between restrict pointers at run time gives undefined behaviour that optimisation can expose.
extended_description: restrict lets the compiler reorder and cache loads and stores on the assumption that no other pointer refers to the same memory; if a caller passes overlapping buffers, for example the same array as source and destination, the generated code can read stale values or write in the wrong order, and nothing checks the promise. The failure often appears only at higher optimisation levels or on a new compiler version. Look for the restrict keyword and its spellings __restrict and __restrict__ in function prototypes in headers, in DSP, copy, filter and math routines in source files, and in macros that expand to these keywords. Standard library prototypes that themselves use restrict, such as memcpy, are not violations by the calling code. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 8.14 (Required).
detection_methods: Search headers and source files for 'restrict', '__restrict' and '__restrict__', including inside macro definitions
At each restrict-qualified parameter, check call sites for arguments that may overlap, such as the same buffer or slices of one array
Check performance-critical modules such as DSP, codec and copy routines, where restrict is typically added
Run a MISRA C checker, which can decide this within a single translation unit
potential_mitigations: Remove restrict qualifiers from project code and rely on clearer algorithms or compiler options for performance
Where restrict is retained for measured performance, record a documented deviation and add run-time or design checks that buffers never overlap
common_consequences: Integrity, Confidentiality; Read Memory, Modify Memory

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Avoid the restrict qualifier

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 8.14 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Use of Automatic Variable Before It Is Assigned
description: The code reads a local variable with automatic storage duration on a path where no value has yet been stored in it, so the program acts on an indeterminate value.
extended_description: C gives automatic (stack) variables no starting value, so reading one before it is written produces whatever bytes remain in that stack slot and is undefined behaviour; optimising compilers may also assume it never happens and remove surrounding logic. In embedded C this usually appears as a local declared without an initialiser that is assigned only in some arms of an if/else or switch (often a switch with no default), only inside a for or while loop that can execute zero times, or only through an out-parameter of a function that can return an error code before writing it, and is then used after the branch, loop or call. Partially filled local arrays and structs that are later passed whole to memcpy, a CRC routine, a send or write function, or returned by value are a frequent variant, as is a variable whose address is taken but which is never actually written. Objects with static storage duration (file-scope globals and static locals) are zero-initialised by the language and do not count, and neither do locals that are initialised at their declaration or assigned unconditionally before first use. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 9.1 (Mandatory).
detection_methods: List local variables declared without an initialiser and follow every control path from the declaration to the first read
Check variables written only in selected if/else arms, switch cases without a default, or loop bodies that may run zero times, and then read afterwards
Check out-parameters such as int *result or struct pointers filled by callees that can return early on error; confirm the caller does not read them on the failure path
Look for local arrays and structs that are only partly assigned before being copied, checksummed, transmitted or returned
Run a MISRA C checker or compiler flow analysis such as -Wmaybe-uninitialized or -Wuninitialized, then confirm each report manually because the property is undecidable
potential_mitigations: Initialise every automatic variable at its declaration with a safe, defined value
Restructure branches and switch statements so that every path, including a default label, assigns the variable before it is read
Make functions with out-parameters write a defined value on every return path, including error returns
Clear whole local buffers and structs with an initialiser such as = { 0 } or memset before partially filling them
common_consequences: Availability; DoS: Crash, Exit, or Restart

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Stack objects written before any read

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 9.1 (Mandatory; Undecidable; System). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Flat Initialiser List for Nested Aggregate
description: The code initialises a multi-dimensional array, an array of structs, a struct containing arrays or a union with a flat or incompletely braced initialiser list, so the mapping of values to members depends on implicit brace elision and is easy to get wrong.
extended_description: C allows inner braces to be omitted in an initialiser, in which case values are assigned to subobjects strictly in declaration order; when a field is added, reordered or resized, every following value silently shifts to the wrong member without any compiler error. Typical findings are lookup tables such as uint8_t tbl[4][2] = { 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8 }, arrays of configuration structs written as one long comma-separated list, structs whose array member is initialised without its own braces, and scalar or union objects initialised with no braces at all where a brace-enclosed list is expected. The rule concerns the shape of the initialiser, not whether every element is given a value. Initialising a whole aggregate or subobject with { 0 }, initialising a char array from a string literal, initialising an automatic struct or union from another expression of the same type, and using designated initialisers for part of a subobject are acceptable. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 9.2 (Required).
detection_methods: Search for initialisers of multi-dimensional arrays ([..][..]) and arrays of struct type and check that each row or element has its own brace pair
Check struct initialisers where a member is itself an array, struct or union and confirm that member's values are enclosed in nested braces
Check union and aggregate initialisers that have no outer braces at all
Run a MISRA C checker or compiler warnings such as -Wmissing-braces, which decide this property directly
potential_mitigations: Add explicit nested braces for every row, element and member subobject in the initialiser
Use designated initialisers such as .field = value or [index] = value for large configuration tables so values cannot drift between members
Use { 0 } where the intent is simply to zero the whole object
Record a documented deviation only where generated code makes nested braces impractical

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Nested braces mirror aggregate structure in initialisers

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 9.2 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Array Initialiser Shorter Than Declared Size
description: The code supplies explicit positional values for only some elements of an array whose size is fixed, so the remaining elements are silently zero-filled and a missing table entry goes unnoticed.
extended_description: When an array has a declared length and its initialiser lists fewer values, C quietly sets the trailing elements to zero; this hides mistakes such as a forgotten entry in a calibration table, a lookup array that was lengthened without adding data, or an enum-indexed table that fell out of step with the enum. Typical findings are declarations like int16_t gains[8] = { 10, 20, 30 }; or const char *names[NUM_STATES] = { "IDLE", "RUN" }; where the count of values is less than the dimension, including inner rows of a two-dimensional array. The concern is an incomplete list, not zero initialisation as such. A single { 0 } that clears the whole array, an array initialised entirely with designated initialisers such as [3] = 1, and a char array initialised from a string literal do not count. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 9.3 (Required).
detection_methods: Find array declarations with both an explicit dimension and a positional initialiser list and compare the number of values with the dimension, including each inner row
Pay particular attention to tables sized by a macro or enum count such as [NUM_MODES] or [CHANNEL_COUNT], since the size can grow without the data growing
Ignore initialisers that are exactly { 0 }, use only designated initialisers, or are string literals
Run a MISRA C checker, which decides this property directly
potential_mitigations: Provide an explicit value for every element, or use { 0 } when the whole array is meant to start at zero
Use designated initialisers keyed by enum constants for state or mode tables
Add a static assertion such as _Static_assert or a sizeof check that ties the table length to the enum count
Record a documented deviation where a partial positional list is deliberate and reviewed

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Positional array initialisers cover every element

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 9.3 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Same Element Given Two Values in One Initialiser
description: The code initialises the same array element or struct member more than once within a single initialiser, so one value silently overrides the other and the intended setting may be lost.
extended_description: With C99 designated initialisers, a later entry for an element or member replaces an earlier one without any diagnostic, and the C standard leaves it unspecified whether side effects in the overridden expression are evaluated. This commonly happens in large tables where two lines use the same index, for example [MODE_RUN] = 3 and later [MODE_RUN] = 5, where two enum constants used as indices share a value, where a designated .field = x repeats a member already set, or where positional values follow a designator and run on into elements that were already set explicitly. Such duplicates often arise from copy and paste or from merges of configuration tables. Initialisers in which every element and member is set exactly once, whether positionally or by designator, do not count. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 9.4 (Required).
detection_methods: Search initialisers containing designators such as [index] = or .member = and check for repeated indices or member names
Resolve enum or macro values used as array designators and check that no two of them evaluate to the same index
Check initialisers that mix designators with following positional values and work out whether the positional values overwrite elements already set
Run a MISRA C checker or compiler warnings such as -Woverride-init or -Winitializer-overrides, which decide this property directly
potential_mitigations: Remove duplicate designators so each element or member is set once
Avoid mixing positional and designated entries in the same initialiser list
Keep enum-indexed tables in enum order and add static assertions on enum values that must be distinct
Record a documented deviation only where an override is deliberate and its expressions have no side effects

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Each subobject set at most once per initialiser

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 9.4 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Array Length Inferred From Designated Initialiser
description: The code declares an array with empty brackets and fills it using designated initialisers, so the array length is set by whichever index happens to be largest and can change unexpectedly when entries are edited.
extended_description: When an array is declared as T a[] and initialised with entries such as [5] = x, C sizes it from the highest designated index, which is not obvious to a reader and changes silently if the last entry is removed or an index constant is renumbered. Code that then loops to a separate macro or enum count, or indexes the array with a value it assumes is in range, may read or write past the real end. Typical findings are lookup tables like static const uint8_t map[] = { [CMD_RESET] = 1, [CMD_READ] = 2 }; and flexible array members initialised with designators. Arrays with an explicit dimension such as map[CMD_COUNT], and unsized arrays initialised only with positional values or a string literal, do not count. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 9.5 (Required).
detection_methods: Search for array declarations with empty brackets [] whose initialiser contains [index] = designators
Check code that iterates over or indexes such arrays using a separate count macro or enum rather than sizeof, and confirm the bound matches
Check flexible array members in structs initialised with designators
Run a MISRA C checker, which decides this property directly
potential_mitigations: Give the array an explicit dimension, ideally the enum or macro count that its indices come from
Add a static assertion that the array length equals the expected count
Record a documented deviation only where the inferred size is intended and checked
common_consequences: Integrity, Confidentiality; Read Memory, Modify Memory

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Explicit dimension for designator-initialised arrays

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 9.5 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Operator Applied to Operand of Unsuitable Kind
description: The code applies an operator to an operand whose underlying kind of value does not suit it, such as arithmetic on a boolean or character, bitwise or shift operations on a signed value, or logical operators on a plain integer, so the result relies on implicit promotions and may be implementation-defined, undefined or simply not what was meant.
extended_description: MISRA's essential type model sorts every expression into a category regardless of C's integer promotions: boolean (results of comparisons, !, && and ||, and _Bool or a project bool type), character (plain char), signed integer, unsigned integer, enumeration and floating. Each operator only makes sense for some categories, and using it on another hides a logic error or reaches implementation-defined or undefined behaviour. Concrete signs in source are: shifts, ~, &, | and ^ on signed values such as int16_t x; x >> 2 or ~x, where a negative value gives implementation-defined or undefined results; a shift count that is signed or could be negative; unary minus on an unsigned value; arithmetic or relational operators on bool-like values, for example flag + 1 or flag > 0; arithmetic on enum constants or enum variables outside simple equality tests; integers used directly as conditions of &&, ||, ! or ?:, for example if (count && ptr); and bitwise or modulo operators on float or double. Character values used in arithmetic are covered separately by Rule 10.2, and a non-negative integer constant used as a shift count or bitwise operand with an unsigned value is acceptable. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 10.1 (Required).
detection_methods: Search for <<, >>, ~, &, |, ^ and their compound forms and check whether either operand is a signed integer type, a bool, an enum or a char
Search for &&, || and ! whose operands are integers or pointers rather than comparison results or bool values
Check arithmetic and relational operators applied to bool variables, comparison results or enum values
Check unary minus applied to unsigned variables and shift counts that are signed or computed
Run a MISRA C checker configured for the essential type model, which decides this property directly
potential_mitigations: Use unsigned types such as uint32_t for any value that is shifted or manipulated bit by bit
Write explicit comparisons such as (count != 0U) instead of using integers or pointers as booleans
Keep bool values out of arithmetic and convert them with an explicit conditional where a number is needed
Convert enum values to an integer type with a deliberate cast before doing arithmetic, or use an integer type instead of the enum
Record a documented deviation for any remaining case that is reviewed and justified

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Operand essential type suits the operator

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 10.1 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.
view_names: MISRA C:2012 - The Essential Type Model

name: Character Value Used in General Arithmetic
description: The code uses plain char values in addition or subtraction other than simple digit and letter offsets, so text characters are treated as numbers and the result depends on the character set and on the implementation-defined signedness of char.
extended_description: Plain char exists to hold text, and whether it is signed or unsigned is chosen by the compiler, so arithmetic on it can give different answers on different targets and turns character data into ordinary numbers without that being visible. The essential type model accepts only a few character arithmetic patterns: adding an integer offset to a character, for example '0' + digit or 'A' + n, giving a character; subtracting one character from another, for example c - '0', giving an integer; and subtracting an integer from a character to step back through the character set. Findings to look for are two characters added together, characters multiplied, divided or used with %, a character subtracted from an integer, character offsets computed with a floating or boolean value, and the result of c - '0' being stored back as a char and treated as text. Treating uint8_t or int8_t buffers as numeric bytes is not affected, since those are not plain char, and the permitted digit and letter conversions above are acceptable. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 10.2 (Required).
detection_methods: Search for + and - expressions involving char variables or character literals such as '0', 'a' and 'A'
Flag char + char, int - char, and any *, / or % applied to plain char operands
Check whether results of char - char are stored back into char variables or passed where text is expected
Run a MISRA C checker configured for the essential type model, which decides this property directly
potential_mitigations: Restrict character arithmetic to char plus integer offset, char minus char, and char minus integer offset
Convert a character to its numeric value with c - '0' into an integer variable before further calculation
Use uint8_t rather than char for buffers that hold binary data rather than text
Record a documented deviation where a reviewed character set dependency is intended

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Character arithmetic limited to offset forms

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 10.2 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.
view_names: MISRA C:2012 - The Essential Type Model

name: Implicit Narrowing or Category Change on Assignment
description: The code stores a value into an object of a smaller type, or of a different kind such as signed into unsigned, floating into integer or integer into bool or enum, without an explicit cast, so the value can be silently truncated, wrapped or sign-changed.
extended_description: C converts values implicitly whenever they are assigned, passed as arguments, returned from a function or used to initialise an object, and those conversions quietly discard high-order bits, wrap negative numbers to large unsigned values, or drop the fractional part of floats. This applies to every assigning context: plain =, compound forms such as +=, initialisers, function arguments matched to prototype parameters, return statements and case constants in a switch. Concrete signs are uint8_t b = some_uint16; int16_t r = a_int32 * k; uint32_t u = signed_val; int n = f_double; enum mode m = 3; bool ok = count; char c = some_int; and a function declared to return uint16_t that returns an int32_t expression. Assigning to a wider type of the same kind, for example uint8_t into uint32_t, and assigning a non-negative integer constant that fits into an unsigned object, for example uint8_t x = 10;, do not count. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 10.3 (Required).
detection_methods: Check assignments, initialisers and compound assignments where the right-hand type is wider than the left, for example 32-bit into 16-bit or 8-bit fields
Check assignments between signed and unsigned integers, floating and integer, and integer and bool or enum types
Compare function call arguments with prototype parameter types and return expressions with the declared return type
Look in register access code, protocol packing and sensor scaling functions where wide intermediate results are stored into narrow fields
Run a MISRA C checker or compiler warnings such as -Wconversion and -Wsign-conversion, which decide this property directly
potential_mitigations: Make every intended narrowing or category change visible with an explicit cast, after checking the value fits
Range-check or saturate values before storing them into smaller types
Choose variable, parameter and return types so that values naturally match their destination
Use unsigned constants with a U suffix when assigning to unsigned objects
Record a documented deviation for reviewed cases where implicit conversion is intended

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: No implicit narrowing or category change when storing values

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 10.3 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.
view_names: MISRA C:2012 - The Essential Type Model

name: Mixed Signed and Unsigned Operands in Arithmetic or Comparison
description: The code combines operands of different kinds, such as a signed and an unsigned integer or an integer and a floating value, in a binary arithmetic, comparison, bitwise or conditional expression, so C's usual arithmetic conversions silently change one of them and the result can be wrong.
extended_description: When the two operands of operators such as +, -, *, /, %, <, >, <=, >=, ==, !=, &, |, ^ and the second and third operands of ?: belong to different categories, C converts one to the type of the other before evaluating; a negative signed value compared with an unsigned one becomes a large positive number, so a test like if (offset < len) with int offset and size_t or uint32_t len can pass for negative offsets. Typical findings are loops such as for (int i = 0; i < sizeof(buf); i++), comparisons of return codes from functions returning int against unsigned lengths, subtraction of unsigned counters producing wrap-around before being compared with a signed value, mixing float and integer operands, and compound forms such as u32 += s16. Enum values compared with plain integers also fall here. Operands of the same category but different widths, for example uint8_t with uint32_t, are a matter of width rather than category and do not count under this weakness, and character plus integer offsets permitted by Rule 10.2 are acceptable. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 10.4 (Required).
detection_methods: Search for relational operators and check whether one side is signed, such as int or a function return value, while the other is unsigned, such as size_t, sizeof, strlen or a uint type
Check for loop conditions comparing a signed index with an unsigned bound
Check arithmetic and compound assignments that combine signed and unsigned operands, or integer and floating operands
Check integer constants without a U suffix used with unsigned variables, and enum values compared with integers
Run a MISRA C checker or compiler warnings such as -Wsign-compare and -Wsign-conversion, which decide this property directly
potential_mitigations: Give both operands the same signedness by choosing matching declared types or adding an explicit, checked cast
Check signed values for negativity before comparing them with unsigned lengths
Use the U suffix on integer constants that are combined with unsigned values
Use size_t or another unsigned type for loop indices that are compared with sizeof or buffer lengths
Record a documented deviation for reviewed cases where the conversion is known to be safe
common_consequences: Integrity, Confidentiality; Read Memory, Modify Memory

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Matching operand categories under arithmetic conversion

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 10.4 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.
view_names: MISRA C:2012 - The Essential Type Model

name: Explicit Cast to Unsuitable Kind of Type
description: The code uses an explicit cast that converts a value into a kind of type that makes no sense for it, such as a number into bool or enum, a bool into a number, or a floating value into char, so the cast hides a likely logic error and may produce an invalid value.
extended_description: Casts silence compiler warnings, so a cast that changes a value's basic meaning can conceal a mistake rather than document an intended conversion. Under the essential type model the doubtful casts are: casting an integer or floating value to bool or a project boolean type, for example (bool)status, where any non-zero value collapses to true; casting a bool result to an integer or floating type to do arithmetic with it; casting an integer to an enum type, for example (enum state)raw_byte, which may yield a value that matches no enumerator; casting between floating types and plain char; and casting one enum type to another. These typically appear in protocol decoders that convert received bytes straight into enum states, in flag handling code, and in macros that coerce values to bool. Casts among signed, unsigned and floating numeric types, and casting the constants 0 or 1 to a boolean type, are acceptable here, although width changes may still be relevant to Rule 10.8. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 10.5 (Advisory).
detection_methods: Search for casts to bool, _Bool or the project boolean type and check that the operand is already a boolean expression or the constant 0 or 1
Search for casts to enum types, especially of raw bytes or integer fields from messages and registers, and check for range validation
Search for casts of boolean expressions to integer or floating types
Search for casts between float or double and plain char
