Run a MISRA C checker configured for the essential type model, which decides this property directly
potential_mitigations: Produce boolean values with explicit comparisons such as (status != 0U) instead of casting
Convert raw integers to enum values through a validating switch or lookup that rejects out-of-range input
Use explicit conditional expressions where a numeric value is needed from a boolean
Record a documented deviation for any reviewed cast that is retained

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Casts keep values within a sensible type category

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 10.5 (Advisory; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.
view_names: MISRA C:2012 - The Essential Type Model

name: Narrow Calculation Stored Into Wider Variable
description: The code assigns the result of an arithmetic or bitwise expression computed in a narrow type to an object of a wider type, so the calculation overflows or wraps in the narrow type before the widening and the destination receives a truncated result.
extended_description: The width of a calculation in C is decided by its operands, not by where the result is stored, so uint32_t total = a16 * b16; or uint64_t ticks = ms32 * 1000U; is computed in the narrower type (or in int after promotion) and may already have overflowed or wrapped before it is widened. The behaviour also differs between 16-bit and 32-bit targets because the size of int determines whether promotion helps. Here a composite expression means one built with binary arithmetic or bitwise operators (+, -, *, /, %, <<, >>, &, |, ^), the conditional operator applied to such operands, or compound assignments; a lone variable, a constant or a function call result is not composite. Typical places are timer and tick conversions, buffer size calculations, fixed-point scaling, checksum accumulation and register value assembly such as uint32_t reg = hi16 << 16. Assigning the composite result to an object of the same width, or widening a simple variable, does not count. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 10.6 (Required).
detection_methods: Search for assignments, initialisers, returns and function arguments where a wider destination, such as uint32_t or uint64_t, receives an expression containing *, +, -, << or similar on narrower operands
Look at time, frequency, size and fixed-point scaling code, where products of 16-bit or 32-bit values are stored into 32-bit or 64-bit variables
Check shifts of 8-bit or 16-bit values into higher bit positions that are then stored in 32-bit registers
Run a MISRA C checker configured for the essential type model, which decides this property directly
potential_mitigations: Cast one operand to the destination width before the operation, for example (uint32_t)a * b, so the calculation is done in the wider type
Declare intermediate variables with the wide type and compute in them
Use suitably suffixed constants such as 1000UL or 1000ULL where a constant sets the calculation width
Record a documented deviation for reviewed calculations that cannot overflow
common_consequences: Availability; DoS: Crash, Exit, or Restart

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Compound results not widened only after evaluation

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 10.6 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.
view_names: MISRA C:2012 - The Essential Type Model

name: Narrow Calculation Combined With Wider Operand
description: The code uses the result of a calculation done in a narrow type as one operand of a binary operator whose other operand is wider, so the inner calculation can overflow before the wider type takes effect, contrary to what the expression appears to compute.
extended_description: In an expression such as u32 + (u16a * u16b) or total_u32 > (len16 << 4), the inner sub-expression is evaluated entirely in its own narrow type and is only widened afterwards to match the outer operand, so any overflow or wrap-around in the inner part is already baked in. Readers usually assume the whole expression is evaluated at the wider width, which is the source of the error, and results can also change between targets with 16-bit and 32-bit int. A composite expression here is one built with binary arithmetic or bitwise operators, or a conditional operator over such results; the concern arises when that composite is one side of an arithmetic, relational, bitwise or conditional operator whose other side has a wider type of the same category. Common places are deadline and timeout checks, address and offset calculations, scaled sensor comparisons and accumulators. Expressions where both operands have the same width, or where the narrow side is a single variable or constant rather than a calculation, do not count. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 10.7 (Required).
detection_methods: Search for binary expressions where one side is a parenthesised or nested calculation on 8-bit or 16-bit (or 32-bit on 64-bit targets) operands and the other side is a wider variable
Check timeout, deadline and address comparisons such as now32 > start32 + (count16 * period16)
Check accumulations such as sum64 += a32 * b32 where the product is formed before widening
Run a MISRA C checker configured for the essential type model, which decides this property directly
potential_mitigations: Cast an operand inside the inner calculation to the wider type so the whole expression is evaluated at that width
Split the calculation into steps using intermediate variables of the wider type
Record a documented deviation for reviewed expressions that are proven not to overflow

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Inner calculation not narrower than its partner operand

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 10.7 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.
view_names: MISRA C:2012 - The Essential Type Model

name: Cast of Whole Calculation to Wider or Different Kind
description: The code casts the result of an arithmetic or bitwise calculation to a wider type, or to a different kind such as signed to unsigned or integer to floating, so the cast appears to control the calculation but is applied only after any overflow, truncation or integer division has already happened.
extended_description: A cast applied around a calculation, as in (uint32_t)(a16 * b16), (float)(sum / count) or (uint32_t)(s32a - s32b), converts only the final result; the multiplication, division or subtraction is still evaluated in the narrower or original type, so overflow, wrap-around or integer division loss occurs first. Developers often write this believing the cast widens or converts the calculation itself, which is why it is a reliable signal of a latent defect, for example averages that are truncated before conversion to float, products that overflow 16 bits before being cast to 32 bits, and negative differences turned into huge unsigned values. A composite expression here means one built with binary arithmetic or bitwise operators or a conditional operator over them. Casting a composite expression to a narrower type of the same category is permitted, since the programmer is deliberately discarding bits, and casting a single variable or constant before the operation, for example (uint32_t)a16 * b16, is the correct form and does not count. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 10.8 (Required).
detection_methods: Search for casts immediately followed by a parenthesised expression containing an operator, such as (type)(x * y), (type)(x / y), (type)(x << n) or (type)(x - y)
Flag such casts when the target type is wider than the operands or belongs to a different category, such as floating from integer or unsigned from signed
Check average, ratio and percentage calculations that cast an integer division to float or double
Run a MISRA C checker configured for the essential type model, which decides this property directly
potential_mitigations: Move the cast onto an operand so the calculation itself is done in the target type, for example (float)sum / (float)count
Use an intermediate variable of the target type for multi-step calculations
Record a documented deviation for reviewed casts where the inner calculation is proven safe

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Casts of compound results neither widen nor change category

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 10.8 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.
view_names: MISRA C:2012 - The Essential Type Model

name: Cast Between Function Pointer and Other Type
description: The code converts a pointer to a function into a pointer to a different function type, an object pointer or an integer (or the reverse), so a later call or access through the result can use the wrong calling convention or an invalid address.
extended_description: Calling a function through a pointer whose type does not match the function's real prototype is undefined behaviour, and converting a function pointer to an object pointer or integer is not portable because code and data addresses may differ in size or address space. In embedded C this shows up in callback and handler tables, ISR vector tables built as arrays of void * or uint32_t, bootloaders that jump to an application with a cast such as ((void (*)(void))0x08004000u), plugin or command dispatch tables that store handlers as void *, and calls such as qsort or thread-create wrappers that are passed a handler cast to a mismatched signature. Look for casts whose target or source type contains (*)( together with a different parameter list, a void *, or an integer type such as uintptr_t or uint32_t. Assigning a function name to a pointer of exactly the same function type, implicit conversion of a null pointer constant to a function pointer, and implicit conversion of a function designator to its own pointer type do not count. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 11.1 (Required).
detection_methods: Search for casts whose type contains (*)( and compare the cast target signature with the prototype of the function or pointer being converted
Inspect vector tables, callback registries and dispatch arrays declared with void *, uint32_t or uintptr_t elements that are filled with function names
Check bootloader and firmware-update code for jumps through integer addresses cast to function pointers
Run a MISRA C checker or compiler warnings such as -Wcast-function-type and -Wpedantic to list every function pointer conversion
potential_mitigations: Declare callback and handler tables with the exact function pointer typedef they will be called through, and give every handler that signature
Use small adapter functions with the required signature instead of casting a handler to a mismatched type
Confine unavoidable conversions such as a bootloader jump to one documented, reviewed function and record a deviation for it
common_consequences: Availability; DoS: Crash, Exit, or Restart
Integrity; Execute Unauthorized Code or Commands

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Function pointers kept separate from other types

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 11.1 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Cast Involving Pointer to Incomplete Type
description: The code converts a pointer to an incomplete (opaque) struct or union type into some other pointer or integer type, or converts another type into it, which defeats the encapsulation the opaque type provides and risks misaligned or mistyped access.
extended_description: Opaque handles such as a pointer to a struct that is only forward-declared in a header exist so that callers cannot see or depend on the layout; casting such a handle to a concrete struct pointer, a byte pointer or an integer bypasses that boundary and can produce a pointer that is wrongly aligned or refers to a different object type, which is undefined behaviour when dereferenced. Typical places are driver and HAL APIs that expose typedef struct foo_ctx *foo_handle_t, RTOS object handles, and library modules where client code casts the handle to an internal struct or to uintptr_t to stash it in a register, message or table. Look for casts where the source or target type is a struct or union declared with no body in the visible translation unit. Converting a null pointer constant to the opaque type, and converting it to or from void *, are not counted here (the void * case is covered by the separate void pointer guideline). Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 11.2 (Required).
detection_methods: List struct and union tags that are only forward-declared in public headers and search for casts to or from pointers to those tags
Check client code of driver, HAL and RTOS APIs for casts of opaque handles to internal structure types, byte pointers or uintptr_t
Check code that packs handles into integer message fields, registers or lookup tables
Run a MISRA C checker, which can decide this rule within a single translation unit
potential_mitigations: Keep opaque handle types opaque and provide accessor functions in the owning module instead of casting the handle in client code
Inside the owning module, convert to the complete type only where the definition is visible and the handle is known to originate from that module
Store handles in fields of the handle type rather than in integers, or document a deviation where an integer encoding is unavoidable
common_consequences: Integrity, Confidentiality; Read Memory, Modify Memory

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Opaque type pointers not converted to other types

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 11.2 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Cast Between Pointers to Different Object Types
description: The code casts a pointer to one object type into a pointer to a different object type and accesses memory through it, so the access may be misaligned or violate the effective type rules.
extended_description: Reinterpreting memory through a pointer of another type can produce a misaligned address, which faults on many microcontrollers, and reading an object through an incompatible lvalue breaks the strict aliasing rules so the optimiser may reorder or drop accesses. The classic embedded patterns are protocol and packet parsing such as (struct hdr *)rx_buf or *(uint32_t *)&buf[3], overlaying structs on DMA or flash buffers, type punning a float as uint32_t via *(uint32_t *)&f for CRC or serialisation, and casting between unrelated struct pointers to fake inheritance. Look for casts of the form (T *)p where p points to a different object type, especially uint8_t or char buffers cast to wider integer or struct pointers. Casting any object pointer to a pointer to char, signed char or unsigned char to inspect its bytes is permitted and does not count, nor does adding const or volatile qualifiers to the same pointed-to type. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 11.3 (Required).
detection_methods: Search for casts of uint8_t, char or byte buffer pointers to wider integer pointers (uint16_t *, uint32_t *) or struct pointers in parsers, DMA handlers and flash or EEPROM code
Check expressions of the form *(T *)&x used for type punning floats, doubles or structures
Check casts between unrelated struct pointer types used to emulate inheritance or message variants
Run a MISRA C checker or compiler warnings such as -Wcast-align and -Wstrict-aliasing
potential_mitigations: Copy bytes into a properly typed local object with memcpy, or assemble multi-byte fields with shifts, instead of dereferencing a cast byte pointer
Use a union or explicit serialisation functions for type punning and data marshalling
Where hardware overlays are unavoidable, guarantee alignment with the buffer declaration and record a documented deviation
common_consequences: Integrity, Confidentiality; Read Memory, Modify Memory
Availability; DoS: Crash, Exit, or Restart

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: No reinterpreting casts between object pointer types

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 11.3 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Conversion Between Object Pointer and Integer
description: The code converts an object pointer into an integer or an integer into an object pointer, so the resulting value or address depends on implementation-defined representation and may be truncated, misaligned or invalid.
extended_description: The mapping between integers and pointers is implementation-defined; an integer type narrower than a pointer truncates the address, and an integer converted to a pointer may not be correctly aligned or may not point to a valid object. In embedded C the dominant case is memory-mapped register access such as #define GPIOA_ODR (*(volatile uint32_t *)0x40020014u), plus pointer arithmetic done in integers for alignment rounding ((uint32_t)p + 3u) & ~3u, storing buffer addresses in uint32_t DMA descriptor fields, and passing pointers through integer message or event fields. Look for casts between pointer types and integer types including uint32_t, unsigned long, size_t, intptr_t and uintptr_t, and for integer literals cast to pointer types. Assigning a null pointer constant, and conversions involving void * or function pointers (handled by neighbouring guidelines), do not count. Because register access is often necessary, hits should be checked for confinement to a hardware abstraction layer rather than scattered through application code. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 11.4 (Advisory).
detection_methods: Search for integer literals or macros cast to pointer types, such as (volatile uint32_t *)0x40000000u, and note whether they are confined to register definition headers
Search for casts of pointers to uint32_t, unsigned long, size_t or uintptr_t used for alignment arithmetic, hashing or storage in descriptors and messages
Check that any integer holding an address is at least as wide as a pointer on the target, preferring uintptr_t
Run a MISRA C checker or compiler warnings such as -Wpointer-to-int-cast and -Wint-to-pointer-cast
potential_mitigations: Confine memory-mapped register addresses to a single hardware definition header or vendor CMSIS-style structures and record a documented deviation for them
Use uintptr_t from <stdint.h> when a pointer must be held as an integer, never a fixed-width type that may be narrower
Prefer pointer arithmetic and alignment attributes over integer manipulation of addresses
common_consequences: Integrity, Confidentiality; Read Memory, Modify Memory

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Avoid mixing object addresses with integers

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 11.4 (Advisory; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Conversion of Void Pointer to Object Pointer
description: The code converts a void * into a pointer to a specific object type, so the compiler can no longer check that the memory really holds an object of that type with suitable alignment.
extended_description: A void * carries no type information, so turning it back into a typed pointer relies entirely on the programmer knowing what it originally pointed to; if that assumption is wrong the access is misaligned or reads the wrong type, which is undefined behaviour. Common embedded locations are generic callback context arguments (void *ctx cast back to a driver struct), message queue and mailbox payloads, memory pool or custom allocator returns, malloc results, and generic container or list nodes. Look for explicit casts such as (struct foo *)arg and implicit conversions where a void * is assigned to or initialises a typed pointer variable. Conversions from an object pointer to void *, and conversions of a null pointer constant, do not count. Because this pattern is sometimes needed for generic interfaces, the useful signal is where the original type of the pointer cannot be established from the surrounding code. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 11.5 (Advisory).
detection_methods: Search for casts from void * parameters such as callback context, user data or argument pointers to concrete struct or integer pointer types
Check assignments of malloc, pool allocator, queue receive and mailbox payload results to typed pointers
Trace each conversion back to where the void * was produced and confirm the original object type and alignment match
Run a MISRA C checker to list implicit and explicit void * to object pointer conversions
potential_mitigations: Use typed interfaces, for example a callback that takes struct foo_ctx * rather than void *, where the set of users is known
Keep each void * round trip local and documented so the original type is evident at the conversion
Record a documented deviation for allocator and generic container code where the conversion is inherent
common_consequences: Integrity, Confidentiality; Read Memory, Modify Memory

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Avoid recovering typed pointers from void *

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 11.5 (Advisory; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Cast Between Void Pointer and Arithmetic Type
description: The code casts a void * to an integer or floating type, or an arithmetic value to void *, so the result depends on implementation-defined representation and may lose address bits or yield an invalid pointer.
extended_description: Converting between void * and an arithmetic type has implementation-defined results, can truncate the address when the integer is narrower than a pointer, and is meaningless for floating types. It typically appears when integers are smuggled through generic void * parameters, for example passing (void *)channel_id as a thread, timer or callback argument and recovering it with (int)arg or (uint32_t)arg, when RTOS task parameters or queue items carry small integers as pointers, and when DMA or peripheral APIs taking void * are given a numeric address. Look for casts such as (void *)n, (void *)0x2000u and (uint32_t)ptr where ptr is void *. Casting the integer constant 0 to void * to form a null pointer is allowed and does not count, nor do conversions between void * and object pointers. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 11.6 (Required).
detection_methods: Search for (void *) applied to integer variables, enum values or numeric literals other than 0
Search for integer or floating casts applied to void * values, especially callback, task and timer argument parameters
Check RTOS task creation, timer and thread APIs for integers passed through the void * argument
Run a MISRA C checker or compiler warnings such as -Wint-to-pointer-cast and -Wpointer-to-int-cast
potential_mitigations: Pass a pointer to a properly typed object, such as a static configuration struct, instead of encoding an integer in a void *
Use uintptr_t via an intermediate object pointer only where unavoidable and document a deviation
Change interfaces that need numeric identifiers to take an integer parameter explicitly
common_consequences: Integrity, Confidentiality; Read Memory, Modify Memory

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Void pointers not cast to or from numbers

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 11.6 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Cast Between Object Pointer and Non-Integer Arithmetic Type
description: The code casts an object pointer to a floating, boolean, character or enum type, or casts such a value to an object pointer, producing a result that is undefined or meaningless as an address or a value.
extended_description: C does not define a conversion between pointers and floating types, and conversions to essentially Boolean, character or enum types throw away address information or rely on implementation-defined behaviour, so the result cannot be trusted. In practice this appears as (bool)ptr or (_Bool)ptr used as a validity test, pointers cast to char or an enum type to fit a narrow message field, addresses squeezed into float or double members of telemetry or logging structures, and enum constants cast to pointers to select a register block. Look for casts whose source is a pointer and whose target is float, double, bool, _Bool, char or an enum type, and the reverse. Ordinary integer-pointer conversions are a separate concern, and a null test written as ptr != NULL is the correct form and does not count. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 11.7 (Required).
detection_methods: Search for casts of pointers to float, double, bool, _Bool, char or enum types
Search for casts of floating, Boolean, character or enum values to pointer types
Check packing of pointers into narrow or floating fields of log, telemetry and message structures
Run a MISRA C checker, which decides this rule within a single translation unit
potential_mitigations: Test pointer validity with an explicit comparison against NULL rather than a cast to a Boolean type
Store addresses only in pointer objects, or uintptr_t where unavoidable, never in floating, character or enum fields
Use lookup tables indexed by an enum to select pointers instead of casting enum values to pointers
common_consequences: Availability; DoS: Crash, Exit, or Restart

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Object pointers kept apart from non-integer arithmetic types

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 11.7 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Cast Discarding Const or Volatile Qualifier
description: The code casts a pointer to a const or volatile qualified type into a pointer that lacks that qualifier, so writes to read-only objects or optimised-away hardware accesses can occur.
extended_description: Modifying an object defined const through a pointer with the qualifier cast away is undefined behaviour and can fault when the object lives in flash or ROM, while accessing a volatile object through a non-volatile pointer lets the compiler cache, merge or remove reads and writes. Typical embedded sites are memory-mapped registers and DMA or shared ISR buffers passed to helper functions such as memcpy, memset or a CRC routine that take plain pointers, (uint8_t *)const_buf to satisfy a non-const library or HAL API, and lookup tables in flash cast to writable pointers. Look for casts where the source pointer type contains const or volatile and the target type omits it, including casts through void *. Casts that add a qualifier, and casts of the pointer value itself (for example a const pointer variable copied to a non-const pointer variable of the same pointed-to type), do not count. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 11.8 (Required).
detection_methods: Search for casts such as (uint8_t *), (char *) or (void *) applied to expressions whose type is a pointer to const or volatile data
Check calls that pass volatile register blocks, DMA buffers or ISR-shared buffers to memcpy, memset, memcmp or checksum functions
Check calls that pass const tables or strings to APIs with non-const parameters
Run a MISRA C checker or compiler warnings such as -Wcast-qual
potential_mitigations: Correct the parameter types of internal helper functions so they accept const or volatile qualified pointers
Copy volatile data element by element through a volatile pointer instead of passing it to library routines that assume ordinary memory
Where a third-party API is not const-correct, wrap it in one documented function and record a deviation
common_consequences: Availability; DoS: Crash, Exit, or Restart

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Pointer casts keep const and volatile

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 11.8 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Literal Zero Used as Null Pointer
description: The code uses the integer literal 0 or a home-made macro instead of NULL to denote a null pointer, which hides pointer intent and makes pointer and integer contexts easy to confuse.
extended_description: Writing 0 where a null pointer is meant compiles silently but obscures whether a variable is a pointer or an integer, so reviewers and tools can miss mismatched arguments, wrong comparisons or a pointer passed where a count is expected, and project-specific null macros may expand differently in different headers. Look for pointer variables initialised or assigned with 0, comparisons such as p == 0 or p != 0, functions returning 0 from a pointer-returning function, 0 passed as a pointer argument (for example to callback registration or memcpy-style APIs), and local macros such as #define NIL 0 or #define MY_NULL ((void *)0). Uses of NULL from <stddef.h> or <stdio.h>, the expression (void *)0 written as the definition of NULL itself, and the integer 0 used in integer contexts do not count. Implicit tests such as if (p) or !p are a separate essential-type concern. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 11.9 (Required).
detection_methods: Search for pointer declarations initialised with = 0 and pointer assignments of the literal 0
Search for comparisons of pointer expressions against 0 using == or !=, and return 0 statements in functions that return a pointer
Search headers for project-defined null macros and check where they are used
Run a MISRA C checker or compiler warnings such as -Wzero-as-null-pointer-constant where supported
potential_mitigations: Replace every literal 0 used as a pointer with NULL from <stddef.h>
Remove project-specific null macros and use the standard NULL macro consistently

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Null pointers written only as NULL

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 11.9 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Reliance on Implicit Operator Precedence
description: The code mixes operators of different precedence without parentheses, so the expression may be grouped differently from what the author intended and compute a wrong value.
extended_description: C's precedence table has several counter-intuitive levels, notably bitwise &, ^ and | binding more loosely than == and !=, shifts binding more loosely than + and -, and && versus || mixing, so unparenthesised expressions are a frequent source of silent logic errors. In embedded code this concentrates in register and flag tests such as if (REG & MASK == MASK), bit-field assembly such as hi << 8 + lo, mixed && and || conditions in state machines and ISR guards, ternary expressions nested in arguments, and macro bodies whose parameters and whole expansion are not parenthesised. Look for expressions combining binary operators from different precedence groups without grouping parentheses, and for macro definitions using parameters without surrounding parentheses. Simple chains of the same operator, such as a + b + c, and the obvious grouping of multiplicative operators inside additive ones are lower risk and generally not worth flagging. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 12.1 (Advisory).
detection_methods: Search conditions for bitwise &, | or ^ combined with ==, !=, < or > without parentheses around the bitwise part
Search for << or >> combined with + or - in the same unparenthesised operand
Check conditions that mix && and || without grouping, and nested ?: expressions
Check #define bodies for parameters and whole expansions that are not enclosed in parentheses
Run a MISRA C checker or compiler warnings such as -Wparentheses
potential_mitigations: Add parentheses so that the grouping of every mixed-precedence expression is explicit
Split complex conditions into named intermediate variables
Parenthesise each macro parameter use and the full macro expansion

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Make expression grouping explicit with parentheses

name: Shift Count Outside Operand Bit Width
description: The code shifts a value by a count that is negative or not less than the bit width of the left operand's essential type, which is undefined behaviour or silently produces an unexpected result.
extended_description: Shifting by a negative amount or by the full width or more of the promoted type is undefined behaviour in C, and different CPUs mask or saturate the count differently, so the same code can give different answers across compilers and targets; shifting a narrow essential type such as uint8_t by 8 or more also discards every bit even where promotion avoids the formal undefined behaviour. In embedded code this appears in bit-mask construction such as 1u << n or (1u << width) - 1u where n or width can reach 32, in loops that build masks over a full register width, in protocol and CRC code that shifts uint8_t or uint16_t values by computed amounts, and in literals such as 1 << 31 on a 32-bit int. Look for << and >> whose right operand is a variable, macro or expression whose range is not obviously bounded below the width of the left operand. Constant shift counts that are clearly within range do not count. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 12.2 (Required).
detection_methods: Search for << and >> with a variable or computed right operand and determine the possible range of that operand
Check mask-building expressions such as (1u << n) - 1u for the case where n equals the full register width
Check shifts whose left operand is uint8_t, uint16_t or a char type against shift counts of 8, 16 or more
Run a MISRA C checker or UBSan shift checks, and confirm by manual range analysis because the property is undecidable across the system
potential_mitigations: Validate or clamp shift counts against the operand width before shifting
Handle the full-width case explicitly, for example with a conditional that returns an all-ones mask
Cast the left operand to a sufficiently wide unsigned type before shifting so the intended bits are kept
Record a documented deviation only where the shift count range is proven by design

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Shift counts kept within the operand width

name: Use of the Comma Operator
description: The code uses the comma operator to combine expressions, which hides side effects and evaluation order and makes the statement easy to misread.
extended_description: The comma operator evaluates its left operand, discards the result and yields the right operand, so it packs several actions into one expression where readers tend to overlook all but one of them, and a misplaced comma can turn an intended argument list or initialiser into a single discarded expression. Typical locations are for loop headers that update several variables, such as for (i = 0, j = n; i < j; i++, j--), multi-statement macros written as expressions, conditions such as while (read_byte(&c), c != END), and return statements like return (log_err(), -1);. Look for commas at expression level outside function call argument lists, parameter lists, declarations with several declarators and initialiser lists, all of which are separators and do not count. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 12.3 (Advisory).
detection_methods: Search for commas in the initialisation and increment clauses of for loops
Search macro bodies for comma-separated expressions used to bundle several actions
Check if, while and return expressions for commas that are not part of a function call argument list
Run a MISRA C checker, which can distinguish the comma operator from comma separators
potential_mitigations: Rewrite comma expressions as separate statements
Move extra loop variable updates into the loop body or restructure the loop
Implement multi-action macros as do { ... } while (0) blocks or as inline functions

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Avoid the sequencing comma operator

name: Unsigned Wrap-Around in Constant Expression
description: The code contains a compile-time constant expression whose unsigned arithmetic wraps around modulo 2^N, so the constant silently takes a value very different from the one the author computed.
extended_description: Unsigned wrap-around is well defined in C, which is why compilers rarely warn about it, but in a constant expression it almost always signals a mistake such as a subtraction in the wrong order, a product that overflows the width of int or unsigned int, or a value that differs between 16-bit and 32-bit targets. In embedded code look for #define constants and enum, static initialiser, array size and #if expressions that combine unsigned literals or macros, for example timer reload values like (CLOCK_HZ / BAUD) - 1u when the division can yield 0, BASE_ADDR - OFFSET with OFFSET larger, delay or timeout products such as DELAY * WIDTH computed in a 16-bit unsigned int, and preprocessor arithmetic in #if directives. Only expressions whose operands are all compile-time constants are in scope; run-time wrap-around in counters, ring buffer indices or deliberate modulo arithmetic does not count. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 12.4 (Advisory).
detection_methods: Evaluate #define, enum, const initialiser and array dimension expressions built from unsigned literals and check whether any intermediate result goes below zero or above the type maximum
Check #if and #elif directives that perform subtraction or multiplication on unsigned values
Check clock, baud rate, timer reload and memory map calculations for subtraction of larger constants and products that exceed 16 or 32 bits on the target
Run a MISRA C checker, or enable compiler diagnostics for integer overflow in constant expressions
potential_mitigations: Reorder or rewrite the expression so intermediate results stay within range, and use a wider type suffix such as UL or ULL where needed
Add static assertions (_Static_assert or #error checks) that verify derived constants fall within the expected range
Record a documented deviation where wrap-around in a constant is intentional

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Constant arithmetic must not wrap unsigned values

name: Order-Dependent Side Effects Inside Brace Initialisers
description: The code places function calls, increments, assignments or volatile reads inside a braced initialiser list for an array, struct or union, so the resulting object contents and program state depend on an evaluation order that C leaves unspecified.
extended_description: C does not define the order in which the expressions inside a brace-enclosed initialiser are evaluated, so if two elements each change shared state, or one element reads what another writes, different compilers or optimisation levels can produce different values. Typical violating code looks like `uint8_t buf[3] = { next(), next(), next() };`, `struct pkt p = { idx++, data[idx] };`, or an initialiser that reads a volatile hardware register or calls a function that updates a static counter, log or peripheral. It is most common in C99 code that initialises local aggregates or compound literals from calls in drivers and protocol encoders. Initialisers made only of constants, plain variable reads, address-of expressions or pure functions with no observable effects are not a concern, nor is a scalar initialiser such as `int x = f();`. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 13.1 (Required).
detection_methods: Search for aggregate and compound literal initialisers of the form `= {` or `(type){` and inspect each element expression
Flag elements containing `++`, `--`, `=` or compound assignment, calls to functions that modify static, global or hardware state, or reads of `volatile` objects
Check whether one element reads an object that another element in the same list modifies
Run a MISRA C checker, and review called functions manually across translation units because whether a call has persistent side effects cannot always be decided
potential_mitigations: Evaluate side-effecting calls and volatile reads into separate local variables in explicit statements before the declaration, then initialise from those locals
Declare the aggregate first and assign its members in sequenced statements where ordering matters
Record a documented deviation only where every element's side effect is shown to be independent of evaluation order

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Keep lasting side effects out of brace initialisers

name: Expression Result Dependent on Unsequenced Evaluation Order
description: The code writes an expression whose value or side effects change depending on which operand, argument or subexpression the compiler evaluates first, which can produce undefined behaviour or results that differ between compilers and builds.
extended_description: Apart from a few sequence points such as `&&`, `||`, `?:` and the comma operator, C leaves the order of operand and argument evaluation unspecified, and modifying an object twice, or modifying and reading it, without an intervening sequence point is undefined behaviour. Concrete forms include `a[i] = i++;`, `x = x++ + 1;`, `f(i++, i);`, `g(read_reg(), read_reg())` where both calls touch the same volatile register, `p->n = update(p)` where `update` changes `p->n`, and macros that expand an argument containing `++` more than once. Two calls in one expression that both modify the same static or global object, or that both access volatile objects, also qualify because their relative order is not fixed. Expressions where each object is modified at most once and is not read elsewhere in the same expression, or where the operations are separated by `;`, `&&`, `||`, `?:` or the comma operator, are not affected. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 13.2 (Required).
detection_methods: Search for `++`, `--`, `=` and compound assignment operators that appear inside a larger expression, function argument list or array index, and check whether the same object is also read or written elsewhere in that expression
Check expressions containing two or more function calls, or two or more `volatile` accesses, for shared state the callees modify or hardware registers they read
Expand function-like macros and check whether an argument with a side effect is evaluated more than once
Enable compiler diagnostics such as -Wsequence-point or -Wunsequenced and run a MISRA C checker, then review callee side effects across translation units manually because the property is undecidable
potential_mitigations: Split the expression into separate statements so each side effect occurs in its own full expression in a defined order
Copy volatile reads and side-effecting call results into local variables before combining them
Rewrite function-like macros as static inline functions, or ensure each macro argument is evaluated exactly once
Record a documented deviation only where analysis shows the outcome is identical under every permitted order
common_consequences: Integrity, Confidentiality; Read Memory, Modify Memory

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Results must not hinge on the compiler's evaluation order

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 13.2 (Required; Undecidable; System). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Increment or Decrement Mixed with Other Side Effects
description: The code embeds a `++` or `--` operator in a full expression that also calls functions, assigns, or accesses volatile objects, which makes the ordering of effects hard to see and can hide sequencing defects.
extended_description: When an increment or decrement shares a statement with other effects, readers must work out whether the old or new value is used and in what order the effects happen, and slight edits can turn the code into an unsequenced modification with undefined behaviour. Typical examples are `buf[n++] = read_byte();`, `x = *p++ + f();`, `send(i++, j);`, `y = a[i++] = 0;` and `while (*dst++ = *src++)` in hand-written copy loops. A statement whose only effect is the increment, such as `i++;`, or a `for` clause like `i++`, is fine, as is an expression that uses `++` alongside plain reads of non-volatile objects with no calls, such as `x = a[i++];`. This guideline concerns clarity and review effort rather than guaranteed misbehaviour. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 13.3 (Advisory).
detection_methods: Search for `++` and `--` tokens that are not the whole of an expression statement or a `for` third clause
At each hit, check whether the same full expression also contains a function call, an assignment or compound assignment, another `++` or `--`, or a `volatile` access
Pay particular attention to pointer walking idioms such as `*p++ = f()` and `*d++ = *s++` in copy and parsing loops
Run a MISRA C checker, since the construct is decidable within a single translation unit
potential_mitigations: Move the increment or decrement into its own statement immediately before or after the expression that uses the value
Assign function results or volatile reads to a local first, then increment the index in a separate statement
Record a documented deviation for an established idiom only where the team agrees it is clear and has no ordering hazard

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Keep ++ and -- out of statements with other effects

name: Assignment Value Used as an Operand
description: The code uses the value produced by an assignment operator inside another expression, such as an `if` or `while` condition, a chained assignment or a function argument, which invites confusion between `=` and `==` and hides state changes.
extended_description: Embedding an assignment in a condition, as in `if (x = read())` or `while ((c = getchar()) != EOF)`, makes it hard to tell an intended assignment from a mistyped comparison, and combining it with other operations raises the risk of sequencing errors. Concrete forms include assignments in `if`, `while`, `for` second clauses and `?:` conditions, chained assignments like `a = b = 0;`, compound assignments used as values like `f(n += 2)`, and assignments inside array subscripts or return expressions such as `return (err = check());`. An assignment that forms a whole expression statement, or the first and third clauses of a `for` statement, does not count, nor do comparisons written with `==`. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 13.4 (Advisory).
detection_methods: Search the controlling expressions of `if`, `while`, `do ... while`, `for` second clauses and `?:` conditions for a single `=` or compound assignment operator
Search for chained assignments matching `x = y =` and for assignments nested inside function arguments, array subscripts or `return` expressions
Enable compiler warnings such as -Wparentheses that flag assignments used as truth values
Run a MISRA C checker, since the construct is decidable within a single translation unit
potential_mitigations: Perform the assignment as its own statement before the condition, then test the variable
Restructure read loops such as `while ((c = getchar()) != EOF)` into a loop that assigns at the end of the body or uses a priming read
Split chained assignments into separate statements
Record a documented deviation for a team-approved idiom only where the intent is unambiguous

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Do not consume the value of an assignment

name: Side Effect Skipped by Logical Operator Short Circuit
description: The code places a state-changing operation on the right of `&&` or `||`, so the operation silently does not happen whenever the left operand alone decides the result.
extended_description: C evaluates the right operand of `&&` only when the left is true and the right operand of `||` only when the left is false, so any increment, assignment, volatile read or function call with lasting effects placed there runs conditionally, which developers often do not intend. Concrete examples are `if (ready && (count++ > 3))`, `if (err || (status = poll_device()))`, `while (n > 0 && read_reg(STATUS) & BUSY)` where the register read has clear-on-read behaviour, and `ok = ok && write_block(b);` patterns where later writes are skipped. It commonly appears in driver polling, error-accumulation chains and input parsing. Right operands that only read non-volatile variables, compare values or call pure functions without observable effects are not a concern. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 13.5 (Required).
detection_methods: Search for `&&` and `||` and inspect each right operand for `++`, `--`, assignment operators, calls to functions that modify state or perform I/O, and `volatile` accesses
Check error-accumulating chains such as `ok = ok && step()` and `if (a() || b())` where every call was expected to run
Check register polling conditions where the right operand reads a hardware register with read side effects
Run a MISRA C checker and review called functions across translation units manually, because whether a callee has persistent side effects is undecidable
potential_mitigations: Evaluate the side-effecting operation in a separate statement before the logical expression and test the stored result
Use nested `if` statements so that the conditional execution of the side effect is explicit
Record a documented deviation only where skipping the effect is the deliberate and reviewed design

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: No lasting effects in conditionally evaluated logical operands

name: Side Effect Placed Inside sizeof Operand
description: The code puts an increment, assignment, function call or volatile access inside the operand of `sizeof`, so the expected effect usually never happens because the operand is not evaluated.
extended_description: For ordinary types, `sizeof` determines its result at compile time and does not evaluate its operand, so `sizeof(i++)`, `sizeof(x = 5)`, `sizeof(get_buffer())` or `sizeof(*next_item())` leave the program state unchanged even though the code appears to change it. For a variable length array operand in C99 the operand may be evaluated, so the same code then behaves differently and it is unspecified whether some subexpressions run. Such code often appears in macros that wrap `sizeof` around an argument, for example a length macro invoked with `p++` or a function call. A plain `sizeof(type)`, `sizeof(var)`, `sizeof(*ptr)` or `sizeof(arr[0])` without any operator that changes state is not affected; a read of a `volatile` object inside `sizeof` does count because it is itself a potential side effect. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 13.6 (Mandatory).
detection_methods: Search for every `sizeof` and inspect its operand for `++`, `--`, `=`, compound assignment, function calls and `volatile` objects
Expand macros that wrap `sizeof` around a parameter, such as array length or field size helpers, and check each call site's arguments
Check C99 code that applies `sizeof` to variable length arrays with non-trivial size expressions
Run a MISRA C checker, since the construct is decidable within a single translation unit
potential_mitigations: Perform the intended side effect in its own statement and apply `sizeof` to a plain variable, type name or dereferenced pointer
Use `sizeof` on the type, or on an existing object, rather than on a function call result
Make size helper macros reject or avoid arguments with side effects, for example by documenting and checking call sites

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: sizeof operands must be free of potential side effects

name: Floating-Point Variable Used as Loop Counter
description: The code controls a loop with a `float` or `double` counter that is stepped and compared against a limit, so rounding error can change the number of iterations or prevent the loop from ending.
extended_description: Most decimal steps such as 0.1 cannot be represented exactly in binary floating point, so repeated addition accumulates error and the iteration count may differ by one from what the code suggests, vary between targets or optimisation levels, or never meet an equality test at all. Typical forms are `for (float t = 0.0f; t < 1.0f; t += 0.1f)`, `for (double x = start; x != end; x += step)`, and `while` or `do ... while` loops that increment a floating-point variable and compare it in the condition. It is common in sampling, interpolation, timing and calibration code. Loops that use an integer counter and compute a floating-point value from it inside the body, such as `t = i * 0.1f`, are not affected, nor are floating-point values that are tested in a loop condition but not stepped as the counter. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 14.1 (Required).
detection_methods: Search `for` statements whose first or third clause declares, assigns or increments a `float`, `double` or `long double` variable, or a typedef of one such as `float32_t`
Search `while` and `do ... while` loops whose condition compares a floating-point variable that is incremented or decremented in the body
Flag floating-point loop conditions using `==` or `!=`, which may never become true
Run a MISRA C checker and review loops manually where the counter's type comes through typedefs or other translation units, because identifying the loop counter is undecidable in general
potential_mitigations: Use an integer loop counter and derive the floating-point value from it inside the body, for example `t = start + (float)i * step`
Precompute the iteration count as an integer before the loop
Record a documented deviation only where the floating-point stepping is shown to terminate with a known iteration count on every target

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Loops must not count with floating-point variables

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 14.1 (Required; Undecidable; System). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Irregular For Loop with Hidden Counter Changes
description: The code writes a `for` statement whose clauses or body do not follow a simple single-counter pattern, such as changing the counter inside the body or testing objects the body modifies, so the number of iterations is hard to predict and verify.
extended_description: A `for` loop is easiest to review when one counter is set in the first clause, tested in the second and changed only in the third; deviating from this makes termination and bounds analysis much harder and is a frequent source of off-by-one and runaway loop defects. Violating shapes include assignments to the counter inside the body such as `i += 2;` or `i--` to retry an element, two counters stepped in the third clause like `i++, j--`, conditions with side effects like `for (i = 0; next(&i) < n; )`, conditions that test a variable other than the counter that the body changes, such as `for (i = 0; i < len; i++) { ... len--; }`, and third clauses that call functions or modify other objects. Functions called from the body count as part of the body if they change the counter or the objects tested. An empty `for (;;)` infinite loop is acceptable, as is a condition that also tests a Boolean flag set in the body to exit early. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 14.2 (Required).
detection_methods: For each `for` statement, identify the counter from the clauses and search the body for assignments, `++`, `--` or address-taking of that variable
Flag third clauses containing the comma operator, more than one modified object, or function calls
Flag second clauses containing side effects, or testing non-Boolean objects that the loop body or its callees modify
Run a MISRA C checker and review callees manually across translation units, because effects of called functions on the counter are undecidable in general
potential_mitigations: Restrict each `for` loop to one counter that is initialised in the first clause, compared in the second and stepped only in the third
Use a `while` loop when the iteration logic genuinely needs to change the index in the body or track several indices
Use a Boolean exit flag in the condition, or `break`, for early termination instead of altering the counter
Record a documented deviation only where the irregular loop is shown to terminate with a bounded iteration count

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: For loops follow a single predictable counter pattern

name: Control Condition That Is Always True or Always False
description: The code uses an `if`, `while`, `for`, `do ... while`, `switch` or `?:` condition whose value can never change, which usually signals a logic error and lets the compiler silently remove the code on the dead path, including defensive checks.
extended_description: A condition that is constant, or that the types involved make constant, means one branch can never run; the compiler may delete it, so error handling that the author believed was present is absent from the binary. Typical causes are comparisons that the operand type makes impossible, such as `if (u8 > 255)`, `if (unsigned_val < 0)` or `while (u >= 0)` with an unsigned `u`, tests repeated after a previous branch already fixed the outcome, `if (x = 0)` style mistakes, conditions built from macros that expand to constants, and `#define DEBUG 0` followed by `if (DEBUG)` that hides dead code. Deliberate infinite loops such as `while (1)`, `for (;;)` and `while (true)` in main loops or task bodies are acceptable, as is `do { ... } while (0)` used to wrap multi-statement macros. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 14.3 (Required).
detection_methods: Search controlling expressions of `if`, `while`, `for`, `do ... while`, `switch` and the first operand of `?:` for literal constants or macros that expand to constants, excluding deliberate infinite loops and `do ... while (0)` macro wrappers
Flag comparisons of unsigned variables with `< 0` or `>= 0`, and comparisons of narrow types against values outside their range
Check conditions that repeat or contradict an enclosing condition on the same variable, making the inner test fixed
Enable compiler warnings such as -Wtype-limits and -Wtautological-compare and run a MISRA C checker, then confirm by manual review because invariance can depend on values from other translation units
potential_mitigations: Correct the condition so it tests the intended variable and range, using types wide enough and signed where negative values are possible
Remove genuinely unreachable branches, or replace build-time switches like `if (DEBUG)` with preprocessor conditionals reviewed as configuration
Write intentional infinite loops in a single recognised form such as `for (;;)`
Record a documented deviation only where an invariant condition is required, for example for configuration that varies between builds

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Control conditions must be able to vary

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 14.3 (Required; Undecidable; System). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Non-Boolean Value Used as Branch or Loop Condition
description: The code tests an integer, pointer, floating-point value or assignment result directly in an `if`, `while`, `for` or `do ... while` condition instead of an explicit comparison, so the intended truth test is implicit and easy to get wrong.
extended_description: C treats any non-zero scalar as true, which lets code such as `if (count)`, `if (ptr)`, `while (n--)`, `if (flags & MASK)`, `if (strcmp(a, b))` or `if (f)` with a float compile without complaint, but the reader must infer whether a zero, a NULL or an error code was meant, and inverted logic like `if (!strcmp(...))` is a common source of bugs. Typical violating places are loop conditions over counters, pointer null checks, bitmask tests and calls returning `int` status codes. Conditions built from relational or equality operators (`==`, `!=`, `<`, `>`), logical operators (`&&`, `||`, `!` applied to Boolean operands), or variables of `bool` or a project Boolean typedef are acceptable. Use of `?:` or `switch` is outside this weakness. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 14.4 (Required).
detection_methods: Search `if`, `while`, `for` second clauses and `do ... while` conditions whose expression is a bare identifier, pointer, function call, arithmetic expression or bitwise `&` result without a comparison
Flag conditions such as `while (n--)`, `if (ptr)`, `if (!ptr)`, `if (strcmp(...))` and `if (status)` where the operand is not of Boolean type
Check project Boolean typedefs and macros to determine which variables are essentially Boolean before flagging
Run a MISRA C checker, since the construct is decidable within a single translation unit
potential_mitigations: Write explicit comparisons, for example `if (ptr != NULL)`, `if (count > 0U)`, `if ((flags & MASK) != 0U)` and `if (strcmp(a, b) == 0)`
Store status results in a variable and compare it against a named success or error constant
Use `bool` from <stdbool.h> or a project Boolean typedef for flags that are tested directly

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Branch and loop conditions must be genuinely Boolean

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 14.4 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Use of goto for Unstructured Control Transfer
description: The code transfers control with `goto`, which creates paths that bypass the normal block structure and make the function harder to review, test and analyse.
extended_description: Unrestricted jumps break the correspondence between source layout and execution order, so reviewers and tools find it harder to confirm that variables are initialised, resources released and loops bounded on every path. Typical uses in C are `goto cleanup;`, `goto err;` or `goto out;` error-handling ladders in drivers and parsers, `goto retry;` loops that jump backwards, and jumps out of nested loops. Any `goto` statement counts under this advisory guideline, even where it follows a well-understood cleanup idiom; teams often permit that idiom by deviation while relying on the stricter goto-direction and goto-scope weaknesses for the remaining cases. Labels used only by `switch` (`case` and `default`) and `break` or `continue` statements are not `goto` and do not count. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 15.1 (Advisory).
detection_methods: Search for the `goto` keyword and for identifier labels of the form `name:` at statement level
At each hit, note whether the jump is forward to a cleanup label, backward to form a loop, or out of nested loops
Check whether a documented project deviation covers single-exit cleanup patterns before reporting those
Run a MISRA C checker, since the construct is decidable within a single translation unit
potential_mitigations: Replace backward `goto` jumps with `while`, `do ... while` or `for` loops
Replace nested-loop escapes with a Boolean exit flag tested in the loop conditions, or move the loops into a helper function that returns
Restructure error handling with nested `if` blocks or helper functions that release resources
Record a documented deviation for a reviewed forward-only cleanup idiom where restructuring would reduce clarity

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Avoid goto altogether

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 15.1 (Advisory; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Backward goto Forming a Hidden Loop
description: The code uses `goto` to jump to a label that appears earlier in the function, creating a loop that is not expressed as a loop statement and whose termination is hard to verify.
extended_description: A backward jump produces iteration without any visible loop construct, so reviewers and analysis tools may miss that code repeats, and the loop bound, exit condition and re-initialisation of variables are easy to get wrong, leading to hangs or repeated side effects. Typical shapes are `retry: ... if (fail) goto retry;`, `again:` labels in I/O and lock acquisition code, and state machines where several `goto` statements jump back to a dispatch label near the top of the function. Forward jumps to a label later in the same function, such as a `goto cleanup;` to an exit section, are not this weakness, though they still fall under the general goto concern. Jumps between functions using `setjmp` and `longjmp` are a separate issue. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 15.2 (Required).
detection_methods: Search for `goto` statements and locate the matching label; flag any whose label appears on an earlier line in the same function
Look for label names such as `retry:`, `again:`, `restart:`, `loop:` and `top:` near the start of functions
Check each backward jump for a guaranteed bound on the number of repetitions
Run a MISRA C checker, since the construct is decidable within a single translation unit
potential_mitigations: Rewrite the backward jump as a `while`, `do ... while` or `for` loop with an explicit and bounded exit condition
Add a retry counter with a fixed maximum when converting retry patterns
Record a documented deviation only where a backward jump is shown to be bounded and clearer than the loop alternative

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: goto may only jump forward within its function

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 15.2 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: goto Jumping Into a Nested or Sibling Block
description: The code uses `goto` to reach a label inside a block that does not enclose the `goto`, such as the body of another `if`, loop or `switch` case, so control enters that block while skipping its declarations and setup.
extended_description: Jumping into the middle of a block bypasses the code that would normally run on entry, so local variables may be read before initialisation, loop counters may never be set and invariants of the target block are broken; jumping into the scope of a variable length array is undefined behaviour in C99. Violating shapes include a `goto` in one branch of an `if` aimed at a label inside the `else` branch, a `goto` from outside a loop to a label in the loop body, a jump from one `switch` case's braces into another case's braces, and a jump from before a nested `{ ... }` block into it. Jumps to a label in the same block as the `goto`, or in any block that encloses it, such as a function-level `cleanup:` label reached from inside nested loops, are not this weakness. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 15.3 (Required).
detection_methods: For each `goto`, find its target label and compare their enclosing compound statements; flag targets that sit inside a block not containing the `goto`
Check labels placed inside loop bodies, `if` or `else` branches and braced `switch` cases that are reached from outside those blocks
Check variables declared, and especially variable length arrays, between the start of the target block and the label for use without initialisation
Run a MISRA C checker, since the construct is decidable within a single translation unit
potential_mitigations: Move the label to the same block as the `goto` or to an enclosing block
Restructure the logic with flags, loops or helper functions so that blocks are always entered from the top
Record a documented deviation only where entry into the block is shown not to bypass any initialisation

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: goto targets must be in the same or an enclosing block

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 15.3 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Loop with Multiple break or goto Exits
description: The code leaves a single `while`, `do ... while` or `for` loop through two or more `break` or `goto` statements, so the loop has several hidden exit points and the state on exit is hard to reason about.
extended_description: Each extra exit adds a path on which the loop's post-conditions, such as an index value, a buffer length or a lock state, must be checked separately, and maintenance changes often update one exit but not the others. Typical shapes are search and parse loops with several `if (...) break;` lines, loops containing both a `break` and a `goto error;`, and polling loops that break out on timeout, on error and on success separately. Only exits that terminate the same loop count: a `break` that ends an inner `switch` or an inner nested loop belongs to that inner statement, and `continue` and `return` are not counted here. A loop with a single `break` or a single `goto` is acceptable. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 15.4 (Advisory).
detection_methods: For each loop, count the `break` statements that are not inside a nested `switch` or nested loop, plus any `goto` statements that jump to a label outside the loop
Flag loops where that count is two or more
Check the code after each such loop for assumptions about index or status values that hold only on some exit paths
Run a MISRA C checker, since the construct is decidable within a single translation unit
potential_mitigations: Combine the exit conditions into the loop's controlling expression or into a single Boolean done flag
Record the exit reason in a status variable and use one `break`, then branch on the status after the loop
Move the loop into a helper function that returns the result
Record a documented deviation where multiple exits are clearer and every exit path has been reviewed

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Limit each loop to one break or goto exit

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 15.4 (Advisory; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Function with Early or Multiple Return Points
description: The code returns from a function at several places, or from somewhere other than its final statement, so clean-up and post-condition code at the end can be skipped on some paths.
extended_description: When a function has more than one `return`, every exit must release locks, free memory, restore interrupt masks and set out-parameters, and later edits that add clean-up at the bottom frequently miss the earlier exits, causing leaks or stuck resources. Typical shapes are guard clauses such as `if (p == NULL) { return ERR; }` at the top of a function, `return` statements inside loops or `switch` cases, and error paths that return in the middle of a sequence of hardware or allocation steps. A single `return` as the last statement of the function, or a `void` function that simply falls off its closing brace, is compliant. This is an advisory, style-driven guideline; early returns that hold no resources carry lower risk but still count. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 15.5 (Advisory).
detection_methods: Count `return` statements in each function body and flag functions with more than one, or with a `return` that is not the final statement
Prioritise functions that acquire resources, such as calls to `malloc`, `fopen`, mutex lock functions or interrupt disable macros, before an early `return`
Check `return` statements inside loops and `switch` cases for skipped clean-up or unset out-parameters
Run a MISRA C checker, since the construct is decidable within a single translation unit
potential_mitigations: Store the result in a local status variable and return it once at the end of the function
Use nested `if` blocks or a status check before each step so that control always reaches the common exit
Record a documented deviation for simple parameter-validation guard clauses where no resources are held

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Prefer one return located at the function end

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 15.5 (Advisory; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Control Statement Body Without Braces
description: The code writes the body of an `if`, `else`, `while`, `do`, `for` or `switch` as a single statement without `{ }`, so later edits or a stray semicolon can change which statements are controlled without the change being visible.
extended_description: Without braces, indentation is the only cue to what a condition controls, so adding a second statement under an unbraced `if`, or a macro that expands to two statements, silently moves code out of the branch, and a semicolon right after the condition, as in `if (x);` or `while (busy);`, makes an empty body. Dangling `else` problems, where an `else` binds to an inner unbraced `if`, are another result. Typical violating lines look like `if (err) return;`, `for (i = 0; i < n; i++) sum += a[i];`, `else x = 0;` and `while (!ready) ;`. The `else if` chain is acceptable without braces around the inner `if`, and bodies already enclosed in `{ }`, including an empty `{ }`, are fine. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 15.6 (Required).
detection_methods: Search for `if (...)`, `else`, `while (...)`, `for (...)`, `do` and `switch (...)` that are not followed by `{`, other than `else if`
Flag a semicolon directly after a closing parenthesis of `if`, `while` or `for`
Check unbraced bodies that invoke function-like macros which might expand to multiple statements
Enable compiler warnings such as -Wmisleading-indentation and -Wempty-body and run a MISRA C checker
potential_mitigations: Enclose every control statement body in braces, even when it is a single statement or empty
Apply a code formatter or linter rule that inserts braces automatically
Wrap multi-statement macros in `do { ... } while (0)` as an additional safeguard

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Always brace loop and selection bodies

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 15.6 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Else-If Chain Without Final Else Branch
description: The code writes an `if ... else if` chain that stops without a closing `else`, so values not matched by any condition fall through silently with no handling or record that the case was considered.
extended_description: Chains of `else if` usually decode a state, command, mode or range; without a final `else`, an unexpected value such as a corrupted state variable or an out-of-range sensor reading is ignored, and reviewers cannot tell whether the omission was deliberate. Typical violating code tests a variable against several constants, such as `if (mode == A) { ... } else if (mode == B) { ... }`, or several ranges of a measurement, and then simply ends. The final `else` may contain error handling, a safe default, or just a comment explaining why nothing is needed. A lone `if` without any `else if` is not affected, nor is an `if ... else` pair. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 15.7 (Required).
detection_methods: Search for `else if` and follow each chain to its last branch; flag chains whose final branch is an `else if` rather than a plain `else`
Prioritise chains that decode state variables, message types, modes or value ranges
Check whether unmatched values should raise an error, set a safe state or be logged
Run a MISRA C checker, since the construct is decidable within a single translation unit
potential_mitigations: Add a final `else` that handles unexpected values, for example by reporting an error or entering a safe state
Where no action is needed, add a final `else` containing a comment that explains why
Consider a `switch` with a `default` label when the chain compares one variable against constants

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Close every else-if chain with a plain else

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 15.7 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Switch Statement With Irregular Body Structure
description: The code uses a switch statement whose body is not a plain sequence of case groups each ending in an unconditional exit, so control flow through the switch is hard to follow and easy to break during maintenance.
extended_description: C allows almost any statement to follow switch, including bodies with no braces, statements before the first case label, labels buried inside loops or if blocks, and clauses that run into each other. Such shapes compile but make it unclear which code runs for which value, and they defeat tools and reviewers that assume one clause per group of labels. In source this looks like a switch whose body is a single statement without braces, declarations or code placed between the opening brace and the first case, case or default labels inside nested blocks, or clauses that end without break, return, continue, goto or a call to a noreturn function. A conventional switch with braces, one or more labels per clause, a final break in each clause and a default clause is the expected shape and is not a finding. This entry is the umbrella for the narrower switch weaknesses on label placement, fall-through and default handling. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 16.1 (Required).
detection_methods: Search for the switch keyword and check that its body is a braced compound statement whose first item is a case or default label
Flag any statement, declaration or label inside the switch body that is not part of a case clause, such as code before the first case
Check each clause for a terminating break or equivalent unconditional exit before the next label
Run a MISRA C checker, since the shape of a switch body is decidable within one translation unit
potential_mitigations: Rewrite each switch as braces containing case groups, each group followed by its statements and a final break
Move setup code and declarations out of the switch body to before the switch statement
Where an irregular shape is genuinely required, record a documented deviation with the justification

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Switch bodies follow a single regular layout

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 16.1 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Case Label Nested Inside Inner Block of Switch
description: The code places a case or default label inside a loop, if statement or inner block within a switch body, so a jump into the middle of that construct can bypass its entry logic.
extended_description: Because case labels are just jump targets, C lets them appear inside any nested statement of the switch body, the best known example being Duff's device where labels sit inside a do-while loop. Jumping into a nested block skips its controlling expression, loop initialisation and any variable initialisers at the top of the block, so the code then runs with state that was never set up. In source, look for case or default appearing after an opening brace of an if, else, for, while or do inside a switch, or labels interleaved with loop bodies in hand-unrolled copy routines and protocol state machines.
