Labels that sit directly in the outermost compound statement of the switch are correct, and a nested switch with its own labels is not a finding for the outer switch. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 16.2 (Required).
detection_methods: Search for case and default labels and check that the innermost enclosing compound statement is the body of the owning switch
Look for unrolled copy loops and state machines in the style of Duff's device where labels sit inside do or while bodies
Flag case labels inside if or else blocks within a switch body
Run a MISRA C checker to confirm label nesting within the translation unit
potential_mitigations: Move all case and default labels to the top level of the switch body
Replace label-in-loop tricks such as Duff's device with a plain loop followed by a remainder loop
Where nesting is unavoidable in legacy code, record a documented deviation and review the skipped initialisation

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Switch labels belong at the top level of the switch body

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 16.2 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Switch Clause Falls Through to Next Case
description: The code has a switch clause containing statements that does not end with break or another unconditional exit, so execution silently continues into the following clause.
extended_description: C switch clauses do not end on their own; unless a clause finishes with break, return, continue, goto or a call that never returns, control drops into the next label's statements. A forgotten break is a classic cause of commands or state transitions running the wrong handler, often only for one rarely seen input value. In source this appears as a case group with one or more statements followed directly by another case or default label, sometimes marked with a fall-through comment or __attribute__((fallthrough)), and often in message dispatchers, state machines and command parsers. Several labels stacked together with no statements between them, such as case 1: case 2: shared handling, are not a finding. The last clause in the switch also needs an explicit break so that adding a new clause later cannot create fall-through. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 16.3 (Required).
detection_methods: For each case or default clause that contains statements, check that the last statement is break, return, continue, goto or a noreturn call
Search for comments such as fall through, FALLTHRU or fallthrough attributes, which mark deliberate fall-through that still breaks the rule
Check the final clause of each switch for a closing break
Compile with -Wimplicit-fallthrough or run a MISRA C checker and review each hit
potential_mitigations: End every non-empty switch clause with break, including the last clause
Factor shared handling into a function called from each clause rather than falling through
Group labels that need identical handling directly above a single statement list
Where intentional fall-through is retained, record a documented deviation

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Each non-empty switch clause ends with break

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 16.3 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Switch Statement Without Default Clause
description: The code has a switch statement with no default label, so an unexpected controlling value is silently ignored instead of being handled.
extended_description: When no case matches and there is no default, a C switch simply does nothing, which hides corrupted state variables, out-of-range sensor or message codes and enum values added later without updating every switch. A default clause gives a single place to report the error, enter a safe state or at least document that doing nothing is intended. In source, look for switch statements over state variables, message identifiers, error codes and enum types that contain only case labels, and for default clauses that exist but are empty without any comment or action. Switches over an enum where every enumerator is listed still need a default, because a corrupted or cast value can hold something else. A default that contains a defensive action, an assertion or a comment explaining why nothing is needed is acceptable. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 16.4 (Required).
detection_methods: Search for switch statements and flag any whose body contains no default label
Review default clauses that are empty or contain only break and check whether a comment or error handling is present
Pay particular attention to switches over enum types and state variables in state machines and protocol handlers
Use -Wswitch-default or a MISRA C checker to list switches missing a default
potential_mitigations: Add a default clause to every switch that reports, logs or recovers from an unexpected value
In safety-related state machines, have the default clause drive the system to a defined safe state
If no action is needed, add a default with a comment explaining why, or record a documented deviation

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Every switch provides a default path

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 16.4 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Default Label Placed in Middle of Switch
description: The code places the default label somewhere other than the first or last clause of a switch, so readers can miss it and later edits can introduce unintended fall-through around it.
extended_description: C lets the default label appear anywhere among the case labels, and the language still only takes it when nothing else matches. When it sits between ordinary cases, a reviewer scanning the switch can overlook the catch-all path, and clauses added above or below it can accidentally fall into or out of the default handling. In source this looks like case A: ... default: ... case B: ..., or default stacked together with other case labels in the middle of the list. A default label that is the very first or very last clause, including one combined with other labels in that first or last position, is acceptable. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 16.5 (Required).
detection_methods: Search for default labels and check whether any case label appears both before and after them in the same switch
Check switches where default shares a clause with other case labels and confirm that clause is first or last
Run a MISRA C checker to flag default label placement automatically
potential_mitigations: Move the default clause to the end of the switch, or to the start if that is the project convention
Keep a consistent default position across the code base so reviewers know where to look
Record a documented deviation if generated code cannot be reordered

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: The default clause sits at one end of the switch

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 16.5 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Degenerate Switch With Single Clause
description: The code uses a switch statement that contains only one clause, such as only a default or a single case group, so the switch adds no real branching and may hide a missing or deleted case.
extended_description: A switch whose body holds only default, or one case group with or without labels stacked together, behaves like an if statement or straight-line code dressed up as a multi-way branch. This usually indicates leftover code after cases were removed, a placeholder never completed, or a misunderstanding of what the switch handles, and it misleads readers into thinking several values are being distinguished. In source, look for switch (x) { default: ... } or switch (x) { case A: case B: ... break; } with no other clause, often in stubbed handlers and code generated from tables that became empty. A switch with at least two separate clauses, for example one case group plus a default, is not a finding. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 16.6 (Required).
detection_methods: Count the distinct clauses in each switch body and flag those with fewer than two
Look for switches whose only label is default, which are effectively unconditional blocks
Check stubbed or generated handler functions for single-clause switches left after cases were removed
Run a MISRA C checker to list these switches
potential_mitigations: Replace a single-clause switch with an if statement or plain code that states the intended condition
Restore any missing cases and add a default so the switch genuinely distinguishes values
Record a documented deviation for generated code where the clause count varies with configuration

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: A switch must offer at least two distinct clauses

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 16.6 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Switch Controlled by Boolean Expression
description: The code switches on an expression that is essentially Boolean, such as a comparison or logical test, so a two-way decision is written as a multi-way branch and labels other than true and false can never match.
extended_description: A comparison like a > b or a logical expression with &&, || or ! produces only 0 or 1, so using it as a switch controlling expression is really an if/else in disguise. It often signals a mistake, such as writing switch (x == MODE_A) when switch (x) was meant, in which case labels for other values are dead and the intended dispatch never happens. In source, look for switch whose parentheses contain a relational or equality operator, a logical operator, a bool variable, or a call returning bool. Switching on an integer, character or enum variable is the normal use and is not a finding. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 16.7 (Required).
detection_methods: Search for switch ( followed by an expression containing ==, !=, <, >, <=, >=, &&, || or ! at its top level
Flag switches on variables or function results declared as bool or _Bool
Check case labels in such switches for values other than 0 and 1, which indicate an intended different controlling expression
Run a MISRA C checker that applies the essential type model
potential_mitigations: Replace a switch on a Boolean condition with an if/else statement
If multi-way dispatch was intended, switch on the underlying integer or enum variable instead
Record a documented deviation only where a tool-generated pattern cannot be changed

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Switch selectors are not true/false expressions

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 16.7 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Use of Variadic Argument Facilities from stdarg.h
description: The code defines or processes variable argument lists with <stdarg.h> facilities such as va_list, va_start and va_arg, so argument types and counts are not checked and mismatches lead to undefined behaviour.
extended_description: With va_arg the callee must guess the type and number of the arguments it reads, and the compiler cannot check that the caller supplied matching values, so a wrong type, a missing argument or a promoted float read as float silently yields garbage or corrupts the stack. Calling va_arg on a va_list that has not been started, omitting va_end, or using a va_list after passing it to another function adds further undefined behaviour. In source, look for #include <stdarg.h>, va_list declarations, va_start, va_arg, va_copy and va_end, typically in home-grown logging, printf-like trace and debug helpers, and command formatting routines in drivers. Merely calling standard library functions such as printf is a separate concern; this weakness targets code that defines or forwards variadic argument lists itself. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 17.1 (Required).
detection_methods: Search for #include <stdarg.h> and for the tokens va_list, va_start, va_arg, va_copy and va_end
Check functions declared with an ellipsis parameter (...) in project code, especially logging and trace helpers
At each va_arg use, confirm how the expected type and argument count are determined and whether callers can violate it
Run a MISRA C checker, which can flag stdarg usage directly
potential_mitigations: Replace variadic functions with fixed-signature functions, one per argument shape
Pass a pointer to a struct or an array plus a count instead of a variable argument list
Where a printf-style logger must remain, confine it to one audited module, annotate it with format attributes and record a documented deviation
common_consequences: Integrity, Confidentiality; Read Memory, Modify Memory
Availability; DoS: Crash, Exit, or Restart

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Variable argument list machinery is avoided

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 17.1 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Direct or Indirect Function Recursion
description: The code contains a function that calls itself, either directly or through a chain of other functions, so stack usage cannot be bounded and deep inputs can overflow the stack.
extended_description: Each recursive call consumes another stack frame, and on embedded targets with small fixed stacks and no guard pages an unexpectedly deep recursion silently overwrites adjacent memory or triggers a hard fault. Static stack-usage analysis cannot give a worst case for recursive call graphs unless depth is provably bounded, which undermines timing and memory budgets in safety-related software. In source, look for functions that call themselves by name, mutual recursion such as parse_expr calling parse_term calling parse_expr, and recursion through function pointers or callbacks, common in tree walkers, parsers, JSON or TLV decoders and recursive sort routines. Iterative loops with an explicit bounded stack or work queue are not recursion. Detecting indirect recursion needs a call graph across all translation units. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 17.2 (Required).
detection_methods: Search each function body for a call to its own name
Build a whole-program call graph, including calls through function pointers where targets are known, and look for cycles
Review parsers, decoders, tree or list traversals and sort routines, which are common places for recursion
Use a stack-usage analyser or MISRA C checker with system-wide analysis, and manually review function-pointer calls it cannot resolve
potential_mitigations: Rewrite recursive algorithms as loops using an explicit, fixed-size stack or queue with an overflow check
Where recursion is retained, enforce and document a hard maximum depth and verify the worst-case stack usage
Record a documented deviation that includes the stack bound justification
common_consequences: Availability; DoS: Crash, Exit, or Restart

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Call graphs contain no cycles

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 17.2 (Required; Undecidable; System). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Call to Function With No Visible Declaration
description: The code calls a function for which no declaration or prototype is in scope, so a C90-style compiler assumes it returns int and takes unchecked arguments, causing wrong return values and argument passing.
extended_description: Under C90 rules a call to an undeclared identifier creates an implicit declaration returning int with no parameter checking; C99 removed this, but many embedded compilers still accept it with only a warning. If the real function returns a pointer, long, float or struct, or expects arguments of different types, the caller reads the wrong register or stack slot and passes mis-sized values, which is undefined behaviour and frequently truncates 64-bit pointers. In source this shows up as calls to library or project functions in files that lack the matching #include, such as using malloc without <stdlib.h>, memcpy without <string.h>, or a driver function whose header was not included, and as compiler diagnostics like implicit declaration of function. Calls through a function pointer of a declared type, and calls to functions declared earlier in the same file, are not findings. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 17.3 (Mandatory).
detection_methods: Compile with -Werror=implicit-function-declaration or the equivalent and list every implicit declaration diagnostic
For each source file, check that standard library calls such as malloc, free, memcpy, strlen and printf are matched by the correct #include
Look for project functions called in one file but declared only in another file's header that is not included
Run a MISRA C checker; this property is decidable within a translation unit
potential_mitigations: Include the header that declares every function before its first call
Give every external function a full prototype in a shared header included by both caller and definition
Build in C99 or later mode with implicit declarations treated as errors
common_consequences: Integrity, Confidentiality; Read Memory, Modify Memory
Availability; DoS: Crash, Exit, or Restart

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Functions are declared before they are called

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 17.3 (Mandatory; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Non-Void Function Exits Without Returning a Value
description: The code has a function declared to return a value in which some path reaches the closing brace or a bare return; statement, so the caller receives an indeterminate result.
extended_description: If a function with a non-void return type finishes without an expression in return and the caller uses the result, behaviour is undefined, and in practice the caller sees whatever was left in the return register. This typically arises where every branch of an if/else chain or switch returns except one, where an error path uses a bare return;, or where a loop is expected to always return from inside and the code after it is assumed unreachable. In source, look for functions returning int, bool, a status enum or a pointer whose last statement is not a return expression, and for return; inside such functions. void functions, and functions whose final statement is a call to a noreturn function such as abort or a reset routine, are not findings. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 17.4 (Mandatory).
detection_methods: Compile with -Wreturn-type or the equivalent and treat each warning as an error
For every non-void function, check that each path ends in return followed by an expression
Search for bare return; statements inside functions with a non-void return type
Check functions ending in a switch or if/else chain for a missing branch, and run a MISRA C checker
potential_mitigations: Add an explicit return with a defined value, such as an error status, at the end of every non-void function
Replace bare return; in non-void functions with a return of the appropriate error value
Use a single result variable initialised to a safe default and returned at the end of the function

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Value-returning functions return a value on every path

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 17.4 (Mandatory; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Array Argument Smaller Than Declared Parameter Size
description: The code declares a function parameter with an array type of a given size but passes arrays with fewer elements, so the callee may index past the end of the caller's object.
extended_description: A parameter written as uint8_t buf[16] is adjusted to a pointer, so the compiler does not enforce the size, yet both the author of the function and its readers assume that 16 elements are available. If a caller passes a shorter array, or a pointer into the middle of an array with fewer elements remaining, the callee's loops over the declared size read or write out of bounds. In source, look for prototypes and definitions with sized array parameters such as void crc(const uint8_t data[8]) and compare against the declared sizes of the arguments at every call site. Parameters declared as plain pointers or as unsized arrays like int a[] together with a separate length argument are not findings for this weakness. Verifying the property needs call sites across all translation units. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 17.5 (Advisory).
detection_methods: Search function declarations for parameters of the form type name[N] with a constant size
At each call site, compare the argument's array size or the elements remaining after a pointer offset with N
Check callers that pass a pointer to a smaller buffer, a struct member array, or buf + offset
Use a MISRA C checker with system-wide analysis and manually review calls through pointers it cannot size
potential_mitigations: Ensure every argument for a sized array parameter has at least the declared number of elements
Prefer an explicit element-count parameter or a struct that wraps a fixed-size array so the size is checked
Add assertions or static checks on buffer sizes at call boundaries, or record a documented deviation
common_consequences: Integrity, Confidentiality; Read Memory, Modify Memory
Availability; DoS: Crash, Exit, or Restart

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Array arguments match the size a parameter declares

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 17.5 (Advisory; Undecidable; System). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Static Keyword in Array Parameter Brackets
description: The code declares an array parameter with static inside the brackets, such as int a[static 10], so the compiler may assume at least that many valid elements and any caller passing fewer triggers undefined behaviour.
extended_description: The C99 form type name[static N] promises the compiler that every call supplies a non-null pointer to at least N elements, and optimisers are allowed to rely on that promise, for example by removing null checks or reading ahead. The promise is not enforced at call sites in other translation units, so a shorter buffer or a null pointer leads to undefined behaviour that the optimiser can make worse. In source, look for the static keyword appearing inside square brackets in function prototypes and definitions, often in performance-oriented utility or DSP code. Ordinary uses of static for file-scope or function-scope storage, and sized array parameters without static, are not findings. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 17.6 (Mandatory).
detection_methods: Search for the pattern [static inside function parameter lists, for example with a regular expression such as \[\s*static
Check headers as well as source files, since the qualifier usually appears in shared prototypes
Run a MISRA C checker; this property is decidable within a translation unit
potential_mitigations: Remove static from inside array parameter brackets and declare the parameter as a pointer or unsized array
Pass an explicit length and validate it, or check pointers for null, inside the function
common_consequences: Integrity, Confidentiality; Read Memory, Modify Memory

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: No minimum-size static qualifier on array parameters

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 17.6 (Mandatory; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Discarded Return Value of Non-Void Function
description: The code calls a function that returns a value and ignores that value without an explicit (void) cast, so error statuses and results are silently lost.
extended_description: Many C functions report failure only through their return value, so calling them as a bare expression statement means a failed write, a short read, a full queue or a rejected configuration goes unnoticed and the program continues with wrong assumptions. In source this looks like statements such as HAL_UART_Transmit(&h, buf, n, 10);, fclose(fp);, snprintf(buf, sizeof buf, ...);, memcpy-like helpers returning status, or project functions returning a status enum, called on their own line with no assignment, condition or (void) cast. It is especially significant in driver initialisation, flash and EEPROM writes, communication stacks and RTOS calls such as queue sends and semaphore takes. A call explicitly cast to (void) documents that the value is deliberately unused and is not a finding, nor are calls to void functions. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 17.7 (Required).
detection_methods: Find expression statements consisting only of a call to a function whose declared return type is not void
Prioritise calls to I/O, memory, flash, communication, RTOS and HAL functions that return a status code
Check whether ignored values are error indicators, such as negative returns, NULL or non-OK status enums
Compile with warn_unused_result attributes or -Wunused-result where available and run a MISRA C checker
potential_mitigations: Assign the result and test it, handling failure explicitly on every call that can fail
Where the value is genuinely not needed, cast the call to (void) and add a comment explaining why
Mark project status-returning functions with a warn_unused_result attribute so the compiler flags ignored results
Record a documented deviation for specific library functions whose result is never meaningful in the project
common_consequences: Availability; DoS: Crash, Exit, or Restart

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Returned values are used or explicitly discarded

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 17.7 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Assignment to Function Parameter Inside Function Body
description: The code assigns to or increments a function parameter within the function, so later code in the function no longer sees the value the caller passed and readers may wrongly believe the caller's variable changes.
extended_description: C passes arguments by value, so changing a parameter only changes the local copy; developers sometimes expect the caller's variable to be updated, and later edits to the function can use the parameter assuming it still holds the original argument. In source, look for parameters used as working variables, such as len-- or ptr++ in copy loops, count = count * 2, or clamping like if (x > MAX) { x = MAX; } applied to the parameter itself, common in buffer and string helpers. Writing through a pointer parameter, as in *out = value or ptr[i] = 0, modifies the pointed-to object and is not a finding; only changes to the parameter variable itself count. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 17.8 (Advisory).
detection_methods: For each function, find assignment, compound assignment, ++ and -- operators whose operand is a parameter name
Check pointer parameters advanced in loops, such as src++ or dst += n, inside copy and parse helpers
Distinguish modifying the parameter from writing through it, and only flag the former
Run a MISRA C checker, and review cases where macros hide parameter updates
potential_mitigations: Copy the parameter into a local working variable and modify the local instead
Declare scalar and pointer parameters const where they should not change, for example const uint8_t *const p
Record a documented deviation where a project coding style deliberately reuses parameters

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Parameters are treated as read-only inputs

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 17.8 (Advisory; Undecidable; System). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Pointer Arithmetic Leaving Bounds of Array Object
description: The code adds to, subtracts from or indexes a pointer so that the result points outside the array it was derived from, beyond the one-past-the-end position, which is undefined behaviour even before any dereference.
extended_description: C only defines pointer arithmetic within an array object and the position just past its last element; computing anything further away, or before the first element, is undefined behaviour, and dereferencing the one-past-the-end pointer is also invalid. Compilers may optimise on the assumption that such pointers never exist, so even a bounds check written as if (p + n > end) can be removed or misbehave. In source, look for expressions like buf + len, &arr[i], p[idx], p++ in loops, and end - 1 on possibly empty buffers, where the offset comes from a length field in a message, a loop counter with an off-by-one condition such as i <= N, or arithmetic on header offsets in parsers. Indexing that is provably within the declared array size, and pointers compared against a correctly computed end pointer, are not findings. Proving the property usually requires tracing lengths across functions and translation units. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 18.1 (Required).
detection_methods: Find array indexing and pointer offsets whose index comes from external data, message length fields or loop counters and check them against the array bound
Check loop conditions using <= with an array length, and decrements such as p - 1 or end - 1 where the buffer may be empty
Review bounds checks written as pointer comparisons, such as p + n > end, which themselves form out-of-range pointers
Use a MISRA C checker, sanitisers such as AddressSanitizer in host tests, and manual review across functions because the property is undecidable
potential_mitigations: Validate indices and lengths against the array size before forming the pointer, using integer comparisons such as n <= (size_t)(end - p)
Use index-based access with explicit bounds checks instead of free-running pointer increments
Fix off-by-one loop conditions so the index stays strictly below the element count
Record a documented deviation only for audited low-level code with a proven bound
common_consequences: Integrity, Confidentiality; Read Memory, Modify Memory
Availability; DoS: Crash, Exit, or Restart

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Derived pointers stay within their source array

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 18.1 (Required; Undecidable; System). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Subtraction of Pointers Into Different Objects
description: The code subtracts one pointer from another when the two do not point into the same array, so the resulting distance is undefined and any length or index computed from it is meaningless.
extended_description: C defines p - q only when both pointers refer to elements of the same array or one past its end; for unrelated objects, such as two separate buffers, two struct instances or a stack variable and a heap block, the result is undefined and can differ between builds and memory layouts. This often appears when code computes a length as end - start where start and end were obtained from different allocations or different calls, when it measures the gap between two global variables, or when it uses pointer difference to locate a struct from a member pointer without offsetof. In source, look for subtraction expressions whose operands are both pointers and trace where each operand came from, especially in buffer managers, memory pools and linked-list code. Subtracting two pointers that both derive from the same array, such as cursor - buf_start in a parser, is valid. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 18.2 (Required).
detection_methods: Search for binary - between two pointer-typed operands, and for ptrdiff_t results
For each hit, trace both operands back to their base object and confirm they derive from the same array
Check memory pool, allocator and container code that computes offsets between separately allocated blocks or global objects
Run a MISRA C checker with system-wide analysis and review undecidable cases manually
potential_mitigations: Track lengths and offsets as integer counts alongside the base pointer instead of subtracting unrelated pointers
Use offsetof to relate a struct member to its containing struct
Where pool addresses must be compared numerically, convert through uintptr_t in one audited place and record a documented deviation
common_consequences: Integrity, Confidentiality; Read Memory, Modify Memory

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Pointer differences only within one array

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 18.2 (Required; Undecidable; System). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Relational Comparison of Pointers to Unrelated Objects
description: The code compares pointers with <, <=, > or >= when they do not point into the same object, so the outcome is undefined and range or ordering checks built on it cannot be trusted.
extended_description: C only defines ordering between pointers to elements of the same array, members of the same struct, or one past the end of an array; comparing addresses of separate objects is undefined behaviour and optimisers may fold such comparisons to constants. Code commonly does this to test whether a pointer lies inside a buffer or memory region, as in if (p >= pool_start && p < pool_end) where p may come from elsewhere, to sort or order unrelated objects by address, or to detect stack direction or overlap between two buffers before memmove-style copies. In source, look for relational operators whose operands are both pointers, and for macros that implement is-in-range or overlap checks on arbitrary pointers. Equality comparisons with == and != are not covered, and relational comparisons between pointers that provably derive from the same array, such as while (p < end) in a loop over one buffer, are valid. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 18.3 (Required).
detection_methods: Search for <, <=, > and >= where both operands are pointer expressions
For each hit, confirm both operands derive from the same array or struct object
Review is-in-region, overlap and address-sorting helpers in allocators, memory pools and copy routines
Run a MISRA C checker and review cross-function pointer provenance manually because the property is undecidable
potential_mitigations: Restrict relational pointer comparisons to pointers into the same array, such as a cursor and its end pointer
Track membership with indices or explicit ownership information rather than comparing raw addresses
Where an address-range check is unavoidable, perform it on uintptr_t values in one audited function and record a documented deviation

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Pointer ordering only within a single object

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 18.3 (Required; Undecidable; System). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Explicit Additive Arithmetic on Pointer Values
description: The code moves pointers with +, -, += or -= instead of array indexing, which obscures which element is accessed and makes out-of-bounds pointer creation easier to miss in review.
extended_description: Expressions such as p + i, p += len or p - 4 compute addresses implicitly scaled by the element size, and when chained through a function they hide the base array and the offset, which is where off-by-one and wrong-scaling bugs typically live. Array subscript notation like buf[i] keeps the base and index visible and makes it easier for reviewers and tools to check against the array bound. In source, look for arithmetic operators applied to pointer variables in parsers, packet builders, ring buffers and string handling, for example hdr = (struct hdr *)(pkt + off) or out += n after a write. Increment and decrement with ++ and -- are not covered by this weakness, nor is subtraction of two pointers into the same array to get a count, nor array indexing itself. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 18.4 (Advisory).
detection_methods: Search for +, -, += and -= where one operand has pointer type and the other is an integer
Check casts combined with pointer arithmetic, such as (uint8_t *)p + offset, for wrong scaling
Review parsers, packet and frame builders, and ring buffer code where pointers are advanced by computed lengths
Run a MISRA C checker; the property is decidable within a translation unit
potential_mitigations: Use array indexing such as &buf[i] or buf[i] instead of buf + i
Keep a base pointer and an integer offset, and bounds-check the offset before indexing
Record a documented deviation for audited low-level code where pointer stepping is clearer
common_consequences: Integrity, Confidentiality; Read Memory, Modify Memory

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Prefer subscripts over additive pointer operators

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 18.4 (Advisory; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Excessive Levels of Pointer Indirection in Declarations
description: The code declares objects or parameters with three or more levels of pointer indirection, such as int ***p, so the meaning and lifetime of each level become hard to follow and dereference errors become likely.
extended_description: Each extra level of indirection adds another pointer that may be null, dangling or pointing to the wrong level, and declarations like char ***argvp or struct node ****table are hard to read correctly, especially when combined with arrays and const qualifiers. Mistakes show up as dereferencing the wrong number of times, allocating the wrong size for an intermediate level, or freeing only part of a multi-level structure. In source, look for declarations with three or more consecutive asterisks, typedefs that hide pointer levels and are then combined with further *, and parameters like type **arr[] which also amount to three levels. One or two levels, such as char **argv or an out-parameter of type T **, are acceptable. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 18.5 (Advisory).
detection_methods: Search declarations and parameter lists for three or more consecutive * tokens
Expand pointer typedefs and check whether further * or [] in parameters push the total past two levels
Review dynamic multi-dimensional array allocation and matrix code, where deep indirection is common
Run a MISRA C checker to count indirection levels after typedef expansion
potential_mitigations: Wrap intermediate levels in structs with named fields so each level has clear meaning
Use contiguous arrays with computed indices instead of arrays of pointers to arrays of pointers
Record a documented deviation where an external API forces deeper indirection

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Keep pointer indirection to at most two levels

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 18.5 (Advisory; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Address of Automatic Object Escapes Its Lifetime
description: The code stores or returns the address of a local variable with automatic storage so that the pointer is still reachable after the variable's block ends, leaving a dangling pointer to reused stack memory.
extended_description: When a function returns or a block closes, its automatic variables cease to exist and any pointer to them becomes indeterminate; later reads see whatever the next call placed in that stack slot and later writes corrupt unrelated frames. Typical forms are return &local; or return local_array;, assigning &local to a global, static or struct field that outlives the function, registering a stack buffer with a DMA engine, ISR, callback list or RTOS queue that uses it later, and keeping a pointer to a variable declared inside a loop or inner block after that block ends. In source, look for the & operator applied to locals and for local array names flowing into return statements, global assignments or registration and send calls. Passing the address of a local to a function that only uses it during the call is fine, and so are locals declared static. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 18.6 (Required).
detection_methods: Search for return statements whose expression is &local or the name of a local array
Find assignments of &local or local array names to globals, static variables, heap structs or output parameters
Check registrations with DMA, interrupt, callback, timer and RTOS queue APIs that are given pointers to stack buffers
Compile with -Wreturn-local-addr and -Wdangling-pointer where available, and run a MISRA C checker with manual review across functions
potential_mitigations: Return data by value, or have the caller supply the buffer as a parameter
Use static or heap storage with a defined lifetime for data that must outlive the function
Ensure asynchronous consumers such as DMA or queues finish with a buffer before its owning function returns, and clear stored pointers when the object goes out of scope
common_consequences: Integrity, Confidentiality; Read Memory, Modify Memory
Availability; DoS: Crash, Exit, or Restart

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Stack object addresses must not outlive the object

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 18.6 (Required; Undecidable; System). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Struct Declared With Flexible Array Member
description: The code declares a struct whose last member is an array with empty brackets, so the struct's real size depends on how it was allocated and copies, sizeof and assignments silently omit the trailing data.
extended_description: A C99 flexible array member such as uint8_t data[]; at the end of a struct has no storage of its own, so the struct only works when allocated with malloc(sizeof(struct s) + n) and the extra length is tracked separately. Declaring such a struct on the stack or statically, copying it by assignment or memcpy(sizeof), or computing the allocation size wrongly leads to reads and writes past the allocated block. In source, look for struct definitions ending in a member declared with [], and the older pre-C99 idiom of a trailing array of size 0 or 1 used the same way, typically in message, packet and variable-length record types. Arrays with a fixed constant size and pointer members to separately allocated buffers are not findings. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 18.7 (Required).
detection_methods: Search struct definitions for a final member declared with empty brackets, such as type name[];
Also look for trailing arrays declared [0] or [1] that are used as variable-length tails
At each allocation of such a struct, check the size calculation and that the length is stored and checked on access
Run a MISRA C checker; the declaration is decidable within a translation unit
potential_mitigations: Replace the flexible array member with a fixed-size array sized for the maximum supported length
Use a pointer member and a length field referring to a separately managed buffer
Where the layout is fixed by an external protocol, isolate access behind bounds-checked helpers and record a documented deviation
common_consequences: Integrity, Confidentiality; Read Memory, Modify Memory

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Structs avoid open-ended trailing arrays

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 18.7 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Variable-Length Array Sized at Run Time
description: The code declares an array whose size is a non-constant expression evaluated at run time, so stack consumption is unbounded and a zero, negative or large size causes undefined behaviour or stack overflow.
extended_description: A C99 variable-length array such as uint8_t buf[len]; is allocated on the stack with no way to report failure, so a large len silently overruns the stack, and a size that evaluates to zero or a negative value is undefined behaviour. VLAs also make worst-case stack analysis impossible and change sizeof into a run-time operation. In source, look for local array declarations whose bracket expression involves a parameter, a variable, a struct field or a function call, and for VLA types in parameter lists or typedefs such as void f(int n, int m[n]). Arrays sized by an integer constant expression, an enum constant or a #define macro that expands to a constant are not findings; note that a const int variable is not a constant expression in C, so int a[N] where N is const int is still a VLA. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 18.8 (Required).
detection_methods: Search local array declarations for bracket expressions that reference variables, parameters or function calls
Check arrays sized by const-qualified variables, which are still variable-length in C
Inspect parameter lists and typedefs for variably modified types such as int a[n] or int (*p)[n]
Compile with -Wvla or -Werror=vla, or run a MISRA C checker, since the construct is decidable
potential_mitigations: Declare arrays with a compile-time maximum size and check the run-time length against it
Use static or pre-allocated pool buffers sized for the worst case
Build with VLAs disabled, for example by defining the compiler to reject them, so new uses are caught
common_consequences: Availability; DoS: Crash, Exit, or Restart
Integrity, Confidentiality; Read Memory, Modify Memory

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Array sizes are fixed at compile time

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 18.8 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Copy Between Partially Overlapping Memory Regions
description: The code assigns or copies an object into storage that partially overlaps the source object, so the bytes written depend on copy order and the result is undefined.
extended_description: The C standard leaves the result undefined when the source and destination of an assignment or a memcpy, strcpy, strncpy, strcat, sprintf or similar library copy share some but not all of their bytes; an optimised memcpy may copy forwards, backwards or in words and silently corrupt data. In source this typically looks like memcpy(&buf[1], &buf[0], n) or memcpy(p + off, p, len) used to shift elements within one array, ring buffer or packet buffer, strcpy(s, s + k) to strip a prefix, sprintf(buf, "%s...", buf) that appends to itself, or assigning one union member from a different, differently sized member of the same union object. Overlap is often hidden behind two pointer parameters that callers sometimes pass aliased pointers into, so check call sites as well as the copy itself. Copying with memmove, which is defined for overlapping regions, and plain assignment between two lvalues that designate exactly the same object with compatible types are not defects. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 19.1 (Mandatory).
detection_methods: Search for memcpy, strcpy, strncpy, strcat, strncat, sprintf and snprintf calls whose source and destination are derived from the same array, buffer or base pointer with different offsets
Check sprintf or snprintf calls where the destination buffer also appears among the format arguments
Inspect functions that take separate source and destination pointers and copy between them, then review callers for arguments that can alias the same buffer
Find assignments of the form u.a = u.b where a and b are different members of the same union object
Run a MISRA C checker or alias analysis, then confirm reports manually because overlap across calls is undecidable
potential_mitigations: Use memmove instead of memcpy whenever the source and destination might share storage
Copy through a separate temporary buffer when shifting or rearranging data within one array
Declare non-aliasing pointer parameters with restrict only where every caller is guaranteed to pass disjoint buffers, and document that precondition
Remove self-referential sprintf calls by formatting into a separate buffer and then copying the result

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: No copying between storage that overlaps

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 19.1 (Mandatory; Undecidable; System). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Union Used to Reinterpret Stored Data
description: The code declares a union and writes one member while reading another, so the value obtained depends on padding, alignment, byte order and bit layout chosen by the implementation.
extended_description: When a union member is stored and a different member is then read, C gives either an unspecified value (when the member read is larger than the one written) or an implementation-defined one, and the result also depends on endianness, structure padding inside members and bit-field allocation. In embedded and protocol code unions commonly appear as type-punning helpers such as a union of uint32_t and uint8_t[4] for byte extraction, a union of float and uint32_t for bit inspection, register overlay unions in hardware abstraction headers, and tagged variant records in message parsers. These constructs behave differently when the code is moved to another compiler or CPU and are easy to read with the wrong tag. The rule is advisory and flags every use of the union keyword, but the highest-risk files are those that write through one member and read through another; a union read back only through the member last written is well defined. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 19.2 (Advisory).
detection_methods: Search for the union keyword in typedefs, declarations and anonymous members in .c and .h files
At each union, find code that assigns one member and later reads a different member of the same object, especially integer to byte array or float to integer pairs
Check tagged unions for reads of a member that do not first verify the discriminator field
Run a MISRA C checker to list every union declaration
potential_mitigations: Replace type-punning unions with explicit shifts and masks for byte extraction, or memcpy into a separate object of the target type
Use separate structures or a struct with a validated discriminator instead of overlaying unrelated data
Where a union is unavoidable, such as a register overlay, record a documented deviation that states the compiler, endianness and padding assumptions and add static assertions on sizes

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Avoid unions as a way of overlaying data

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 19.2 (Advisory; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Header Inclusion After Declarations or Code
description: The code places a #include directive after declarations, definitions or statements in a file, so headers may be pulled into the middle of a construct or after library facilities are already used.
extended_description: Including a standard header inside a declaration or function body, or using a library macro or function before its header has been included, is undefined behaviour, and scattered includes make it hard to see which declarations a file depends on. In source this looks like a #include line that follows variable definitions, function bodies or type declarations, an include placed inside a function or between the type and name of a declaration, or generated table files pulled in with #include "table.inc" partway through a source file. The check is applied to the raw file before preprocessing, so only preprocessor directives and comments may appear before each #include. Includes at the top of the file after #define, #ifndef guard or #pragma lines, and include guards themselves, are not defects. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 20.1 (Advisory).
detection_methods: For every .c and .h file, find #include lines that appear after the first non-directive, non-comment token in the file
Search for #include inside function bodies, initialiser lists, struct or enum definitions and array initialisers
Check uses of standard library names such as NULL, size_t, memcpy or printf that occur above the corresponding #include
Run a MISRA C checker, which can decide this per file
potential_mitigations: Move all #include directives to the top of the file, after any header guard and configuration #define lines
Replace mid-file inclusion of data or table fragments with a proper header that declares the data, or record a documented deviation for an established X-macro pattern

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Keep includes ahead of all code in a file

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 20.1 (Advisory; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Special Characters in Included Header Name
description: The code names a header in a #include directive using a quote, apostrophe, backslash or comment sequence, so the header name has undefined meaning and may resolve differently between toolchains.
extended_description: Header names are a special preprocessing token, and the C standard does not define what happens when they contain an apostrophe, a backslash, the comment openers /* or //, or (inside angle brackets) a double quote. The most common real case is a Windows-style path such as #include "drivers\uart.h" or #include <..\config\board.h>, which may build on one compiler and fail or pick another file on a different host or cross compiler. Generated include lines, vendor SDK headers ported from Windows tools and paths containing apostrophes in folder names are typical places to look. Forward slashes in paths, such as #include "hal/gpio.h", are acceptable, as are ordinary letters, digits, dots, underscores and hyphens. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 20.2 (Required).
detection_methods: Search #include lines for a backslash, apostrophe, /* or // between the delimiters, for example with a regex such as #\s*include\s*[<"][^>"]*(\\|'|/\*|//)
Search angle-bracket includes for an embedded double quote
Review generated or vendor-supplied headers and build scripts that emit include lines with host path separators
Run a MISRA C checker, which can decide this per file
potential_mitigations: Use forward slashes as path separators in every #include directive
Rename headers or directories so that their names contain only letters, digits, underscores, hyphens, dots and slashes
Prefer adding include directories to the compiler search path over embedding long relative paths in source; a documented deviation is possible but rarely justified

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Header names free of quote, backslash and comment characters

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 20.2 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Malformed Operand in Include Directive
description: The code writes a #include directive whose operand, after macro expansion, is neither a single <name> nor a single "name" token, so the file actually included is undefined.
extended_description: A #include must, once any macros in it are replaced, reduce to exactly one header name in angle brackets or double quotes; anything else, including trailing tokens, is undefined behaviour and compilers disagree on how to handle it. Look for include lines with a bare identifier or path such as #include config.h, computed includes such as #include BOARD_HEADER where the macro expands to an unquoted name or to two adjacent string literals like "base" ".h" (string concatenation happens after preprocessing, so this does not form one name), and include lines with stray tokens after the closing delimiter. Computed includes are common in board support packages, port layers and multi-target configuration headers. A macro that expands to one complete quoted or angle-bracketed name, such as #define CFG_HDR "cfg_stm32.h" followed by #include CFG_HDR, and paths with directories inside the quotes, are fine. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 20.3 (Required).
detection_methods: Search for #include lines whose first operand token is not < or " and expand the macro used to confirm it yields exactly one header name
Check computed include macros for definitions that build the name from adjacent string literals, ## pasting or unquoted identifiers
Look for extra tokens after the closing > or " on #include lines
Run a MISRA C checker, which evaluates the directive after macro replacement
potential_mitigations: Write each #include with a single literal "name" or <name>
Where a header must be selected by configuration, define the macro as one complete quoted header name, or use #if and #elif branches each containing a literal #include
Remove trailing tokens and comments that are not separated as proper comments from include lines

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Include operand must reduce to one header name

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 20.3 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Language Keyword Redefined as Macro
description: The code uses #define to give a C keyword a new meaning, so readers and tools misinterpret the code and any standard header included afterwards has undefined behaviour.
extended_description: Redefining a keyword silently changes the meaning of every later use of that word, which defeats code review, and the C standard makes it undefined to include a standard header while such a macro is in force. Typical shapes are #define int long, #define const, #define volatile, #define inline or #define static used to switch linkage for unit testing, #define while(c) for(;c;), #define bool or #define true in pre-C99 portability headers, and macros named after compiler extension keywords such as __asm, __interrupt or __far. These are most often found in compiler abstraction headers, porting layers and test harness shims. Macros with ordinary identifier names that expand to keyword sequences, such as #define FOREVER for(;;) or #define STATIC static, are not defects. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 20.4 (Required).
detection_methods: Search for #define and -D compiler options whose macro name is a C keyword, for example with a regex such as #\s*define\s+(auto|break|case|char|const|continue|default|do|double|else|enum|extern|float|for|goto|if|inline|int|long|register|restrict|return|short|signed|sizeof|static|struct|switch|typedef|union|unsigned|void|volatile|while|_Bool)\b
Also check for macros named after compiler-specific extension keywords used by the project toolchain
Inspect compiler abstraction, portability and unit test shim headers, which commonly contain such redefinitions
Run a MISRA C checker, which can decide this per translation unit
potential_mitigations: Use a distinct macro name such as STATIC_FN or TEST_VISIBLE instead of redefining a keyword
Replace keyword-replacing typedef style macros with real typedefs from <stdint.h> and <stdbool.h>
Where a legacy toolchain requires a keyword to be stubbed out, isolate it in one configuration header and record a documented deviation

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Do not use keywords as macro names

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 20.4 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Macro Removed with Undef Directive
description: The code removes macro definitions with #undef, so the meaning of a macro name depends on its position in the translation unit and is hard to establish by reading.
extended_description: Once macros can be undefined and redefined, the same name may mean different things in different parts of a file, and a reader or reviewer cannot tell which definition applies at a given line without tracing every preceding directive and include. Common shapes are #undef followed by a new #define of the same name to override a value from a vendor header, #undef of a qualifier or attribute macro such as volatile wrappers part way through a file, and X-macro tables that #define and #undef an entry macro around repeated #include of a list file. Hidden removal of a qualifier macro can change code generation, for example dropping volatile from a polled register access. The rule is advisory, so well-understood idioms such as X-macros can be handled by deviation; files with no #undef are unaffected. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 20.5 (Advisory).
detection_methods: Search .c and .h files for #undef directives
At each hit, check whether the macro is later redefined with a different value or whether code below depends on its absence
Pay particular attention to #undef of macros that expand to qualifiers, attributes, sizes or configuration switches
Run a MISRA C checker to list every #undef
potential_mitigations: Give each macro a single definition for the whole program and choose distinct names instead of undefining and redefining
Fix conflicting definitions at their source, such as configuration headers, rather than overriding them with #undef
Record a documented deviation for recognised patterns such as X-macro tables and keep the #define and #undef pair adjacent

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Avoid undefining macros

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 20.5 (Advisory; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Preprocessor Directive Inside Macro Invocation Arguments
description: The code places #if, #ifdef, #else, #endif, #define or similar directive lines inside the argument list of a function-like macro call, so the expansion is undefined and may differ between compilers.
extended_description: Function-like macro arguments are collected before directives would normally be processed, and the C standard does not define what happens when a line starting with # appears among them; one compiler may honour the conditional, another may stringify it, and another may reject it. This often appears when a macro that wraps a function call, such as a logging, assert, trace or register-write macro, has its arguments selected with #ifdef and #else blocks inside the parentheses, for example LOG( on one line followed by #ifdef DEBUG and alternative strings. It is also a risk when a standard library function is implemented as a macro, for example memcpy, printf or assert, and conditional blocks are placed inside its argument list. Conditional directives placed around the whole macro call, outside its parentheses, are not defects. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 20.6 (Required).
detection_methods: Search for lines beginning with # that occur between the opening and closing parentheses of a function-like macro invocation
Check multi-line calls to logging, assert, trace and register access macros and to library functions that may be macros, such as printf, memcpy and assert
Run a MISRA C checker, which can decide this per translation unit
potential_mitigations: Move the conditional directives outside the macro call and write a complete call in each branch
Select the varying argument into a separate macro or const variable before the call, then pass that single name
Treat this as a defect to fix rather than deviate, since the behaviour is undefined

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: No directive lines within macro argument lists

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 20.6 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Unparenthesised Macro Parameter in Expression Expansion
description: The code defines a function-like macro that inserts a parameter into an expression without surrounding parentheses, so an argument containing operators binds to neighbouring operators and computes the wrong value.
extended_description: Macro expansion is textual, so if a parameter is pasted next to an operator without parentheses, an argument such as a + b or x << 2 is regrouped by operator precedence after expansion and the macro silently yields a different result. Typical defective shapes are #define SQUARE(x) x * x, #define BIT(n) 1u << n, #define REG_ADDR(base, off) base + off, #define MIN(a, b) a < b ? a : b and #define SCALE(v) v / 10, which are common in register access headers, unit conversion macros and bit mask helpers. A related problem is the whole replacement list not being parenthesised, as in #define DOUBLE(x) (x) + (x) used inside a larger expression. Parameters used purely as operands of # or ##, as structure member names, as type names, or passed straight to another macro that parenthesises them do not need extra parentheses. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 20.7 (Required).
detection_methods: Search #define lines with a parameter list and check each parameter use in the replacement text that is adjacent to an arithmetic, shift, bitwise, comparison, logical or conditional operator for enclosing parentheses
Check bit mask, register offset, min and max, and unit conversion macros in hardware abstraction and configuration headers
Review call sites that pass compound expressions to such macros to see whether the expanded result changes meaning
Run a MISRA C checker, which can decide this per translation unit
potential_mitigations: Wrap every expression use of a macro parameter in parentheses and wrap the entire replacement list as well, for example #define SQUARE(x) ((x) * (x))
Replace function-like macros with static inline functions where the toolchain supports them, which also gives type checking
Where a parameter is intentionally not an expression, such as a member name, record why it is left unparenthesised in a comment

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Parenthesise macro parameters used as expressions

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 20.7 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Non-Boolean Conditional Compilation Expression
description: The code controls #if or #elif with an expression that can evaluate to a value other than 0 or 1, so a configuration value is treated as a truth test and code may be enabled or excluded unintentionally.
extended_description: The preprocessor treats any non-zero value as true, so writing #if FEATURE_LEVEL or #if BUFFER_SIZE uses a numeric setting as a switch and hides the real intent; changing that value, for example from 1 to 2 or to a negative number, may enable code that was meant to be governed by a comparison. Look for #if and #elif lines whose expression is a bare numeric macro, a literal other than 0 or 1, an arithmetic or bitwise expression such as #if (CFG_FLAGS & 0x04) or #if VERSION - 3, or a macro that expands to a string or version number. These are common in configuration headers, feature toggles and board selection files. Expressions using comparison or logical operators, defined(X), !defined(X), and macros that are documented to be only 0 or 1 are not defects; expressions in branches that are already excluded and never evaluated are also out of scope. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 20.8 (Required).
detection_methods: Search #if and #elif lines whose expression lacks a comparison, logical operator or defined() and resolve the macros used to their values
Flag bare numeric literals other than 0 and 1, bitwise and arithmetic expressions, and macros defined with multi-valued settings
Check configuration headers and build flags such as -D options to find the actual values given to switch macros
Run a MISRA C checker, which can decide this per translation unit for a given configuration
potential_mitigations: Rewrite the condition as an explicit comparison, for example #if (CFG_FLAGS & 0x04) != 0 or #if FEATURE_LEVEL >= 2
Restrict on/off configuration macros to the values 0 and 1 and add a #error check that rejects any other value
Use defined() for presence tests rather than relying on the macro's numeric value

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Conditional compilation tests must yield zero or one

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 20.8 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Undefined Macro Evaluated in Conditional Compilation
description: The code evaluates an identifier in #if or #elif that has not been defined at that point, so the preprocessor silently substitutes 0 and selects a branch the developer may not have intended.
extended_description: An undefined identifier in a preprocessor condition is quietly replaced by 0, so a missing configuration header, a misspelt macro name or a build that omits a -D option changes which code is compiled without any diagnostic. Typical shapes are #if DEBUG_LEVEL > 1, #if USE_DMA, #if TARGET == TARGET_STM32 or #elif CFG_VERSION >= 3 in a file that does not include the header defining those names, or where the name is only set by some build configurations. Files that mix #ifdef X in one place and #if X in another are a strong signal. Identifiers guarded so they are only evaluated when defined, such as #if defined(X) && (X == 2), names tested only with defined() or #ifdef, and names the compiler or build system always predefines are not defects. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 20.9 (Required).
detection_methods: Search #if and #elif lines for identifiers not wrapped in defined() and check that each is #define'd in the file or an included header before that line, or by a mandatory build option
Look for misspelt or inconsistently named configuration macros by comparing names used in #if with names actually defined
Check headers whose configuration macros are used without first including the configuration header
Enable compiler warnings such as -Wundef and run a MISRA C checker for each build configuration
potential_mitigations: Define every configuration macro explicitly with a value of 0 or 1 in a single configuration header included by every user
Guard optional names with defined() before using their value, or add #ifndef X followed by #error so a missing definition fails the build
Turn on -Wundef or the equivalent option and treat it as an error

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Identifiers in preprocessor conditions must be defined first

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 20.9 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Stringising or Token-Pasting Operator in Macro
description: The code uses the # stringising or ## token-pasting preprocessor operator in a macro, so expansion order may be unspecified and generated names are hard to find and review.
extended_description: When a replacement list contains more than one # or ## operator, or mixes them, the order in which they are applied is unspecified, so the resulting tokens can differ between preprocessors; producing an invalid string literal or token is undefined behaviour. Token pasting also creates identifiers such as REG_##name##_MASK or handler_##n that cannot be found by text search, which hinders review and maintenance. These operators are common in register definition headers, logging and assert macros that stringise expressions (#expr), X-macro tables, unit test frameworks and code that builds function or variable names from a prefix. The rule is advisory, so recognised idioms may be accepted by deviation; macros that use neither operator, and a # that starts a directive line rather than appearing inside a replacement list, are not affected. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 20.10 (Advisory).
detection_methods: Search #define replacement lists for ## and for # immediately before a parameter name
Prioritise macros that contain several # or ## operators, or both, since their evaluation order is unspecified
Check that pasted results form valid identifiers or numbers and that stringised arguments form valid string literals
Run a MISRA C checker to list every use
potential_mitigations: Write generated identifiers out in full, or use tables and static inline functions instead of pasted names
Limit each macro to at most one # or ## operator so that the result does not depend on evaluation order
Record a documented deviation for established patterns such as assert message stringising, and keep those macros in one reviewed header

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Avoid stringise and paste operators

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 20.10 (Advisory; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Stringised Macro Parameter Pasted with Another Token
description: The code applies ## directly to the result of #param in a macro, so evaluation order is unspecified and pasting a string literal onto another token usually yields an invalid token.
extended_description: In a replacement list such as #x ## y or #name ## _str, the preprocessor may apply the # and ## operators in either order, and if stringising happens first the paste tries to join a string literal to another token, which rarely forms a valid preprocessing token and is then undefined behaviour. The outcome can differ between compilers or produce confusing errors only on one target. This shape mostly appears in hand-written logging, enum-to-string and register name macros that try to build both a string and a symbol in one step. Using # alone (#x), ## alone (x ## y), or # on one parameter and ## on unrelated tokens elsewhere in the same macro is not this defect. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 20.11 (Required).
detection_methods: Search #define replacement lists for the pattern of # followed by a parameter name followed by ##, for example with a regex such as #\s*\w+\s*##
Check enum-to-string, logging and register name helper macros where this combination is most common
Run a MISRA C checker, which can decide this per translation unit
potential_mitigations: Split the macro so that pasting and stringising are done in separate macro levels, pasting first and stringising the pasted result
Rely on adjacent string literal concatenation, such as #x "_suffix", instead of pasting onto a stringised parameter

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Do not paste onto a stringised parameter

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 20.11 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Macro Parameter Both Expanded and Pasted or Stringised
description: The code uses a macro parameter both as an operand of # or ## and as an ordinary token in the same replacement list, so when the argument is itself a macro the two uses see different text and the expansion is inconsistent.
extended_description: Arguments used with # or ## are inserted exactly as written, while the same argument used elsewhere in the replacement list is fully macro-expanded first, so if a caller passes a name that is itself a macro, one part of the expansion uses the macro name and another uses its value. The result is code such as a pasted identifier built from one spelling next to an expression computed from another, which can compile cleanly and still do the wrong thing. Look for function-like macros where a parameter appears once next to ## or after # and again on its own, for example #define DECL_REG(r) volatile uint32_t r##_val = (r) or #define CHECK(e) if (!(e)) log_fail(#e), and then check whether any call site passes an argument that is defined as a macro, such as a register or configuration constant. If no argument at any call site is a macro, the macro is safe in practice, although a checker will still flag the mixed use. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 20.12 (Required).
detection_methods: Search function-like #define lines for parameters that appear both adjacent to # or ## and elsewhere in the replacement list
For each such macro, check call sites for arguments that are object-like macros, such as register names, configuration constants or other wrapper macros
Run a MISRA C checker, which can decide this per translation unit
potential_mitigations: Use a two-level macro so that the argument is either fully expanded before every use or never expanded, consistently
Use separate parameters for the name to be pasted or stringised and the value to be evaluated
Avoid passing macro names as arguments to macros that stringise or paste their parameters

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Parameters given to # or ## not reused as expanded text

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 20.12 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Invalid Preprocessor Directive Line
description: The code contains a line starting with # that is not a recognised, well-formed preprocessing directive, so inside an excluded conditional block it is silently ignored and can cause more or less code to be compiled than intended.
extended_description: Compilers skip the contents of a conditional block that is not selected and often do not diagnose misspelt directives there, so a typo such as #esle, #elsif, #elseif, #endfi, #ifndfe or #else2 can make the intended branch disappear while the build still succeeds. The same hazard applies to non-standard directives copied from another toolchain, such as #warning or #import on a compiler that does not support them, or to stray # lines left behind by editing. Such typos are most damaging in configuration headers and around feature or target selection blocks, where a lost #else or #elif changes behaviour silently. Directives that are valid in standard C, recognised #pragma lines, a lone # null directive, and # characters inside comments or string literals are not defects; whitespace between # and the directive name is allowed. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 20.13 (Required).
detection_methods: Search every line whose first non-blank token is # and check that the following name is one of define, undef, include, if, ifdef, ifndef, elif, else, endif, line, error or pragma, or that the line is a null directive
