Flag near-miss spellings such as elsif, elseif, esle, endfi and extra tokens glued to directive names such as #else1
Check directives inside #if 0 and other excluded blocks, which compilers often do not diagnose
Run a MISRA C checker, which can decide this per translation unit
potential_mitigations: Correct misspelt directives and remove stray lines that begin with #
Replace toolchain-specific directives with standard ones or guard them in a configuration header with a documented deviation
Build every supported configuration so that each conditional branch is compiled at least once

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Lines starting with # must be well-formed directives

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 20.13 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Conditional Compilation Block Split Across Files
description: The code opens a #if, #ifdef or #ifndef block in one file and closes or continues it with #else, #elif or #endif in another file, so the extent of conditionally compiled code cannot be seen from either file alone.
extended_description: When the start and end of a conditional block live in different files, a reader of either file sees an unbalanced block, editing or reordering includes can change what is compiled, and tools that analyse files one at a time may misjudge which code is live. Typical shapes are a header that ends with an open #ifdef that the including .c file closes with #endif, a pair of begin and end headers such as section_start.h and section_end.h wrapped around code, and a .c file whose #if is closed inside an included file. These patterns occur in compiler-specific memory section or packing headers, generated configuration fragments and legacy multi-target code. A header that opens and closes its own include guard or conditional blocks entirely within itself, and conditionals that merely contain #include lines, are not defects. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 20.14 (Required).
detection_methods: For each .c and .h file, count #if, #ifdef and #ifndef against #endif and flag files where they do not balance
Look for #else, #elif or #endif with no matching opener earlier in the same file
Inspect paired begin and end headers, such as memory section or pragma pack start and stop files, for blocks left open between them
Run a MISRA C checker, which can decide this per file
potential_mitigations: Restructure so that every conditional directive group begins and ends in the same file
Replace begin and end header pairs with self-contained headers or macros, or record a documented deviation for compiler-mandated section mapping files
Keep include guards fully closed at the end of each header

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Keep each conditional directive group within one file

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 20.14 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Redefinition of Reserved or Standard Library Macro Names
description: The code uses #define or #undef on an identifier that the C implementation or Standard Library reserves, so library headers and compiler internals may silently change meaning and behaviour becomes undefined.
extended_description: Names that start with an underscore, names declared at file scope by the standard headers (errno, memcpy, printf, assert, NULL and so on) and macros supplied by those headers belong to the compiler and library, which may depend on them internally. Redefining or undefining one can break inlined library code, change what a later #include expands to, or trip explicitly undefined behaviour, as with #define defined or #undef __FILE__. In practice this shows up as include guards spelt _MODULE_H or __CONFIG_H__, compatibility shims such as #define errno my_errno or #undef assert, and headers that re-#define bool, true, false, offsetof, min/max helpers named after library functions, or __STDC__ style symbols. NDEBUG is not a reserved name and may be defined freely, and names listed only under the Standard's future library directions (for example is* or str* prefixes) are outside this weakness. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 21.1 (Required).
detection_methods: Search all .c and .h files for #define and #undef followed by a name beginning with an underscore, including include guards such as _FOO_H and __FOO_H__
Check #define and #undef targets against the identifiers and macros declared by standard headers, for example errno, assert, NULL, offsetof, EOF, bool, true, false, malloc, printf and memcpy
Flag #define defined and any #undef of predefined macros such as __LINE__, __FILE__, __DATE__ or __STDC__
Run a MISRA C checker, since the rule is decidable within a single translation unit
potential_mitigations: Rename include guards and project macros so they do not begin with an underscore, for example MODULE_H_ or PROJ_MODULE_H
Replace shims that redefine library names with project-prefixed wrappers, such as proj_assert or proj_errno
Remove #undef of standard macros and fix the underlying conflict at its source
Where a vendor toolchain genuinely requires such a definition, record it as a documented deviation with the toolchain version it was verified against

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Preprocessor must not redefine or remove implementation-owned names

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 21.1 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Declaration Using Reserved or Standard Library Identifier
description: The code declares its own variable, function, type or tag with a name reserved for the implementation or already provided by the Standard Library, so the program may bind to the wrong entity and exhibit undefined behaviour.
extended_description: Compilers may treat standard library names specially, for example by replacing calls with built-in sequences, and they use underscore-prefixed names for their own internals, so a user declaration with such a name can collide with or bypass that machinery. Typical forms are hand-written prototypes like extern void *memcpy(...) instead of including <string.h>, project functions that reuse library names such as abs, round, log or time, globals named errno, and types or struct tags such as _Buffer, __lock_t or _state_s. Embedded code often does this in startup files, retargeting stubs and private replacements of printf or malloc. Names under the future library directions, local identifiers that only shadow a library name in a nested scope with no underscore prefix, and NDEBUG are not the target here; macro definitions of reserved names are covered by a separate weakness. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 21.2 (Required).
detection_methods: Search declarations of functions, objects, typedefs, struct, union and enum tags whose names begin with an underscore followed by an uppercase letter or a second underscore, or with an underscore at file scope
Find file-scope declarations or definitions whose names match Standard Library functions or objects, for example memcpy, memset, strlen, printf, malloc, free, abs, exp, log, time or errno
Look for explicit extern prototypes of library functions written by hand instead of including the standard header
Run a MISRA C checker, since the rule is decidable within a single translation unit
potential_mitigations: Include the proper standard header rather than writing your own prototype for a library function
Rename project identifiers that clash with library or underscore-prefixed names, using a module prefix such as app_ or drv_
Where a toolchain retargeting stub must use a reserved name, isolate it in one file and record a documented deviation

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: User declarations must not reuse implementation-owned names

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 21.2 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Use of Standard Library Dynamic Heap Allocation
description: The code allocates or releases memory through malloc, calloc, realloc or free from <stdlib.h>, which exposes the program to leaks, fragmentation, double frees, use after free and allocation failure at run time.
extended_description: Heap management in the Standard Library carries undefined and unspecified behaviour: freeing a pointer that was never allocated, touching a block after it is freed, reading freshly allocated memory before it is written, and an implementation-defined result when zero bytes are requested. In long-running embedded and real-time software the heap can also fragment, making allocation timing and success unpredictable. Search for calls to malloc, calloc, realloc and free, macros that wrap them (for example #define ALLOC(n) malloc(n)), and function pointers initialised with these names. Allocators supplied by an RTOS or a project-specific fixed block pool are not the Standard Library functions and are not covered, although they deserve separate review; stack arrays and static buffers are the intended alternative. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 21.3 (Required).
detection_methods: Search for the identifiers malloc, calloc, realloc and free in all source and header files, including uses through macros, wrappers and function pointers
Check headers that include <stdlib.h> purely for allocation and identify the modules that depend on the heap
At each hit, check whether the result is tested for NULL, whether every path releases it, and whether realloc failure loses the original pointer
Run a MISRA C checker, since the rule is decidable within a single translation unit
potential_mitigations: Replace dynamic allocation with statically sized arrays, static buffers or a fixed-size block pool allocated at start-up
If allocation at initialisation time is unavoidable, confine it to a single module, never free afterwards, and record a documented deviation
Size data structures from compile-time configuration constants so memory needs are known before deployment
common_consequences: Integrity, Confidentiality; Read Memory, Modify Memory
Availability; DoS: Crash, Exit, or Restart

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: No heap management through the stdlib allocator

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 21.3 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Non-Local Jumps Using setjmp and longjmp
description: The code uses setjmp, longjmp or jmp_buf from <setjmp.h> to transfer control across function boundaries, which bypasses normal returns and can leave local variables and resources in an indeterminate state.
extended_description: A longjmp unwinds the stack without running any of the intermediate functions' cleanup, so files, locks and heap blocks acquired in between can leak, and non-volatile automatic variables modified after setjmp have indeterminate values once control comes back. Calling setjmp anywhere other than a few permitted expression contexts, or jumping into a function that has already returned, is undefined behaviour. In C code bases this usually appears as home-made exception or error-recovery schemes, parser error escapes, TRY/CATCH style macros built on jmp_buf, and libraries such as libpng-style error callbacks. Ordinary goto within a single function and return-code based error propagation are not this weakness. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 21.4 (Required).
detection_methods: Search for #include <setjmp.h> and the identifiers setjmp, longjmp, sigsetjmp, siglongjmp and jmp_buf
Find macros such as TRY, CATCH, THROW or ON_ERROR that expand to setjmp or longjmp
At each longjmp, list the resources acquired between the matching setjmp and the jump and check whether any are leaked, and check locals modified after setjmp that are not volatile
Run a MISRA C checker, since the rule is decidable within a single translation unit
potential_mitigations: Replace non-local jumps with explicit error return codes propagated up the call chain
Use a single-exit cleanup pattern within each function so resources are released on every error path
If a third-party library forces setjmp use, wrap it in one isolated module and record a documented deviation

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: No non-local control transfer via setjmp.h

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 21.4 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Asynchronous Signal Handling Through signal.h
description: The code installs or raises signals using signal, raise or sig_atomic_t from <signal.h>, whose implementation-defined and undefined behaviour makes handler execution and shared state unreliable.
extended_description: What happens when a signal arrives, whether a handler is reset to the default after one delivery, and which library calls are safe inside a handler all vary between implementations, and many combinations are undefined. Handlers frequently call non-reentrant functions such as printf, malloc or fclose, modify globals that are not volatile sig_atomic_t, or return from SIGFPE or SIGSEGV, any of which can corrupt program state. Look for #include <signal.h>, calls to signal and raise, handler functions taking a single int argument, and the macros SIGINT, SIGTERM, SIGABRT, SIGFPE, SIGILL, SIGSEGV, SIG_DFL, SIG_IGN and SIG_ERR. Hardware interrupt service routines registered through vendor vector tables or RTOS APIs are not part of <signal.h> and are outside this weakness. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 21.5 (Required).
detection_methods: Search for #include <signal.h> and calls to signal and raise, plus POSIX extensions such as sigaction and kill if present
Locate handler functions passed to signal and check what they call and which globals they write
Search for uses of sig_atomic_t and the SIG* macros to find all code that interacts with signals
Run a MISRA C checker, since the rule is decidable within a single translation unit
potential_mitigations: Replace signal-based event handling with polling, a main-loop flag set by a hardware ISR, or an RTOS event mechanism
Where signals are mandated by the host environment, keep handlers to setting a volatile sig_atomic_t flag and record a documented deviation
Move all non-trivial processing out of handlers into normal program context
common_consequences: Availability; DoS: Crash, Exit, or Restart

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: No reliance on signal.h facilities

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 21.5 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Use of Standard Library Stream Input and Output
description: The code performs file or console I/O through <stdio.h> functions or their <wchar.h> wide-character equivalents, which carry undefined, unspecified and implementation-defined behaviour such as format string mismatches and buffer overruns.
extended_description: Standard I/O mixes several hazards: printf and scanf families trust the format string to match the argument list, gets, sprintf and scanf with %s can overrun buffers, stream buffering and end-of-line handling differ between implementations, and many errors are reported only through return values that are often ignored. Search for #include <stdio.h> and calls such as printf, fprintf, sprintf, snprintf, vprintf, scanf, sscanf, fscanf, gets, fgets, puts, putchar, getchar, fopen, freopen, fclose, fread, fwrite, fseek, ftell, rewind, fflush, setvbuf, remove, rename, tmpfile and tmpnam, plus wide forms like wprintf, fwprintf, swprintf, fgetws and fputwc. Diagnostic tracing compiled only into host test builds, project serial or logging drivers that do not use <stdio.h>, and the bare use of the FILE type in a prototype without calling a stream function are lower priority or not covered. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 21.6 (Required).
detection_methods: Search for #include <stdio.h> and calls to the printf, scanf, gets/puts, getc/putc and f* stream function families
Search <wchar.h> users for wide-character I/O calls such as wprintf, fwprintf, swprintf, wscanf, fgetws, fputws, fgetwc and fputwc
At each formatted I/O call, check that the format string is a literal and that its conversions match the argument types and buffer sizes
Run a MISRA C checker, since the rule is decidable within a single translation unit
potential_mitigations: Route logging and console output through a project-specific driver with a fixed, type-safe interface
Where stdio is needed on a host or tooling build, confine it to a dedicated module and record a documented deviation
Replace gets, sprintf and unbounded %s conversions with bounded alternatives and check every return value
common_consequences: Integrity, Confidentiality; Read Memory, Modify Memory

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: No stdio or wide-character stream I/O

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 21.6 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: String to Number Conversion Without Error Reporting
description: The code converts text to numbers with atof, atoi, atol or atoll, which give no way to detect malformed or out-of-range input, so an invalid string produces undefined behaviour or a silently wrong value.
extended_description: The ato* family has no error channel: an empty or non-numeric string usually yields 0, and a value too large for the target type is undefined behaviour, so the caller cannot tell a genuine zero from a parse failure. This matters wherever numbers come from configuration files, command lines, serial protocols, NMEA style sentences or user input, because a corrupted field is accepted without complaint. Search for calls to atoi, atol, atoll and atof and macros that expand to them. The strtol, strtoul, strtoll, strtoull, strtof, strtod and strtold functions, which report errors through endptr and errno, are the intended replacements and are not this weakness. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 21.7 (Required).
detection_methods: Search for the identifiers atoi, atol, atoll and atof, including wrapper macros and function pointers to them
At each hit, trace the source of the string argument and check whether it can be empty, non-numeric or out of range
Check code paths that treat a zero result as meaningful, since a failed conversion is indistinguishable from zero
Run a MISRA C checker, since the rule is decidable within a single translation unit
potential_mitigations: Replace ato* calls with the matching strto* function and check endptr, errno and the resulting range
Validate the input string format before conversion and reject partial or trailing characters
Provide a project helper that wraps strtol with explicit range limits and an error status

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: No unchecked ato* numeric conversions

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 21.7 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Process Termination and Environment Access via stdlib
description: The code calls abort, exit, getenv or system from <stdlib.h>, so program termination, environment lookup and command execution depend on implementation-defined host behaviour and may skip orderly shutdown.
extended_description: exit and abort end the program from wherever they are called, so callers never get to put actuators into a safe state, flush buffers or release resources, and abort may not flush streams or run atexit handlers at all. getenv returns a pointer into storage the implementation may overwrite on the next call, and whether an environment exists is itself implementation-defined. system hands a string to a host command processor that may not exist and whose result is implementation-defined, which also opens the door to command injection. Search for calls to abort, exit, getenv and system, and related forms such as _Exit, quick_exit, atexit handlers that assume exit is used, and error macros like FATAL() or DIE() that expand to exit. A return from main is not this weakness. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 21.8 (Required).
detection_methods: Search for calls to abort, exit, _Exit, quick_exit, getenv and system, including macros that wrap them such as FATAL, DIE or PANIC
At each exit or abort, check what state the system is left in and which resources are not released
At each getenv, check whether the returned pointer is tested for NULL and whether it is used after another getenv call
At each system call, trace whether any part of the command string comes from external input
Run a MISRA C checker, since the rule is decidable within a single translation unit
potential_mitigations: Propagate fatal errors to a central handler that drives the system to a defined safe state instead of calling exit or abort
Read configuration from a defined source such as a calibration table rather than environment variables
Remove system calls and implement the required action directly in the program
Where a host tool genuinely needs these functions, isolate them and record a documented deviation
common_consequences: Availability; DoS: Crash, Exit, or Restart

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: No host termination, environment or shell calls from stdlib

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 21.8 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Library Sort and Search With Callback Comparators
description: The code calls qsort or bsearch from <stdlib.h>, whose result depends on a user comparison callback and an unspecified, often recursive algorithm, so inconsistent comparators or limited stack can yield undefined behaviour or unpredictable ordering.
extended_description: If the comparison function is not a consistent total order, for example it subtracts two ints and overflows, compares floating values that may be NaN, or modifies the elements it is given, the behaviour of qsort and bsearch is undefined. The order in which equal elements end up is unspecified, so results can change between toolchains, and typical qsort implementations recurse with stack use that is hard to bound on small embedded stacks. bsearch also silently gives wrong answers if the array is not sorted with the same comparator. Search for calls to qsort and bsearch and the comparator functions passed to them, usually of the form int cmp(const void *, const void *). Hand-written sorting or searching routines with bounded behaviour are not this weakness. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 21.9 (Required).
detection_methods: Search for calls to qsort and bsearch, including wrapper macros and function pointers to them
Inspect each comparator for subtraction-based comparisons that can overflow, floating-point comparisons, missing tie breaks and writes through its arguments
For bsearch, check that the array is guaranteed to be sorted with the same comparator before the search
Run a MISRA C checker, since the rule is decidable within a single translation unit
potential_mitigations: Replace qsort and bsearch with a project implementation that has bounded stack use and known worst-case time, such as an iterative insertion or heap sort
Write comparators using explicit less-than and greater-than tests and give a deterministic tie break so they never return 0 for distinct elements
Where library use is retained, document the stack budget analysis as part of a documented deviation
common_consequences: Availability; DoS: Crash, Exit, or Restart

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: No generic stdlib sort or binary search

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 21.9 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Reliance on Standard Library Time and Date Facilities
description: The code obtains or formats time through <time.h> functions or wcsftime, whose encoding, range, epoch and static result buffers are implementation-defined or unspecified, so timing and timestamps can be wrong or overwritten.
extended_description: The representation of time_t and clock_t, the epoch, the resolution of clock, whether a calendar time is available at all, and the handling of time zones and daylight saving are left to the implementation. localtime, gmtime, ctime and asctime return pointers to shared static objects that later calls overwrite, and asctime or strftime can overflow or produce undefined results with out-of-range struct tm fields; 32-bit time_t also overflows in 2038. Search for #include <time.h> and uses of time, clock, difftime, mktime, gmtime, localtime, asctime, ctime, strftime, wcsftime, CLOCKS_PER_SEC, time_t, clock_t and struct tm. Hardware timer drivers, RTOS tick counters and project-defined time types that do not use <time.h> are not this weakness. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 21.10 (Required).
detection_methods: Search for #include <time.h> and the identifiers time, clock, difftime, mktime, gmtime, localtime, asctime, ctime, strftime and wcsftime
Search for the types time_t, clock_t and struct tm and the macro CLOCKS_PER_SEC in declarations and casts
At each localtime, gmtime, ctime or asctime call, check whether the returned pointer is kept across another call or used from multiple threads
Run a MISRA C checker, since the rule is decidable within a single translation unit
potential_mitigations: Use a project time service built on a hardware timer or RTOS tick with a defined width, resolution and wrap-around handling
Represent timestamps in a fixed-width unsigned type with a documented epoch and unit
Where host tooling must use <time.h>, isolate it and record a documented deviation

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: No time.h clock or calendar services

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 21.10 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Type-Generic Math Macros From tgmath.h
description: The code includes <tgmath.h> so that maths calls such as sqrt or pow silently dispatch to float, double, long double or complex variants based on argument type, which can select an unintended precision or trigger undefined behaviour.
extended_description: With <tgmath.h> in scope, an unsuffixed call like sqrt(x), fabs(x) or pow(x, y) becomes a macro whose chosen function depends on the types of its arguments, so a change in a variable declaration or an integer argument quietly changes precision, and some argument combinations have undefined results. The reader cannot see from the call site which function actually runs, which hampers numerical review in navigation, guidance and control code. Search for #include <tgmath.h> and then review the maths calls in those files. Including <math.h> or <complex.h> and calling explicitly typed functions such as sqrtf, sqrt, sqrtl or csqrt is the intended alternative and is not this weakness. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 21.11 (Required).
detection_methods: Search all source and header files for #include <tgmath.h>, including indirect inclusion through project headers
In affected files, list calls to unsuffixed maths names such as sqrt, pow, exp, log, sin, cos, fabs and fmod and identify the argument types
Run a MISRA C checker, since the rule is decidable within a single translation unit
potential_mitigations: Remove <tgmath.h> and include <math.h> or <complex.h> instead
Call the explicitly typed variant that matches the operand type, for example sqrtf for float and sqrt for double
Make argument types explicit with essential-type-consistent declarations rather than relying on macro dispatch

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: No implicit type-generic maths dispatch

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 21.11 (Required; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Reliance on Floating-Point Exception Status Flags
description: The code tests, clears, raises or saves floating-point exception flags through <fenv.h>, whose flag values can be unspecified and whose raise order is unspecified, so error detection based on them may silently fail.
extended_description: Whether the floating-point status flags reflect a given operation depends on the compiler honouring FENV_ACCESS, on optimisation reordering or folding the arithmetic, and on the hardware actually supporting each exception, so a check such as testing for divide-by-zero after a division can miss the event or see a stale flag. Accessing the flags without the proper pragma state is undefined, and feraiseexcept with several exceptions raises them in an unspecified order. Search for #include <fenv.h>, calls to feclearexcept, fetestexcept, feraiseexcept, fegetexceptflag and fesetexceptflag, the macros FE_DIVBYZERO, FE_INEXACT, FE_INVALID, FE_OVERFLOW, FE_UNDERFLOW and FE_ALL_EXCEPT, and #pragma STDC FENV_ACCESS. Rounding mode functions such as fegetround and fesetround are not the target of this weakness. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 21.12 (Advisory).
detection_methods: Search for #include <fenv.h> and calls to feclearexcept, fetestexcept, feraiseexcept, fegetexceptflag and fesetexceptflag
Search for the FE_* exception macros and #pragma STDC FENV_ACCESS
At each fetestexcept, check whether the guarded arithmetic could be reordered or constant folded by the compiler
Run a MISRA C checker, since the rule is decidable within a single translation unit
potential_mitigations: Validate operands before the operation, for example check a divisor against zero or a range limit, instead of testing flags afterwards
Use isnan, isinf or isfinite on results where post-hoc checking is required
If flag-based detection is retained, confine it to one module, verify it on the target compiler and hardware, and record a documented deviation

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Avoid fenv.h exception flag handling

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 21.12 (Advisory; Decidable; Single Translation Unit). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Heap Block or File Stream Never Released
description: The code obtains memory with malloc, calloc or realloc, or a stream with fopen, and has a path on which the matching free or fclose never happens, so memory or file handles are exhausted over time.
extended_description: Each leaked allocation or open stream permanently consumes a limited resource, and in software that runs for weeks the slow loss eventually causes allocation failures, fopen returning NULL or the process being killed. Leaks typically occur on early-return error paths, when a pointer or FILE * is overwritten by a second malloc or fopen before the first is released, when realloc fails and the original pointer is replaced by NULL, and when ownership passes between functions without a clear rule about who frees. Search each function that calls malloc, calloc, realloc, strdup, fopen, freopen or tmpfile and follow every exit path to a corresponding free or fclose; data structures that store the pointers need checking for a teardown routine. Allocations deliberately held for the whole program lifetime, such as a single start-up buffer, are lower priority but still technically covered. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 22.1 (Required).
detection_methods: Find every call to malloc, calloc, realloc, strdup, fopen, freopen and tmpfile and trace each return, goto and error branch to confirm a matching free or fclose
Look for a pointer or FILE * variable assigned from an allocator or fopen a second time before being released
Check realloc calls of the form p = realloc(p, n), which leak the original block when the call fails
Check structures and lists that store allocated pointers for a destroy or close function that releases every member
Use a leak detector or MISRA C checker with inter-procedural analysis, and review manually across translation units because the property is undecidable
potential_mitigations: Use a single-exit cleanup block in each function so every allocated block and opened stream is released on all paths
Assign realloc results to a temporary and only overwrite the original pointer on success
Define and document ownership for every allocated object, including which function is responsible for releasing it
Avoid run-time allocation and file handles altogether by using static buffers and pre-opened resources where possible

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Every dynamically acquired library resource must be given back

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 22.1 (Required; Undecidable; System). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Free of Non-Heap or Already Freed Memory
description: The code passes to free or realloc a pointer that did not come from malloc, calloc or realloc, or whose block has already been released, which is undefined behaviour that commonly corrupts the heap.
extended_description: free and realloc may only be given a pointer previously returned by the Standard Library allocator and not yet released; anything else, such as the address of a local or static variable, a string literal, a pointer offset into the middle of a block, or a second free of the same block, corrupts allocator metadata and can crash later in unrelated code. Double frees often arise through aliases, where two pointers share one block and both are freed, through error paths that free and then fall into common cleanup that frees again, and through realloc, which may already have released the old block. Search for every call to free and realloc and determine where the argument came from; also check frees of pointers that were advanced with ++ or pointer arithmetic. free(NULL) is well defined and is not this weakness, and memory from RTOS or custom pool allocators released with their own matching function is outside scope. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 22.2 (Mandatory).
detection_methods: Find every call to free and realloc and trace the argument back to confirm it was returned by malloc, calloc or realloc
Flag free applied to &local, arrays, string literals, static or global buffers, and pointers advanced by arithmetic
Look for aliases of one allocated block that are freed separately, and for cleanup labels reached after an earlier free on the same path
Check that pointers are set to NULL after free in long-lived structures, and that the old pointer is not freed after a successful realloc
Use a MISRA C checker or heap sanitiser with inter-procedural analysis, and review manually across translation units because the property is undecidable
potential_mitigations: Assign NULL to a pointer immediately after freeing it so a repeated free has no effect
Give each allocated block a single owning pointer and release it only through that owner
Never free memory that was not obtained from the Standard Library allocator; use the matching release function of any other allocator
Prefer static allocation so that free is not needed at all
common_consequences: Integrity, Confidentiality; Read Memory, Modify Memory
Availability; DoS: Crash, Exit, or Restart

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Only release live blocks that the stdlib allocator handed out

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 22.2 (Mandatory; Undecidable; System). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Same File Opened for Writing and Reading on Separate Streams
description: The code holds two open streams to the same file at once where at least one permits writing, so buffered data from one stream may not be seen by the other and the file contents become implementation-defined.
extended_description: Each FILE stream has its own buffer and file position, so a write through one stream may still sit in its buffer when another stream reads, or both streams may write at overlapping positions, and the Standard leaves the outcome to the implementation. This usually appears as a logger or data store module that keeps a writer stream open in "w", "a", "r+" or "w+" mode while another function calls fopen on the same path in "r" mode to read back or verify, or as two modules that each open a shared configuration or log file. Look for fopen and freopen calls that use the same path literal, macro or path variable, and check whether their lifetimes overlap. Opening one file several times for reading only is acceptable, and opening, closing and then reopening in a different mode is not this weakness. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 22.3 (Required).
detection_methods: Collect every fopen and freopen call with its path argument and mode string, grouping calls that use the same literal, macro or path variable
For each group with a writing mode (w, a, r+, w+, a+), check whether another stream on the same file can be open at the same time
Check global or static FILE * variables that stay open across calls while other functions open the same path
Review across translation units manually, because the property is undecidable and paths are often built at run time
potential_mitigations: Use a single stream opened in an update mode such as r+ and reposition with fseek or fflush between reads and writes
Close the writing stream before opening the file again for reading
Centralise access to each shared file in one module that owns its stream
Where unavoidable, record a documented deviation describing how buffers are flushed and synchronised

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: No concurrent read and write streams on one file

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 22.3 (Required; Undecidable; System). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Write Operation on Stream Opened Read-Only
description: The code writes to a FILE stream that was opened only for reading, so the outcome is not defined by the Standard and data may be lost or the program may fail.
extended_description: A stream opened with fopen mode "r" or "rb", or obtained as stdin, supports only input, and calling an output function on it has no behaviour the Standard specifies; the write may be silently dropped, return an error that is ignored, or corrupt the stream state. This typically appears when one FILE * variable is reused for both reading and writing across a module, when a helper accepts a FILE * and writes to it regardless of how the caller opened it, or when the mode string is chosen at run time. Search for fopen and freopen calls with read-only modes and follow the resulting pointer to calls such as fprintf, fputs, fputc, putc, fwrite, vfprintf, fputws and fwprintf. Streams opened in update modes such as "r+", "w+" or "a+" can legitimately be written and are not this weakness. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 22.4 (Mandatory).
detection_methods: Find fopen and freopen calls whose mode string is "r" or "rb" and track the returned FILE * through assignments and function arguments
Flag any fprintf, vfprintf, fputs, fputc, putc, fwrite, fputws, fputwc or fwprintf call reached with such a stream, or with stdin
Check helper functions that take a FILE * parameter and write to it, and confirm every caller passes a writable stream
Use a MISRA C checker with data-flow analysis and review across translation units manually, because the property is undecidable
potential_mitigations: Open the file with a mode that permits writing, such as "r+" or "w", when output is required
Use separate, clearly named variables for input and output streams rather than reusing one FILE * for both
Record the open mode alongside the stream in a wrapper and assert it before every write

taxonomy_mappings.entry_name: Output must not target an input-only stream

mapping_rationale: Adapted from MISRA C:2012 Rule 22.4 (Mandatory; Undecidable; System). Written for Scorpius localisation in original wording; consult a licensed copy of MISRA C:2012 for the normative text.

name: Direct Access to or Copying of FILE Object Contents
description: The code dereferences a FILE pointer, reads or writes its members, or copies the FILE object itself, so the stream's internal state is bypassed or duplicated and the copy may not behave as a valid stream.
extended_description: FILE is an opaque type whose layout belongs to the library, and the Standard warns that its address can matter, so a copy of a FILE object is not guaranteed to work as a stream and poking its fields can desynchronise the library's buffering. Problem code includes expressions like *fp, fp->_ptr, fp->_cnt or fp->_flags (often in old embedded or performance hacks), assigning one FILE object to another, declaring FILE variables by value, and passing a FILE * to memcpy, memcmp or memset. Search for -> or unary * applied to any FILE * variable and for FILE used as a non-pointer type in declarations or sizeof. Copying the pointer value itself (FILE *a = b;) and passing FILE * to standard stdio functions are fine. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 22.5 (Mandatory).
detection_methods: Search for declarations of FILE by value (FILE f;), sizeof(FILE) and struct copies involving FILE objects
Search for the -> operator or unary * applied to variables and parameters of type FILE *, including fields such as _ptr, _cnt, _base, _flags, _fileno or _IO_read_ptr
Search for memcpy, memmove, memcmp or memset calls whose pointer argument is a FILE *
Run a MISRA C checker with type tracking, and review indirect accesses through casts manually because the property is undecidable
potential_mitigations: Treat FILE as opaque and interact with streams only through standard functions such as fread, fwrite, ftell and fileno where available
Pass and store FILE * pointers rather than FILE objects
Replace field-level hacks with documented library calls such as setvbuf or fflush

name: Use of FILE Pointer After fclose
description: The code uses a FILE pointer after fclose has been called on its stream, whose value is then indeterminate, so later reads, writes, comparisons or copies are undefined behaviour.
extended_description: Once fclose returns, the FILE object may be freed or reused for another stream, so calling fprintf, fread, fflush or fclose again on the old pointer can write to the wrong file, crash or corrupt the library's state, and even copying or comparing the pointer value is not defined. Typical forms are a second fclose in shared cleanup code, a global or static FILE * left pointing at a closed stream and reused by a later function, logging after the log file has been closed during shutdown, and a closed pointer stored in a struct and passed on. Search for fclose and freopen calls and follow the same FILE * variable, and any aliases, forward along every path. Assigning a fresh fopen result or NULL to the variable after the close ends the hazard, and using a different, still open stream is not this weakness. Maps to MISRA C:2012 Rule 22.6 (Mandatory).
detection_methods: Find every fclose call and trace the closed FILE * and its aliases forward to any later read, write, fflush, fseek, fclose, comparison or assignment
Check cleanup labels and shutdown routines for a second fclose on a stream that may already be closed
Check global, static and struct-member FILE * variables to see whether they are reset to NULL after closing
Use a MISRA C checker with inter-procedural data-flow analysis and review across translation units manually, because the property is undecidable
potential_mitigations: Set the FILE * variable to NULL immediately after fclose and test for NULL before any use
Give each stream a single owner responsible for both opening and closing it
Wrap fclose in a helper that takes FILE ** and clears the caller's pointer

name: Catastrophic Cancellation When Subtracting Nearly Equal Computed Values
description: The code subtracts two nearly equal quantities that already carry rounding error, such as `b*b - 4*a*c` or `E[x^2] - E[x]^2`, so the matching leading digits cancel and the result is dominated by earlier rounding noise.
extended_description: When two values that agree in most of their leading digits are subtracted, the shared digits vanish and only the trailing digits survive; if those operands were produced by rounded multiplications, squares or sums, the trailing digits are mostly rounding error, so the difference can be wrong in every digit even though the subtraction itself was exact. Typical code includes the discriminant `b*b - 4*a*c` in equation solvers and ray-sphere intersection tests, `x*x - y*y`, Heron's area `sqrt(s*(s-a)*(s-b)*(s-c))` applied to thin triangles or needle-shaped mesh elements, the one-pass variance `sumsq/n - mean*mean` or `np.mean(x**2) - np.mean(x)**2` in statistics, telemetry, finance and ML feature scaling, `1 - cos(x)` for small angles, and differences of large epoch timestamps or geographic coordinates held as `double`. The damage is greatest when the operands are close relative to their own size, for example data with a large mean and small spread, nearly degenerate geometry, small angles or nearby points far from the origin. Subtracting exact inputs (values read straight from storage, small integers, or two error-free numbers within a factor of two of each other) is benign, as is subtraction where the operands differ greatly in magnitude or where only a coarse result is needed. Derived from Goldberg (1991), Section 1.4.
detection_methods: Search for discriminant expressions such as `b*b - 4*a*c`, `b**2 - 4*a*c` and `pow(b, 2) - 4*a*c` and check whether b^2 can be close to 4ac for the inputs the code receives

Search for one-pass variance and standard deviation code (`sumsq / n - mean * mean`, `mean(x**2) - mean(x)**2`, `E[x^2] - E[x]^2`) and check whether inputs can have a large mean relative to their spread
Search for `x*x - y*y`, `1 - cos(`, `1.0 - Math.cos(` and Heron-style `s*(s-a)*(s-b)*(s-c)` area or triangle-quality code and check whether nearly equal operands occur
Check subtractions of large absolute coordinates, epoch timestamps or accumulated totals stored as `float` or `double` where only the small difference is used afterwards
potential_mitigations: Rewrite differences of squares as `(x - y) * (x + y)` and replace `1 - cos(x)` with `2 * sin(x / 2) ** 2` for small x.
Compute variance with Welford's online algorithm or a two-pass method that subtracts the mean first, or call `numpy.var`, `statistics.variance` or `pandas.Series.var`.
Compute triangle areas with Kahan's stable rearrangement of Heron's formula on sorted sides, or with a cross product of edge vectors taken relative to one vertex.
Shift coordinates and timestamps to a local origin before subtracting, and use an `fma`-based compensated product for discriminants when near-double roots matter.

name: Numerically Unstable Quadratic Formula Root Computation
description: The code computes both roots of a quadratic with the textbook `(-b +/- sqrt(b*b - 4*a*c)) / (2*a)` expression, so the root whose numerator subtracts nearly equal values loses most of its accuracy or comes out as zero.
extended_description: When b^2 is much larger than |4ac|, the square root of the discriminant is almost equal to |b|, so one of the numerators `-b + sqrt(d)` or `-b - sqrt(d)` cancels and the smaller-magnitude root can have few correct digits or collapse to exactly zero. A second, separate loss occurs when b^2 is close to 4ac (near-double roots): the discriminant itself cancels and roughly half the digits of both roots can be lost, which no rearrangement of the final division repairs unless the discriminant is formed more accurately. The pattern appears in hand-written `solve_quadratic`, `quadratic_roots` and `roots` helpers, ray-sphere, ray-cylinder and swept-sphere intersection in graphics, games and collision detection, ballistic and kinematic time-to-impact or closest-approach calculations, circle intersection and closed-form eigenvalues of 2x2 matrices, in any language (`sqrt` in C and C++, `Math.sqrt` in Java, C# and JavaScript, `math.sqrt` or `cmath.sqrt` in Python, `f64::sqrt` in Rust, `math.Sqrt` in Go). Code that uses the sign-aware form `q = -(b + copysign(sqrt(d), b)) / 2` with roots `q / a` and `c / q`, code that calls a library polynomial solver, and code that only ever uses the larger-magnitude root computed with the non-cancelling sign are not a concern. Derived from Goldberg (1991), Sections 1.4 and 4.1.
detection_methods: Search for `sqrt(` used together with `2*a`, `2.0 * a` or `(2 * a)` and for both `-b +` and `-b -` forms in the same function, and check whether the smaller-magnitude root is formed by direct subtraction
Search for functions named like `solve_quadratic`, `quadratic`, `roots`, `intersect_sphere`, `ray_sphere`, `time_to_impact` or `closest_approach` and inspect how both roots are produced
Check whether the discriminant `b*b - 4*a*c` is evaluated in the same precision as the inputs when tangent or grazing cases (near-double roots) are expected and their accuracy matters
Check handling of a zero or tiny leading coefficient `a`, where dividing by `2*a` amplifies the same cancellation and a linear solution should be used instead
potential_mitigations: Compute `q = -0.5 * (b + copysign(sqrt(d), b))` and take the roots as `q / a` and `c / q`, so neither root involves a cancelling subtraction.
Evaluate the discriminant in higher precision or with an `fma`-based compensated product when inputs can approach the double-root case.
Use a library solver such as `numpy.roots`, `numpy.polynomial.Polynomial.roots`, GSL `gsl_poly_solve_quadratic` or Boost.Math where available.
Treat a zero or negligible leading coefficient as a linear equation before applying any quadratic formula.

name: Small Quantity Lost When Added to a Much Larger Value
description: The code adds a small quantity to 1 or another much larger value before applying a power, logarithm or subtraction, such as `pow(1 + r/n, n)`, `log(1 + x)` or `exp(x) - 1`, so the low-order digits of the small quantity are discarded and the loss is then amplified.
extended_description: Adding a value x that is tiny relative to 1 keeps only the digits of x that fit beside the leading 1, so `1 + x` already misrepresents x by a relative amount that can be large; taking a logarithm, raising to a high power or subtracting 1 again exposes and magnifies that loss, and when x is below machine epsilon `log(1 + x)` and `exp(x) - 1` return exactly zero. Common forms are compound interest, annuity and discounting code using `Math.pow(1 + rate / periods, periods * years)` or `(1 + r) ** n` with daily or per-second rates, continuous growth and decay models, `log(1 + x)`, `log(1 - p)` and `exp(x) - 1` in probability, survival analysis and log-likelihoods, ML losses and activations such as softplus written as `log(1 + exp(x))`, physics and control code with small time steps, and expressions like `x / (exp(x) - 1)`. The effect is pronounced in single precision, with per-period rates around 1e-4 or smaller, or with many compounding periods; in double precision with moderate rates and few periods the error may be negligible, so check the expected magnitudes before reporting. Calls to `log1p` and `expm1` (`Math.log1p`, `Math.expm1`, `np.log1p`, `np.expm1`, `math.log1p`, `f64::ln_1p`, `f64::exp_m1`), decimal or arbitrary-precision implementations, and additions where both operands are of similar size are not a concern. Derived from Goldberg (1991), Section 1.4.
detection_methods: Search for `log(1 +`, `log(1.0 +`, `Math.log(1 +`, `np.log(1 +`, `log(1 -` and `.ln()` applied to `1.0 + x`, and check whether the added term can be small
Search for `exp(x) - 1`, `Math.exp(` followed by `- 1`, `np.exp(...) - 1` and `1 - exp(` and check whether the argument can be near zero

Search for compounding expressions such as `pow(1 +`, `Math.pow(1 +`, `(1 + r) **`, `(1 + rate / n)` and `powf(1.0f +` in finance, growth, decay and discounting code, and check the rate size, exponent and precision
Search for hand-written softplus and log-sum-exp forms such as `log(1 + exp(x))` and check both the small-argument loss and large-argument overflow
potential_mitigations: Replace `log(1 + x)` with `log1p(x)` and `exp(x) - 1` with `expm1(x)` using the language's library version (`Math.log1p`, `Math.expm1`, `np.log1p`, `np.expm1`, `f64::ln_1p`, `f64::exp_m1`).
Compute compound growth as `exp(n * log1p(r))` and the matching annuity factor as `expm1(n * log1p(r)) / r`.
Use `decimal.Decimal`, `java.math.BigDecimal` or C# `decimal` with an explicit rounding rule where financial results must match contractual or statutory calculations exactly.
Use library implementations of softplus and log-sum-exp (`np.logaddexp`, `scipy.special.logsumexp`, `torch.nn.functional.softplus`) rather than hand-written forms.

name: Decimal Fractions Assumed Exactly Representable in Binary Floating Point
description: The code holds decimal quantities such as money, rates or 0.1 increments in binary `float` or `double` and expects exact decimal results, so values like 0.1 and 0.01 are silently approximated and totals, comparisons and conversions come out wrong.
extended_description: Binary floating point represents a fraction exactly only when its denominator is a power of two, so most short decimal fractions (0.1, 0.2, 0.01, 1.15) have infinite binary expansions and are stored as the nearest binary value; arithmetic on them gives results such as `0.1 + 0.2 != 0.3` or `1.15 * 100` evaluating to 114.99999999999999, and the tiny discrepancies become visible after truncation, `floor`, equality tests, string formatting or summation. Typical sites are currency amounts, prices, tax and GST rates, interest rates, percentages and invoice totals held in `double`, `float`, JavaScript `Number`, Python `float`, Go `float64`, Rust `f64` or SQL `FLOAT`, `REAL` and `DOUBLE` columns; cent conversions such as `(int)(amount * 100)` or `Math.floor(price * 100)`; `parseFloat`, `float()` or `Double.parseDouble` on user-entered amounts; and configured step sizes, thresholds or intervals that the code assumes are exact. It also appears when tests compare a computed double with a decimal literal using `==` or `assertEquals` without a delta. Values that are exactly representable (integers below 2^53 in double, halves, quarters and other dyadic fractions), money held as integer minor units or in `decimal.Decimal`, `BigDecimal`, C# `decimal` or SQL `DECIMAL`/`NUMERIC`, and scientific measurements where a relative error near 1e-16 is acceptable are not a concern. Derived from Goldberg (1991), Section 1.1.
detection_methods: Search for money and rate identifiers (`price`, `amount`, `balance`, `total`, `cost`, `fee`, `tax`, `gst`, `rate`, `percent`, `cents`) declared as `float`, `double`, `float64`, `f64`, `Number` or SQL `FLOAT`/`REAL`/`DOUBLE` and check whether exact decimal results are expected
Search for truncating conversions of scaled values such as `(int)(x * 100)`, `(long)(amount * 100)`, `Math.floor(x * 100)`, `int(x * 100)` and `math.trunc` and check for off-by-one-cent results
Search for equality tests between computed floating values and decimal literals, such as `== 0.3`, `== 0.1`, `=== 0.3` or `assertEquals(0.3, x)` without a delta
Check ORM, JSON and serialisation mappings that turn database `DECIMAL` or `NUMERIC` columns, or decimal strings, into binary floating types
potential_mitigations: Represent money as integer minor units (cents in a 64-bit integer) or as a decimal type such as `decimal.Decimal`, `java.math.BigDecimal`, C# `decimal` or SQL `DECIMAL`/`NUMERIC`.
Construct `BigDecimal` and `Decimal` values from strings rather than from `double` literals, so the binary approximation is not imported.
Round explicitly with a defined mode (`BigDecimal.setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN)`, `Decimal.quantize`, `Math.round` on an integer-scaled value) instead of truncating scaled binary values.
Compare binary floating results with a tolerance (`math.isclose`, `numpy.isclose`, `assertEquals(expected, actual, delta)`) where approximation is acceptable.

name: Naive Summation of Many Floating-Point Terms
description: The code adds a long sequence of floating-point values one at a time into a single running total, so rounding errors accumulate with the number of terms and small terms are absorbed into a large partial sum.
extended_description: Every addition rounds the running total, and the worst-case error of a plain left-to-right sum grows roughly in proportion to the number of terms multiplied by the size of the values, with the earliest terms perturbed most; once the total is large, any increment smaller than half a unit in the last place of the total is lost entirely. This affects loops like `for (...) sum += x[i];`, `total += value` in aggregations, `reduce((a, b) => a + b)` in JavaScript, `std::accumulate` over `double`, `mapToDouble(...).sum()` in Java, numerical integration with many steps (Riemann, trapezoid, Simpson), time integration in simulations and control loops (`position += velocity * dt`), long-running sensor, energy, distance or flow totalisers, Monte Carlo averages and hand-written dot products and norms. The risk scales with the term count (millions of terms in double, thousands in float), with a wide spread of magnitudes and with terms of mixed sign. Short sums of a few terms, sums of integers that remain exact, `math.fsum`, `numpy.sum` (which uses pairwise summation), Python 3.12 and later built-in `sum` over floats (which applies compensation), Kahan or Neumaier compensated loops, BLAS reductions and sums accumulated in a wider type are not a concern. Derived from Goldberg (1991), Sections 3.2.3 and 4.3.
detection_methods: Search for accumulation loops (`sum +=`, `total +=`, `acc +=`, `s = s +`) over `float`, `double`, `float32`, `float64`, `f64` or `Number` values and check the expected term count and range of magnitudes

Search for JavaScript `reduce(` with addition, C++ `std::accumulate`, Java `reduce(0.0, Double::sum)` and Python `sum(` on interpreters before 3.12 over large float collections, and check whether accuracy matters
Search for integration and time-stepping accumulators such as `area += f(x) * dx`, `pos += vel * dt` and `energy += power * dt` in simulation, control and analytics code
Check long-running running totals (energy, distance, revenue, counters) that are never reset and are stored in floating types
potential_mitigations: Use `math.fsum` in Python, `numpy.sum` or `numpy.add.reduce`, or a Kahan-Babuska-Neumaier compensated summation loop for long sums.
Accumulate in a wider type than the data (a `double` accumulator for `float` data, double-double or `long double` for `double` data) when compensation is impractical.
Use pairwise or tree reduction, or group terms by magnitude, when values vary widely in size.
Use exact integer or decimal accumulators for counts and money, and periodically rebase or reset long-running floating totals.

name: Accumulator or Intermediate Product Kept at Insufficient Precision
description: The code accumulates sums, dot products or residuals in a type no wider than the data, or rounds products to the narrow type before adding them to a wider accumulator, so the extra precision the algorithm needs is lost.
extended_description: Some computations need a short burst of extra precision to be accurate: a long sum of single-precision values loses many digits if the total is also single precision, a dot product forfeits most of the benefit of a double accumulator if each `x[i] * y[i]` is first rounded to float, and residuals such as `b - A*x` in iterative refinement or Newton steps are differences of nearly equal values that carry little information unless formed in higher precision than the solution. Look for `float sum = 0.0f` or `float32` accumulators in loops over large arrays, `np.float32`, `torch.float16` or `bfloat16` reductions in ML and signal-processing code, `half` or `__half` accumulators in GPU kernels, C and C++ loops of the form `double acc; acc += a[i] * b[i];` where `a` and `b` are `float` so the product is rounded to float first, `std::accumulate(v.begin(), v.end(), 0)` whose integer initial value truncates every partial sum, mixed-precision solvers that compute residuals in working precision, and narrow fixed-point or float accumulators in DSP filters. The issue is strongest for single and half precision with thousands of terms or more and in iterative methods that depend on residual accuracy. Double accumulators over float data, operands explicitly promoted before multiplying (`(double)a[i] * b[i]`), BLAS, NumPy or framework reductions that already accumulate in a wider type, and tensor-core APIs configured to accumulate in float32 are not a concern. Derived from Goldberg (1991), Sections 3.1, 3.2.1 and 4.3.
detection_methods: Search for accumulators declared as `float`, `float32`, `np.float32`, `half`, `__half`, `float16` or `bfloat16` that are updated with `+=` in loops over large arrays, and check the term count
Search for dot-product, convolution and matrix loops `acc += a[i] * b[i]` where `acc` is `double` but `a` and `b` are `float`, and check whether the operands are promoted before multiplication

Search for `std::accumulate(` with an integer literal initial value such as `0` over floating data, and for `dtype=np.float32`, `.half()` or `astype('float32')` followed by `sum`, `mean`, `var` or `dot`
Check iterative refinement, Newton and Krylov solver code for residuals `r = b - A*x` computed in the same precision as `x` when the method is meant to improve accuracy
potential_mitigations: Declare accumulators one precision wider than the data (`double` for `float`, double-double or `long double` for `double`) and promote operands before multiplying, as in `acc += (double)a[i] * (double)b[i]`.
Pass an explicit accumulation type to reductions, for example `np.sum(x, dtype=np.float64)`, `torch.sum(x, dtype=torch.float32)` or `std::accumulate(begin, end, 0.0)`.
Use `fma` or a library compensated dot product when a wider type is unavailable, and compute residuals for iterative refinement in higher precision than the working solution.

name: Floating-Point Loop Counter or Repeated Increment Used to Reach a Target
description: The code drives a loop, timer or schedule by repeatedly adding a fractional step such as 0.1 to a floating-point variable and testing it against an end value, so accumulated error causes an extra or missing iteration or a final value that never equals the target.
extended_description: A step such as 0.1 or 0.01 is not exact in binary and each addition contributes a further rounding error, so after many steps the counter differs from the step multiplied by the count by an amount that grows with the count; a loop such as `for (double x = 0; x != 1.0; x += 0.1)` may never terminate, a bound like `x <= 1.0` may stop one iteration early or late, and code waiting for `t == t_end` or `angle == 360.0` may never fire. Typical locations are `for (float t = 0.0f; t < 1.0f; t += 0.1f)` in C, C++, Java, C# and JavaScript, `while x < end: x += step` in Python, animation and easing loops, plotting and tabulation ranges, sweep and calibration schedules, simulation clocks advanced with `time += dt`, embedded control loops, and `numpy.arange(0, 1, 0.1)` whose length depends on how the end point rounds. At each hit, check how the iteration count or final value is used, because an extra sample, a skipped final step or a missed trigger can break downstream logic. Loops driven by an integer counter with the floating value derived as `start + i * step`, `numpy.linspace`, steps that are exact powers of two over small ranges, and loops whose exit uses a tolerant bound and whose correctness does not depend on the exact count are not a concern. Derived from Goldberg (1991), Sections 1.1 and 1.2.
detection_methods: Search for `for` and `while` loops whose control variable is `float`, `double`, `float64`, `f32`, `f64` or a JavaScript `Number` incremented by a fractional step (`x += 0.1`, `t += dt`, `v += 0.01`)
Search for loop or wait conditions that compare an accumulated floating value with `==` or `!=` against an end value or trigger time
Search for `np.arange(` and `numpy.arange(` with non-integer steps and check whether the code assumes a particular element count or inclusion of the end point
Check simulation clocks, schedulers and animation timers that advance by repeated addition and trigger events when the clock reaches a specific value
potential_mitigations: Drive loops with an integer counter and compute the floating value as `start + i * step`, deriving the count once with `round((end - start) / step)`.
Use `numpy.linspace(start, stop, num)` or an equivalent fixed-count generator instead of `arange` with a fractional step.
Represent time in integer ticks (milliseconds, microseconds or nanoseconds) and convert to seconds only for display or physics.
Never use `==` or `!=` on an accumulated floating counter as an exit condition; where a floating bound is unavoidable, compare with an ordered test that includes a half-step margin.

name: Biased Hand-Rolled Rounding of Floating-Point Values
description: The code rounds values with a hand-written rule such as `floor(x + 0.5)` or `(int)(x + 0.5)`, or always rounds halfway cases upward, so results are biased in one direction, some inputs round incorrectly and repeated rounding drifts.
extended_description: Sending every halfway case in the same direction introduces a systematic bias; when values are rounded repeatedly, aggregated or fed back into further arithmetic the bias accumulates and totals drift, whereas round-half-to-even keeps the average error near zero and cannot drift in this way. Hand-written idioms add further faults: `floor(x + 0.5)` returns 1 for the largest double below 0.5 (0.49999999999999994) and misrounds large odd values near 2^52 because the addition itself rounds, `(int)(x + 0.5)` and `int(x + 0.5)` move negative numbers toward zero instead of to the nearest integer, and `Math.round` in Java and JavaScript rounds -2.5 to -2 while C `round` gives -3, so ports between languages change results. Look for these idioms in billing and invoicing (rounding each line then summing), tax and GST calculation, pixel and grid snapping, quantisation of sensor and audio samples, resampling, statistical reporting and fixed-point conversion in embedded code. Also check the opposite surprise, where requirements call for half-up but the code uses Python 3 `round()`, `np.round` or .NET `Math.Round`, which default to half-to-even, or rounds binary values to decimal places (`round(2.675, 2)` yields 2.67 because 2.675 is stored slightly low). Rounding done with a documented, intended mode (`BigDecimal.setScale` with an explicit `RoundingMode`, `Decimal.quantize` with an explicit rounding constant, `Math.Round(x, MidpointRounding.AwayFromZero)` where a rule requires it, C `rint` or `nearbyint` under the default mode) is not a concern. Derived from Goldberg (1991), Section 1.5.
detection_methods: Search for `floor(x + 0.5)`, `Math.floor(x + 0.5)`, `(int)(x + 0.5)`, `(long)(x + 0.5)`, `int(x + 0.5)` and `trunc(x + 0.5)` and check handling of negative values, values just below 0.5 and large magnitudes
Search for custom rounding helpers (`roundHalfUp`, `round2`, `roundToCents`, `round_to`, `toFixed`) and check which way halfway cases go and whether results are later summed or rounded again
Check monetary and reporting code that rounds each item or intermediate result inside a loop before aggregating
Check `Math.round`, `round(`, `np.round`, `Math.Round` and `toFixed` calls against the rounding rule the requirements specify, especially in code ported between languages
potential_mitigations: Use library rounding with an explicit mode, such as `Math.rint`, C `nearbyint` or `lrint`, `BigDecimal.setScale(n, RoundingMode.HALF_EVEN)`, `Decimal.quantize(..., rounding=ROUND_HALF_EVEN)` or `Math.Round(x, MidpointRounding.ToEven)`.
Prefer round-half-to-even for repeated or aggregated rounding, and use another mode only where a regulation or contract specifies it, documenting the choice in the code.
Round once at the output or reporting boundary rather than at every intermediate step, and perform decimal-place rounding on decimal types rather than on binary floating values.

name: Exact Equality Comparison of Computed Floating-Point Values
description: The code tests the result of floating-point arithmetic with `==` or `!=` against another computed or decimal-literal value, so tiny rounding differences make logically equal quantities compare unequal (or vice versa) and the wrong branch runs.
extended_description: Most decimal fractions such as 0.1, 0.2 and 0.3 have no exact binary representation, and every arithmetic step may round, so two expressions that are equal on paper (for example `0.1 + 0.2` and `0.3`, or a running total and the sum of its parts) usually differ in the last bit or two; mixing `float` and `double` adds another source of mismatch because a value rounded to single precision when stored no longer equals the same expression evaluated in double. Typical hits are `if (total == expected)`, `while (t != 1.0) t += 0.1;` loops that never terminate, `if (balance == 0.0)` after a series of debits in finance code, `if (angle == M_PI / 2)` in geometry, `float f = 0.7f; if (f == 0.7)` in C, C++, Java or C#, `x == 0.3` in Python or NumPy, `a === b` on computed `number` values in JavaScript, and unit tests using `assertEquals(double, double)` or `assert result == 1.1` with no delta. Look especially at sensor, control, statistics, ML and simulation code where a computed value selects a mode, ends a loop or matches a lookup. It is not a defect to compare against a value that was assigned or copied unchanged (a sentinel `0.0` that was never computed, a value read back from the same variable), to compare integer-valued doubles produced only by integer operations well below 2^53, or to use exact equality deliberately in a well-understood numeric algorithm or in a bit-exact regression test. Derived from Goldberg (1991), Sections 3 and 3.2.1.
detection_methods: Search for `==`, `!=`, `===` and `!==` whose operands have type `float`, `double`, `float32`, `float64`, `f32`, `f64`, JavaScript `number` or `real`, and check whether either side is the result of arithmetic, a division, a library maths call or a parsed decimal
Inspect loop conditions such as `while (x != limit)` or `for (t = 0.0; t != end; t += step)` where a fractional step must land exactly on the end value
Check comparisons that mix `float` and `double` variables or `f`-suffixed and unsuffixed literals, such as `if (f == 0.1)` where `f` is `float`
Search test code for `assertEquals(double, double)` without a delta, `Assert.AreEqual(double, double)` without a tolerance, `assert a == b` on floats and `expect(x).toBe(0.3)` in JavaScript
Use compiler warnings such as GCC and Clang `-Wfloat-equal` or static analysers that flag floating-point equality
potential_mitigations: Compare with a tolerance appropriate to the magnitudes involved, for example Python `math.isclose(a, b, rel_tol=1e-9, abs_tol=...)`, NumPy `numpy.isclose`, or a helper that combines relative and absolute bounds
Use relational tests (`<`, `>=`) for loop termination and thresholds instead of waiting for exact equality, or drive loops with an integer counter and compute the floating-point value from it
Represent money and other exact decimal quantities with `Decimal` (Python, C#), `BigDecimal` (Java) or scaled integers so that equality is exact by construction
In tests use the delta overloads, such as `assertEquals(expected, actual, delta)`, `pytest.approx`, `numpy.testing.assert_allclose` or `toBeCloseTo`

name: Fixed Absolute Tolerance Used for Floating-Point Equality
description: The code decides that two floating-point values are equal when `abs(a - b)` is below one hard-coded constant, so the test is meaningless for values much larger or smaller than the constant, is not transitive, and treats values of opposite sign as equal.
extended_description: Rounding error grows with the magnitude of the numbers, so a single absolute bound such as `1e-9` is far smaller than one ulp for values around 1e8 (making the test behave like exact equality) and far larger than the values themselves for quantities around 1e-12 (making everything equal, including a small positive and a small negative number). Because the relation is not transitive, a = b and b = c under the tolerance does not give a = c, so code that deduplicates, clusters, merges vertices, groups readings or builds equivalence classes with such a helper gets results that depend on input order. Typical hits are `fabs(a - b) < EPSILON`, `Math.abs(a - b) < 1e-6`, `abs(x - y) <= 0.0001` in Python, `Math.abs(a - b) < Number.EPSILON` in JavaScript, `if (std::abs(d) < DBL_EPSILON)` or `FLT_EPSILON` used as an absolute bound (they are relative spacings at 1.0, not general tolerances), and `nearlyEqual` or `approxEqual` helpers in geometry, physics, finance, sensor fusion and ML metric code. Also flag sign-sensitive decisions such as zero-crossing detection or direction choice that call such a helper and therefore cannot tell -1e-10 from +1e-10. Not a concern: tolerances chosen from known domain units and scales (for example 0.5 mm for survey coordinates documented as metres), combined relative and absolute checks such as `math.isclose`, ulp-distance comparisons, and tolerance tests used only for reporting rather than for identity, hashing or ordering. Derived from Goldberg (1991), Section 3.
detection_methods: Search for `abs(`, `fabs(`, `Math.abs(`, `std::abs(` and `math.Abs(` applied to a difference and compared with a literal or a constant named `EPS`, `EPSILON`, `TOL` or `TOLERANCE`, and check whether the operands can span many orders of magnitude
Flag uses of `DBL_EPSILON`, `FLT_EPSILON`, `Number.EPSILON`, `Double.MIN_VALUE`, `float.Epsilon` (C#) or `std::numeric_limits<double>::epsilon()` as an absolute comparison bound
Inspect deduplication, clustering, vertex welding, union-find and grouping code that calls an approximate-equality helper and check whether the result depends on processing order
Check sign or direction decisions (zero crossings, orientation tests, buy or sell signals) that treat values within the tolerance as equal and so lose the sign
Review NumPy `numpy.isclose` and `numpy.allclose` calls that rely on the default `atol=1e-08` for data that is very small or very large in magnitude
potential_mitigations: Use a relative tolerance combined with a small absolute floor, for example Python `math.isclose(a, b, rel_tol=..., abs_tol=...)` or `abs(a - b) <= max(rel * max(abs(a), abs(b)), abs_floor)`
Derive the tolerance from the expected error of the computation and the units of the data, and document it next to the constant
For ulp-level comparisons, compare ulp distance using `Math.ulp`, `nextafter` or `std::numeric_limits<double>::epsilon()` scaled by the operand magnitude

Do not use tolerance equality to define identity for sets, hashing, sorting or clustering; snap values to an explicit grid (for example `round(x / step)`) or use exact representations such as `Decimal` instead
Make sign-dependent decisions with explicit `< 0` and `> 0` tests and a documented dead band rather than an equality helper

name: NaN-Unaware Comparison and Loop Condition Logic
description: The code writes branch or loop conditions that assume every floating-point comparison is either true or false in a complementary way, so a NaN operand silently takes the else branch, inverts a negated test, or makes a loop run forever or exit immediately.
extended_description: With IEEE 754 every ordered comparison involving NaN (`<`, `<=`, `>`, `>=`, `==`) is false and only `!=` is true, so `!(a < b)` is not the same as `a >= b`, `if (x > max) ... else ...` sends NaN down the else path as if it were in range, and `x == x` is false for NaN. This entry is about the control-flow logic itself rather than validating where the NaN came from (see REL-193) or sorting and min/max (see REL-194). Typical hits are range checks written as `if (!(v > limit)) accept(v)` or `if (v < lo || v > hi) reject(); else use(v);` which accept NaN, a `do { ... } while (!(err < tol))` or `while (err >= tol)` iteration where NaN either loops until a timeout or exits at once as converged, `while (x < target) x += step;` when `step` can be NaN, alarm or watchdog code such as `if (temp > threshold) alarm()` that never fires on NaN, and hand-written NaN tests `x != x` or `x == x` that are optimised away under `-ffast-math`, `-ffinite-math-only`, MSVC `/fp:fast` or `fast-math` flags in Rust and CUDA. In Python and NumPy the same applies to `if a > b`, `np.where(a > b, ...)` masks and `while not converged` built from comparisons; in JavaScript to `if (!(n >= 0))`, and in Java and C# comparisons on `double` (but not `Double.compare`, `Double.equals` or `CompareTo`, which order NaN). Comparisons on integer types, on values already proven finite by `isfinite` or `isnan` checks, and branches where NaN is explicitly tested first are not a concern. Derived from Goldberg (1991), Sections 2.2.1, 2.3.1 and 3.2.2.
detection_methods: Search for negated comparisons on floating-point operands, such as `!(a < b)`, `!(x > limit)`, `not a < b` and `!(err <= tol)`, and check whether the code relies on them meaning the opposite relation

Inspect `while`, `do ... while`, `for` and `until` conditions that compare a computed floating-point value with a limit or tolerance (`err > tol`, `x < end`, `delta >= eps`), and check what happens when that value becomes NaN
Review range-check and alarm code where the in-range or safe action is in the else branch of a floating-point comparison

Search for self-comparison idioms `x != x`, `x == x`, `a !== a` and `v == v` and check the build for `-ffast-math`, `-ffinite-math-only`, `/fp:fast`, `-Ofast` or `--use_fast_math`, which permit removing them
Check iterative solvers, convergence loops and retry loops for an iteration cap that still applies when the error metric is NaN
potential_mitigations: Test for NaN explicitly before relying on a comparison result, using `std::isnan`, C `isnan`, `Double.isNaN`, `double.IsNaN`, `Number.isNaN`, `math.isnan`, `numpy.isnan`, `f64::is_nan` or Go `math.IsNaN`
Write range checks so that the accepting branch requires positive evidence, for example `if (v >= lo && v <= hi) use(v); else reject(v);`, which rejects NaN
Give every convergence or stepping loop an iteration limit and treat a NaN error metric as a failure rather than as convergence
Use library NaN tests instead of `x != x`, and avoid fast-math flags (or re-enable `-fno-finite-math-only`) in code that must detect NaN
