name: Missing NaN or Infinity Validation at Input and Output Boundaries
description: The code accepts floating-point values from outside or emits computed results to storage, other systems or actuators without checking that they are finite, so NaN or infinity enters or leaves the system and silently corrupts everything it touches.
extended_description: IEEE 754 arithmetic does not stop on invalid operations: `0/0`, `sqrt(-1)`, `log(-1)` and `inf - inf` give NaN, overflow and division of a non-zero value by zero give infinity, and once present these values propagate through every later sum, mean and product. This entry is about the boundaries where such values should be caught, not about comparison logic (REL-192) or ordering (REL-194). On the input side many parsers accept special values: C `strtod` and `atof`, Java `Double.parseDouble("NaN")` and `"Infinity"`, C# `double.Parse`, Python `float("nan")` and `float("inf")`, the Python `json` module (which reads and writes bare `NaN` and `Infinity`), JavaScript `parseFloat("Infinity")` and `Number(...)`, Go `strconv.ParseFloat` and Rust `str::parse::<f64>`, so values from HTTP parameters, config files, CSV, sensors and message queues can be NaN or infinite without any check. On the output side look for computed doubles written to databases, serialised to JSON (JavaScript `JSON.stringify` turns NaN into `null`; Python writes invalid JSON), sent as prices, quantities, setpoints or actuator commands, or used as array sizes and indices after conversion to integer, where NaN-to-int conversion is undefined in C and C++ and yields 0 in Java. Code is not affected when it validates with `isfinite`, `std::isfinite`, `Double.isFinite`, `double.IsFinite`, `Number.isFinite`, `math.isfinite` or `numpy.isfinite` before use, when the domain arithmetic provably cannot produce special values, or when NaN is a deliberate, documented missing-value marker (for example in pandas) that every consumer handles. Derived from Goldberg (1991), Sections 2.2.1 and 2.2.2.
detection_methods: Search for numeric parsing calls (`strtod`, `atof`, `sscanf` with `%f` or `%lf`, `Double.parseDouble`, `Double.valueOf`, `double.Parse`, `float(`, `parseFloat`, `Number(`, `strconv.ParseFloat`, `.parse::<f64>`) on external input and check whether the result is tested with an `isfinite`-style call before use

Inspect `json.loads`, `json.dumps`, Jackson, Gson and `JSON.stringify` usage on floating-point fields and check whether NaN or Infinity can be read in or written out unchecked (for example Python `allow_nan` left at its default)

Review code that writes computed doubles to databases, files, network messages, control outputs or financial records and check for a finiteness check after divisions, `sqrt`, `log`, `pow`, `acos` and `asin`
Check conversions of computed floats to integers (`(int)x`, `static_cast<int>`, `int(x)`, `as i32`, `Math.trunc`, `long` casts) that size buffers, index arrays or count iterations
Check aggregations such as means, variances and normalisations over input data for an upstream guard against NaN or infinite elements
potential_mitigations: Validate every externally supplied floating-point value with `isfinite`, `std::isfinite`, `Double.isFinite`, `double.IsFinite`, `Number.isFinite`, `math.isfinite`, `numpy.isfinite`, `f64::is_finite` or Go `math.IsInf` and `math.IsNaN`, and reject or explicitly map special values
Check computed results for finiteness before persisting, transmitting or acting on them, and fail safe (hold last good value, raise an error) when the check fails
Configure serialisers to refuse special values, for example Python `json.dumps(..., allow_nan=False)` and strict Jackson or System.Text.Json number handling

Guard domain-restricted calls (`sqrt`, `log`, `acos`, division) by checking their arguments, or test IEEE status flags with `fetestexcept(FE_INVALID | FE_OVERFLOW | FE_DIVBYZERO)` after a block of computation in C and C++
common_consequences: Availability; DoS: Crash, Exit, or Restart

name: Ordering, Min/Max or Sorting over Values That May Contain NaN
description: The code sorts, ranks, searches or takes the minimum or maximum of a collection of floating-point values using plain `<` or `>`, so a single NaN element makes the result depend on element order, breaks the sort contract, or poisons the aggregate.
extended_description: NaN is unordered with respect to every value, so a comparator built from `<` no longer defines a strict weak ordering once NaN is present; sorts may then leave the data partly unsorted, and in C++ `std::sort`, `std::set` and `std::map` with such keys the behaviour is undefined and can crash. This entry concerns collections and aggregates, not single branch conditions (REL-192) or validating the source of the NaN (REL-193). Typical hits are JavaScript `arr.sort((a, b) => a - b)`, C `qsort` comparators returning `a < b ? -1 : a > b`, C++ `std::sort`, `std::max_element`, `std::min` and `std::max` on doubles (whose result depends on argument order when one is NaN, unlike `std::fmax` and `std::fmin`), Python `sorted`, `min`, `max`, `heapq` and `bisect` on lists of floats, hand-written running maximum loops `if (x > best) best = x;` that skip NaN only when it is not first, and medians, percentiles, top-k selection, priority queues and plot axis scaling. Library behaviour differs and must be checked: JavaScript `Math.max` returns NaN if any argument is NaN, NumPy `np.max` and `np.argmax` propagate NaN while `np.nanmax` ignores it, Rust `f64` is only `PartialOrd` so `sort_by(|a, b| a.partial_cmp(b).unwrap())` panics, and Go `sort.Float64s` places NaN first. Not a concern: Java `Arrays.sort(double[])`, `Double.compare` and `Collections.sort` on `Double`, C# `Array.Sort` on `double[]`, Rust `f64::total_cmp`, Go `slices.Sort` and `cmp.Compare` (which give NaN a defined position), and collections already filtered with an `isnan` check. Derived from Goldberg (1991), Section 3.2.2.
detection_methods: Search for sort and ordered-container calls on floating-point data (`std::sort`, `std::stable_sort`, `std::set<double>`, `std::map<double, ...>`, `qsort`, `Array.prototype.sort`, `sorted(`, `.sort(`, `heapq`, `bisect`, `PriorityQueue`, `sort_by`) and check the comparator and whether NaN can be present

Search for `std::min`, `std::max`, `std::max_element`, `Math.max`, `Math.min`, Python `min(` and `max(`, `np.max`, `np.argmax`, `np.percentile` and `np.median` on floating-point data and check the documented NaN behaviour
Inspect hand-written extremum loops (`if (v > best) best = v`, `if (v < lo) lo = v`) and check what happens when the first or a later element is NaN
Check Rust code for `partial_cmp(...).unwrap()` in sort comparators and Go code for comparators built from `<` on `float64`
Review median, percentile, ranking, top-k, histogram binning and chart scaling functions that consume sensor, model or user data
potential_mitigations: Filter or reject NaN before ordering, using `std::isnan`, `Double.isNaN`, `Number.isNaN`, `math.isnan` or `numpy.isnan`, and report how many values were removed
Use total-order comparators that define a place for NaN, such as Java `Double.compare`, Rust `f64::total_cmp`, Go `cmp.Compare`, or C++ comparators that test `std::isnan` explicitly
Choose NaN-aware aggregates deliberately: `std::fmax` and `std::fmin` or `np.nanmax` and `np.nanmin` to ignore NaN, or `np.max` to propagate it, and document which is intended
In C++ never key `std::set`, `std::map` or `std::priority_queue` on doubles that may be NaN
common_consequences: Availability; DoS: Crash, Exit, or Restart

name: Floating-Point Values Used as Hash, Map or Set Keys
description: The code uses floating-point numbers, or records containing them, as keys in hash maps, sets, dictionaries or caches, so NaN, the two signed zeros and rounding noise create duplicate entries and failed lookups.
extended_description: Hash containers need an equality that is reflexive and consistent with the hash, but floating-point equality is not: NaN never equals itself under `==`, `+0.0` and `-0.0` compare equal yet have different bit patterns, and values computed by different routes (for example `0.1 + 0.2` and `0.3`) differ in the last bit, so a key stored from one calculation is not found from another. Language behaviour varies and each case needs checking: Python `dict` and `set` treat distinct NaN objects as different keys and merge `0.0` with `-0.0`; Go maps let every `m[math.NaN()] = v` add a new unreachable entry; Java `HashMap<Double, ...>` uses `Double.equals`, which matches NaN to NaN but separates `0.0` from `-0.0`, unlike `==`; JavaScript `Map` and `Set` use SameValueZero (NaN matches NaN, the zeros merge), while plain objects stringify keys; and C++ `std::unordered_map<double, ...>` cannot find NaN keys at all. Typical hits are memoisation caches keyed on a `double` argument, lookup tables keyed by computed prices, coordinates, timestamps in seconds or sensor readings, `groupby` on float columns, deduplication via `set(floats)` and composite keys such as `(x, y)` tuples or records with `double` fields whose `equals` and `hashCode` include them. Keys that are exact by construction (values parsed once from the same text and never recomputed, or small integers stored as doubles) and keys that are quantised first, such as `round(price * 100)`, are not a concern. Derived from Goldberg (1991), Sections 2.2.3 and 3.2.2.
detection_methods: Search for map, set and dictionary types keyed on floating-point types (`HashMap<Double`, `Map<Double`, `HashSet<Double>`, `Dictionary<double`, `std::unordered_map<double`, `std::map<double`, `map[float64]`, `HashMap<f64` via wrappers such as `OrderedFloat`) and check how the keys are produced
In Python and JavaScript, inspect `dict`, `set`, `Map`, `Set`, `functools.lru_cache` and `@cache` usage where keys or arguments are computed floats or tuples containing floats
Check `equals` and `hashCode`, `__eq__` and `__hash__`, `Equals` and `GetHashCode`, and `#[derive(Hash, PartialEq)]` implementations on records with floating-point fields
Review pandas, SQL and NumPy group-by, join and unique operations on float columns, where NaN groups may be dropped or split and near-equal values form separate groups
potential_mitigations: Quantise floating-point values to an integer grid before using them as keys, for example `Math.round(x * 1000)` or `round(x / step)`, or use exact types such as `Decimal`, `BigDecimal` or scaled integers
Normalise keys before insertion and lookup: reject or map NaN to a dedicated sentinel and convert `-0.0` to `+0.0` (for example by adding `0.0`)
Exclude floating-point fields from `equals` and `hashCode` or implement them on a quantised representation, and document the rule
Key caches on the original inputs (strings, integers, identifiers) rather than on intermediate computed doubles

name: Mishandled Signed Zero in Floating-Point Code
description: The code assumes floating-point zero has no sign, for example negating with `0 - x` or testing sign with `x < 0`, so `-0.0` is produced, lost or misclassified and functions that depend on the sign of zero return the wrong branch or display "-0".
extended_description: IEEE 754 has both `+0.0` and `-0.0`; they compare equal with `==`, but the sign survives multiplication and division and changes the result of `1/x` (plus or minus infinity), `atan2`, `copysign`, complex square roots and logarithms near branch cuts. Because `0.0 - x` gives `+0.0` when `x` is `+0.0` while `-x` gives `-0.0`, rewriting one as the other changes results, and `x < 0` or `x >= 0` cannot see the sign of a zero, so code that needs the sign (direction of approach, wind or heading vectors, underflowed negative quantities, interval endpoints) must use `signbit`. Typical hits are `y = 0 - x` or `0.0 - x` used as negation in C, C++, Java, C#, Go and Rust, `sign = (x < 0) ? -1 : 1`, `if (1.0 / x < 0)` used to detect negative zero without documenting it, `atan2(y, x)` where `y` can be `-0.0` and yields -pi instead of pi, JavaScript `Math.round(-0.3)`, `Math.sign(-0)` and `Object.is` comparisons, formatted output showing "-0.00" in reports and UIs, and builds with `-ffast-math` or `-fno-signed-zeros` that let the compiler ignore the distinction. Ordinary tests such as `if (x == 0.0)` where either zero should be treated the same, and arithmetic whose result does not depend on the sign of a zero, are not affected. Derived from Goldberg (1991), Sections 2.2.3 and 3.2.2.
detection_methods: Search for negation written as subtraction from zero (`0 - x`, `0.0 - x`, `0.0f - x`) on floating-point values, including in macros, code generators and refactored expressions, and check whether `-0.0` matters downstream

Search for sign tests on floats (`x < 0`, `x >= 0`, `x > 0 ? 1 : -1`, `Math.sign`, `np.sign`) whose results choose a branch cut, direction, quadrant or display sign, and check whether `-0.0` can reach them
Inspect calls to `atan2`, `copysign`, `csqrt`, `clog`, `1.0 / x` and `std::complex` operations where an operand may be a signed zero
Check report and UI formatting of rounded floats (`printf("%.2f")`, `toFixed`, `String.format`, f-strings) for "-0" or "-0.00" output
Check build flags for `-ffast-math`, `-fno-signed-zeros`, `/fp:fast` or `-Ofast` in code that relies on signed zero
potential_mitigations: Write negation as unary minus (`-x`) rather than `0 - x`, and keep the two forms distinct when refactoring
Test the sign of a possible zero with `std::signbit`, C `signbit`, `Math.copySign`, `math.copysign(1.0, x)`, `Object.is(x, -0)`, `f64::is_sign_negative` or Go `math.Signbit`
Normalise `-0.0` to `+0.0` (for example `x + 0.0` or `if (x == 0) x = 0.0`) before formatting, hashing or storing when the sign is not meaningful
Avoid `-fno-signed-zeros` and fast-math modes in modules that depend on branch cuts or the sign of zero

name: Division Guard Defeated by Flush-to-Zero Underflow
description: The code protects a division by checking that two floating-point operands differ (or that a value is non-zero) and then divides by a difference or derived quantity, so with flush-to-zero or denormals-are-zero enabled the denominator can still be exactly zero and the result is infinity or NaN.
extended_description: IEEE 754 gradual underflow (subnormal numbers) guarantees that if `x != y` then `x - y` is not zero, but many builds and processors switch this off: x86 FTZ and DAZ bits in MXCSR, ARM flush-to-zero modes, GPU and shader arithmetic, DSPs, and compilers that set FTZ at start-up when linking with `-ffast-math` or `-Ofast` (GCC and Clang `crtfastmath.o`), Intel `-fp-model fast`, CUDA `--use_fast_math` or `-ftz=true`, or code calling `_MM_SET_FLUSH_ZERO_MODE` and `_MM_SET_DENORMALS_ZERO_MODE` for audio or ML performance. In those environments two tiny but different values give a difference that flushes to zero, so a guard such as `if (x != y) r = 1.0 / (x - y);`, `if (a != b) slope = (fa - fb) / (a - b);` or `if (v != 0) w = 1 / (v * v);` still divides by zero. Typical locations are secant and Newton steps, finite-difference derivatives, interpolation between close samples, normalising by small norms, audio filters and physics or ML kernels on GPUs, in C, C++, CUDA, OpenCL, GLSL and HLSL, and in Rust, Go, C#, Java or Python native extensions that call such code or run in a process where a library has set FTZ. Code built with strict IEEE settings that never changes the floating-point environment, and guards that test the actual denominator (`d = x - y; if (d != 0) ... / d`) or a magnitude threshold, are not affected. Derived from Goldberg (1991), Section 2.2.4.
detection_methods: Search for conditions of the form `x != y`, `a == b` (in the negative branch) or `v != 0` that guard a division whose denominator is a different expression, such as `x - y`, `a - b` or `v * v`
Check build files and compiler options for `-ffast-math`, `-Ofast`, `-fp-model fast`, `/fp:fast`, `--use_fast_math`, `-ftz=true`, `-fdenormal-fp-math=preserve-sign` and similar flags
Search for `_MM_SET_FLUSH_ZERO_MODE`, `_MM_SET_DENORMALS_ZERO_MODE`, `_mm_setcsr`, `fesetenv`, `_controlfp`, `torch.set_flush_denormal` and ARM FPCR settings that enable flush-to-zero
Review finite-difference, secant, interpolation and normalisation code, especially in GPU kernels and shaders, for divisions by differences of values that can be very small
potential_mitigations: Compute the denominator first and guard on it directly, for example `d = x - y; if (d != 0.0) r = 1.0 / d;`, or better test `fabs(d) > threshold` chosen from the problem scale
Avoid enabling flush-to-zero or denormals-are-zero process-wide; if needed for performance, restrict it to specific kernels and document that division guards there must test the denominator
Check results with `isfinite` after divisions in code that may run with FTZ or DAZ, and handle infinity or NaN explicitly
Use `std::numeric_limits<double>::min()` or `DBL_MIN` (the smallest normal value) as a lower bound when deciding whether a denominator is safe to divide by
common_consequences: Availability; DoS: Crash, Exit, or Restart

name: Infinity Arithmetic Yielding a Plausible but Wrong Finite Result
description: The code evaluates a formula whose intermediate result overflows to infinity and is then divided into or otherwise absorbed, so the final value is a normal-looking finite number such as 0 or 1 that is badly wrong and passes any NaN or infinity check.
extended_description: In IEEE 754 an overflowing intermediate becomes infinity, and later operations such as `finite / inf = 0`, `atan(inf) = pi/2` or `exp(-inf) = 0` turn it back into an ordinary number, so the error disappears from the output instead of propagating like NaN. A typical case is normalising a component by a norm computed by squaring, such as `u = a / sqrt(a*a + b*b)`, which returns 0 instead of a value near 1 once `a*a` overflows (around 1e154 for `double`, and only about 1.8e19 for `float`, so it is common in `float32` ML and graphics code); similar forms are `x / (x*x + c)`, `p / (p*q + 1)`, `cosh`, `sinh` and `pow` inside ratios, and products of many factors in likelihood or probability code. Look in C, C++, Java, C#, Go and Rust numeric code, NumPy and PyTorch vector normalisation and softmax or sigmoid implementations, JavaScript chart and geometry code, and finance or physics formulas applied to unscaled inputs. Not a concern: formulas where the limiting value really is the correct answer (for example `1 / (1 + x*x)` tending to 0), inputs bounded well below the overflow threshold by validation, and code that already uses rescaled or library forms such as `hypot`, `log1p`, `logsumexp` or `scipy.special.expit`. Derived from Goldberg (1991), Sections 2.2.2 and 2.3.
detection_methods: Search for ratios whose denominator contains a square, product or exponential of a numerator variable, such as `x / (x*x + ...)`, `a / sqrt(a*a + b*b)`, `v / Math.sqrt(dot(v, v))` and `exp(x) / (...)`, and check the possible input range
Inspect hand-written norms, vector normalisation, softmax, sigmoid and likelihood products (`np.exp(x) / np.sum(np.exp(x))`, `np.prod(p)`) on `float32` or unscaled data
Check for `pow`, `exp`, `cosh` and `sinh` calls whose results feed a division, `atan` or `exp(-...)` that can convert an infinity back into a finite number
Review tests and validation that only check for NaN or infinity on the final output, since this defect produces finite values
potential_mitigations: Rewrite formulas to avoid forming large intermediates, for example `hypot(a, b)` or `std::hypot`, `Math.hypot`, `math.hypot`, dividing numerator and denominator by the largest term, or using `1 / (x + c / x)` style rearrangements
Use numerically stable library routines such as `logsumexp`, `scipy.special.softmax`, `scipy.special.expit`, `log1p` and `expm1`, or work in the log domain for products of probabilities
Bound or rescale inputs before evaluation, and check intermediates with `isfinite` or the `FE_OVERFLOW` flag via `fetestexcept` in C and C++
Promote `float` to `double` for intermediate squares and products when inputs can exceed about 1e19

name: Premature Overflow or Underflow in Magnitude Computation
description: The code computes a length, norm or distance by squaring components and taking a square root, so intermediate squares overflow to infinity or underflow to zero even though the true magnitude is well within range.
extended_description: Squaring a value doubles its binary exponent, so in double precision any component above roughly 1e154 makes `x*x` overflow to infinity and any component below roughly 1e-154 makes it underflow to zero or a subnormal, giving an infinite, zero or badly inaccurate magnitude although the correct answer is representable; for float the limits are near 1e19 and 1e-19. Typical forms are `sqrt(x*x + y*y)`, `Math.sqrt(dx*dx + dy*dy + dz*dz)`, `math.sqrt(sum(v*v for v in vec))`, `np.sqrt(np.sum(a**2))`, and hand-written Euclidean distance, vector length and normalisation helpers in geometry, physics, astronomy, graphics, sensor fusion and ML code; NumPy `numpy.linalg.norm` on a vector also sums unscaled squares and is affected for extreme inputs. Related forms such as `a*b/c` or `x*x/y` fail the same way when the intermediate product leaves the range before the division brings it back. Single-precision code in shaders, embedded control and float32 tensors is at greater risk because its range is much narrower. Code that already uses `hypot` (`std::hypot`, `Math.hypot`, `math.hypot`, `math.dist`, Go `math.Hypot`, Rust `f64::hypot`), BLAS `nrm2` or an explicit scaling step is not affected, and neither is code whose inputs are provably moderate, for example pixel coordinates or unit vectors. Derived from Goldberg (1991), Section 2.2.2.
detection_methods: Search for `sqrt(`, `Math.sqrt(`, `math.sqrt(`, `np.sqrt(`, `math.Sqrt(` and Rust `.sqrt()` whose argument is a sum of squared terms (`x*x + y*y`, `pow(x, 2) + pow(y, 2)`, `x**2 + y**2`, `dot(v, v)`) and check whether component magnitudes can exceed about 1e150 for double or 1e18 for float, or fall below their reciprocals
Search for `np.linalg.norm`, `numpy.linalg.norm` and hand-written `norm`, `length`, `magnitude`, `distance` and `normalize` helpers and check whether inputs can be extremely large or small
Check float32 data (`float`, `Float32Array`, `np.float32`, `f32`, GLSL or HLSL `length`) used in such formulas, where the safe range is far smaller than for double
Look for products or squares that are divided later (`a*b/c`, `x*x/y`) where the intermediate value can overflow or underflow before the final division
potential_mitigations: Replace `sqrt(x*x + y*y)` with `hypot(x, y)` (C, C++ `std::hypot`, Java and JavaScript `Math.hypot`, Python `math.hypot` or `math.dist`, Go `math.Hypot`, Rust `f64::hypot`, .NET `double.Hypot`), which avoids spurious overflow and underflow.
For long vectors, divide by the largest absolute component before squaring and multiply the result back afterwards, or call BLAS `nrm2` (for example `scipy.linalg.blas.dnrm2`).
Reorder products and quotients so intermediate values stay in range, for example `(a / c) * b` when both a and c are large.
Compute in double precision when values stored as float can approach the float range limits, and validate input magnitudes where the domain allows.

name: Complex Division Using Unscaled Textbook Formula
description: The code divides complex numbers with the textbook formula that divides by c^2 + d^2, so the quotient overflows, underflows or loses accuracy when the divisor has very large or very small components even though the true result is in range.
extended_description: Dividing (a + ib) by (c + id) by multiplying through by the conjugate forms `c*c + d*d`, which overflows to infinity once either divisor component exceeds roughly the square root of the largest double (about 1e154) and underflows to zero or a subnormal for tiny components, so the result becomes zero, infinity, NaN or a value with few correct digits. Smith's algorithm avoids forming the squared magnitude by first dividing by whichever of c and d is larger in magnitude, and later refinements (Priest; Baudin and Smith) improve it further. The defect appears in hand-written complex types (`class Complex`, `struct { double re, im; }`, `real`/`imag` pairs) and their `operator/` or `div` methods, in signal processing, FFT post-processing, impedance, transfer-function and control-system code, in GPU kernels and embedded firmware that implement complex arithmetic by hand, and in C or C++ built with `-fcx-limited-range` or `-ffast-math`, which allow GCC and Clang to use the naive formula for `_Complex` and `std::complex` division. Standard library division (C99 `_Complex` and `std::complex` without those flags, Python `complex`, NumPy complex dtypes, .NET `System.Numerics.Complex`, Apache Commons Math `Complex`) is generally not affected, and neither is code whose operands are known to have moderate magnitude, such as unit phasors. Derived from Goldberg (1991), Section 2.2.4.
detection_methods: Search complex number classes and structs (`Complex`, `cplx`, `re`/`im` or `real`/`imag` fields) for division operators or `div` methods that compute `c*c + d*d`, `norm_sqr()` or `abs2()` and divide both parts by it
Search build files for `-fcx-limited-range`, `-ffast-math`, `-Ofast` and `/fp:fast` in targets that divide `_Complex` or `std::complex` values
Check FFT, filter design, impedance, transfer-function and rotation code that divides complex values whose magnitudes can be very large or very small
Check vendored or third-party complex types to confirm that their division routine scales the divisor
potential_mitigations: Use the standard library complex division (C99 `_Complex`, `std::complex`, Python `complex`, NumPy, `System.Numerics.Complex`, Apache Commons Math `Complex`) instead of a hand-written formula.
Where division must be hand-written, implement Smith's algorithm: when |d| <= |c| compute r = d/c and den = c + d*r, otherwise swap the roles of c and d, so that no squared magnitude is formed.
Remove `-fcx-limited-range` and `-ffast-math` from translation units that divide complex numbers of arbitrary magnitude.

name: Long Floating-Point Product Without Log-Space or Scaling
description: The code multiplies many floating-point factors into a running product, so the product overflows to infinity or underflows to zero although the quantity actually needed, such as a ratio, normalised probability or logarithm, is representable.
extended_description: Every multiplication adds the exponents of its operands, so a product of a few hundred probabilities around 0.01 falls below the smallest double (about 1e-308, or 1e-45 for float) and becomes zero, while a product of many growth factors or counts reaches infinity; after that, later divisions give zero, infinity or NaN, and comparisons between candidates become ties or meaningless. Typical code is a loop such as `likelihood *= p[i]` or `prob = prob * model.prob(token)`, or a call such as `np.prod(probs)`, `math.prod(factors)`, `functools.reduce(operator.mul, xs)`, `xs.reduce((a, b) => a * b)` or `std::accumulate(..., std::multiplies<double>())`, found in naive Bayes, hidden Markov model, Bayesian network and language-model scoring, sequence alignment, compound growth over many periods, factorials and binomial coefficients computed as floats, and determinants formed as a product of pivots. Before an outright zero, values drifting into the subnormal range silently lose precision and can slow computation sharply on some processors. Products with a small, bounded number of moderate factors, and code that already sums logarithms, uses `logsumexp`, `lgamma`, `math.comb`, `slogdet`, or rescales the running product while tracking an integer exponent (`frexp`/`ldexp`), are not affected. Derived from Goldberg (1991), Section 2.3.1.
detection_methods: Search loops for `*=` or `x = x * ...` on float or double accumulators named like `prob`, `likelihood`, `product`, `score`, `growth` or `factor`, and estimate how many factors of what size can accumulate
Search for `np.prod`, `numpy.prod`, `math.prod`, `torch.prod`, `functools.reduce(operator.mul`, `reduce((a, b) => a * b)` and `std::accumulate` with `std::multiplies` over floating-point data
Check factorial, binomial, gamma and determinant code implemented as repeated floating-point multiplication, including `np.linalg.det` on large matrices
Check whether the product is later divided, normalised or compared, where a zero or infinite intermediate turns into NaN or a false tie
potential_mitigations: Accumulate logarithms (`sum(log(p))`) and combine alternatives with `logsumexp` (`scipy.special.logsumexp`, `torch.logsumexp`) when sums of products are required.
Use `lgamma`, `math.lgamma`, `scipy.special.gammaln`, `math.comb` or exact integer arithmetic for factorials and binomial coefficients.
Use `numpy.linalg.slogdet` instead of `det` for large matrices.
Where full precision is needed, periodically rescale the running product with `frexp`/`ldexp` (Java `Math.getExponent`/`Math.scalb`) and carry the exponent separately as an integer.

name: Insufficient Digits When Serialising Floating-Point Values
description: The code writes floating-point values as decimal text with fewer significant digits than needed to identify them uniquely, so parsing the text back yields a different value and stored or transmitted data silently changes.
extended_description: A double needs up to 17 significant decimal digits, and a float up to 9, for its decimal text to convert back to exactly the same binary value; with fewer digits several distinct binary values print identically, so save and reload cycles, text protocols, caches keyed on printed values, checksums and equality checks after a round trip all break. Common causes are `printf`-style formats `%f`, `%g`, `%.6g`, `%.7g` or `%.15g` used for data rather than display, C++ `std::to_string` (which uses `%f`) and streams with default precision 6 or `std::setprecision(15)`, `String.format("%.10f")`, .NET Framework `double.ToString()` (15 digits by default) or `ToString("F6")`, JavaScript `toFixed` and `toPrecision`, Python `'%g' % x`, `str(round(x, 6))` or `f"{x:.10f}"` in exports, and JSON, XML, YAML or CSV writers configured with fixed decimal places (for example RapidJSON `SetMaxDecimalPlaces` or custom encoders). Fixed-point formats such as `%f` also discard all significance for very small values. Shortest round-trip formatting is not affected: Python `repr`, `str` and `json.dumps`, Java `Double.toString` and `Float.toString`, JavaScript `String(x)` and `JSON.stringify`, Go `strconv.FormatFloat(x, 'g', -1, 64)`, Rust `Display`, .NET Core 3.0 and later default `ToString()` or `"R"`, C++17 `std::to_chars`, and `%.17g`, `%.9g` for float, or `%a`; values formatted purely for people to read are also not a concern. Derived from Goldberg (1991), Sections 2.1.2 and 4.2.
detection_methods: Search for `printf`, `fprintf`, `sprintf`, `snprintf`, `std::format` and `String.format` format strings with `%f`, `%e`, `%g` or an explicit precision below 17 for double (below 9 for float) whose output is stored, transmitted or parsed again

Search for `std::to_string`, `std::setprecision`, `toFixed`, `toPrecision`, `ToString("F`, `ToString("G15`, `round(x, n)` before string conversion, and `:.Nf` or `%.Nf` formatting in serialisation, export, configuration and persistence code
Check JSON, XML, YAML and CSV writers (custom encoders, `SetMaxDecimalPlaces`, decimal-place or precision options) for truncated float output
Check .NET Framework code that calls `double.ToString()` without `"R"` or `"G17"`, and tests that compare printed numbers instead of parsed values
potential_mitigations: Use shortest round-trip conversions: Python `repr`, Java `Double.toString`, JavaScript `String(x)`, Go `strconv.FormatFloat(x, 'g', -1, 64)`, C++17 `std::to_chars`, .NET `ToString("R")` or the .NET Core default `ToString()`.
Where a printf-style format is required, use `%.17g` for double and `%.9g` for float, or `%a` for exact hexadecimal output.
Keep display formatting separate from storage formatting so that values rounded for people never flow back into data.
Add a round-trip test that formats, parses and compares bit patterns for representative values including very small and very large ones.

name: Double Rounding Through an Intermediate Precision
description: The code rounds a value first to an intermediate precision and then again to the target precision, so results lying near a halfway point end up one ulp away from the correctly rounded value.
extended_description: Rounding twice is not equivalent to rounding once: if the first rounding lands exactly on a halfway point of the narrower format, the second rounding applies round-half-to-even to a value that was not genuinely halfway, and the final result differs in its last bit from the correctly rounded answer. This happens with x87 code generation (32-bit x86 builds without SSE2, `long double` intermediates, `FLT_EVAL_METHOD == 2`), where results are rounded to 64-bit extended precision and then again to double when stored; when decimal text is parsed to float via double, as in `(float)strtod(s, NULL)`, `(float)atof(s)`, `(float)Double.parseDouble(s)`, `(float)double.Parse(s)`, `np.float32(float(s))`, `Math.fround(parseFloat(s))` or `s.parse::<f64>()? as f32`; when a 64-bit integer is converted to float through double; and when decimal values are rounded in stages, such as `round(round(x, 3), 2)` or a `BigDecimal` rounded with `setScale` and then converted with `doubleValue()`. The error is rare and usually one ulp, but it breaks bit-for-bit reproducibility across platforms, golden-file and cross-language consistency tests, hashing of numeric results, and financial rounding rules. A single direct conversion to the target type (`strtof`, `Float.parseFloat`, .NET Core `float.Parse`, Go `strconv.ParseFloat(s, 32)`, Rust `s.parse::<f32>()`), 64-bit or SSE2 builds without `long double` intermediates, and staged conversions whose first step is exact are not affected. Derived from Goldberg (1991), Section 4.2.
detection_methods: Search for parsed doubles narrowed to float: `(float)strtod`, `(float)atof`, `(float)Double.parseDouble`, `(float)double.Parse`, `np.float32(float(`, `Math.fround(parseFloat(` and `as f32` applied to a parsed `f64`
Check C and C++ build settings for 32-bit x86 targets without `-msse2 -mfpmath=sse`, MSVC `/arch:IA32`, `long double` intermediates, and code that depends on `FLT_EVAL_METHOD`

Search for nested or staged rounding such as `round(round(x, a), b)`, consecutive `setScale` or `quantize` calls followed by `doubleValue()` or `float()`, and `int64` to `float` conversions routed through `double`
Prioritise code with bit-exact expectations: reproducibility checks, golden outputs, numeric hashing and regulated rounding
potential_mitigations: Convert text directly to the target precision with `strtof`, `Float.parseFloat`, `float.Parse`, Go `strconv.ParseFloat(s, 32)` or Rust `s.parse::<f32>()`.

Build x86 code with SSE2 floating point (`-msse2 -mfpmath=sse`, or 64-bit targets) so that each double operation is rounded once, and avoid `long double` intermediates where results must match other platforms.
Round decimal values once, directly to the required number of places, with `Decimal.quantize` or `BigDecimal.setScale` and an explicit `RoundingMode`.
Where an intermediate format cannot be avoided, use round-to-odd for the first step or verify against a correctly rounded reference in tests.

name: Narrow Precision Variable Compared With Wider Expression
description: The code compares a variable stored in a narrower floating-point type with an expression evaluated in a wider type, so a value assigned from that same expression no longer compares equal to it.
extended_description: When a quotient such as one third, or a decimal such as 0.1, is computed in double and stored in a float, the stored value is rounded to 24 significand bits; comparing it later with the same expression evaluated in double compares a rounded value with an unrounded one, so the test fails even though the source code looks symmetrical. The same effect occurs in C and C++ when `FLT_EVAL_METHOD` is 1 or 2, or on x87 targets, where expressions are evaluated in double or extended precision while variables in memory hold the declared type, so `x == y` can depend on whether a value stayed in a register, on optimisation level, and on debug versus release builds. Typical cases are `float ratio = 1.0 / 3.0; if (ratio == 1.0 / 3.0)` and `float f = 0.1f; ... if (f == 0.1)` in C, C++, Java and C#, a `float` struct field or `Float32Array` element compared with a double literal in JavaScript, `np.float32` arrays compared with Python floats, and threshold or sentinel checks like `if (gain == 0.7)` where gain is a float. Comparisons where both sides have the same type and no excess precision is used, comparisons with values exactly representable in both types (0.5, 2.0, small integers), and Go or Rust code, which cannot mix widths without an explicit conversion, are not affected. Derived from Goldberg (1991), Section 3.2.1.
detection_methods: Search for `==` and `!=` (and `<=` or `>=` used as equality guards) where one operand is a `float`, `Single`, `f32`, `np.float32` or `Float32Array` element and the other is a double literal without an `f` suffix or a double-typed expression
Search for float variables or fields initialised from double expressions (`float x = a / b;` with double operands, `float f = 0.1;`) that are later compared with the same expression
Check C and C++ builds for 32-bit x87 code generation, `FLT_EVAL_METHOD` values other than 0, and `-ffloat-store` or `volatile` workarounds that indicate register-precision comparison problems
Check unit tests and assertions that use exact equality between float results and double expected values
potential_mitigations: Compare values of the same type: narrow the wider expression explicitly (`ratio == (float)(1.0 / 3.0)`) or store both values in double.

Use a tolerance suited to the narrower type, for example a relative bound based on `FLT_EPSILON` or `Math.ulp(f)`, `math.isclose` with a float32-sized `rel_tol`, or `np.isclose`, instead of exact equality.
Write float literals (`0.1f`) consistently in float code and enable warnings such as `-Wfloat-equal`, `-Wdouble-promotion` and `-Wfloat-conversion`.
On x86, compile with SSE2 floating point so that evaluation width matches the declared types.

name: Single-Precision Constant or Operand Limiting Double Computation
description: The code mixes a single-precision literal, field or variable into a double-precision calculation, so the result is only as accurate as the float value even though the computation and the result type are double.
extended_description: A float holds only about 7 significant decimal digits, and widening it to double does not recover the digits already lost: `0.1f` promoted to double is 0.100000001490116..., so every result derived from it carries a relative error near 1e-8 instead of 1e-16. In C, C++, Java and C# this shows up as `f`-suffixed literals (`0.1f`, `3.14159f`, `1e-3f`) inside double expressions, float constants such as `static const float PI = 3.14159265f` or `FLT_EPSILON` used in double code, float struct fields, configuration values or sensor readings feeding double maths, and single-precision functions (`sqrtf`, `sinf`, `powf`, `std::sin` on a float argument) inside double code paths; in Python and JavaScript it arrives through `np.float32` arrays, `astype(np.float32)`, `torch.float32` tensors and `Float32Array` storage mixed into double computations; in Go and Rust through stored `float32` or `f32` values widened with `float64(v)` or `as f64`. It matters most for long integrations, timekeeping, geodesy and coordinate code (latitude and longitude in float32 resolve only to around a metre), and scientific or financial code that expects double accuracy. Code that is deliberately single precision throughout (graphics, ML inference, DSP) and float literals whose values are exactly representable (`0.5f`, `2.0f`, `1024.0f`) are not affected. Derived from Goldberg (1991), Section 3.2.1.
detection_methods: Search for literals with an `f` or `F` suffix (regex `[0-9.]f\b`) and `(float)` casts inside expressions whose result is assigned to a `double`, passed to a double parameter or combined with double variables

Search for `float`, `Single`, `f32` and `float32` fields, constants and configuration values (`static const float`, `FLT_EPSILON`, `float PI`) used in double arithmetic, especially time, coordinate, distance and money calculations
Search for single-precision maths calls (`sqrtf`, `sinf`, `cosf`, `powf`, `expf`, `logf`) and `Math.fround` in otherwise double code
Search for `np.float32`, `astype(np.float32)`, `dtype=np.float32`, `torch.float32` and `Float32Array` data that feeds computations whose outputs are expected to have double accuracy
potential_mitigations: Remove `f` suffixes and float casts from constants and operands in double computations, and declare such constants as `double` (or use `M_PI`, `Math.PI`, `math.pi`).
Store quantities that need double accuracy, such as timestamps, coordinates and accumulators, in double fields and arrays (`float64`, `Float64Array`).
Enable diagnostics such as `-Wdouble-promotion` and `-Wfloat-conversion`, clang-tidy `bugprone-narrowing-conversions`, and equivalent Java and C# analysers.
Where data must be stored as float, document the reduced accuracy and confirm that downstream tolerances allow for about 7 significant digits.

name: Integer Division Where Floating-Point Division Was Intended
description: The code divides two integer operands and only afterwards converts or combines the quotient with floating-point values, so the fractional part is discarded and averages, ratios and percentages are wrong.
extended_description: In C, C++, Java, C#, Go and Rust the kind of division performed by `/` is chosen from its operand types, not from the variable that receives the result or the surrounding expression, so `double avg = total / count;` with integer `total` and `count`, `offset + hits / attempts`, `pct = 100 * done / all`, `ratio = (double)(a / b)` or `scale = 1 / n` truncate toward zero before any conversion happens; `1 / 2` is 0 and `-7 / 2` is -3. The bug is frequent in averaging and statistics code, progress and percentage reporting, scale factors, timing and unit conversion (`elapsed_ms / 1000`, `bytes / 1024`), resampling ratios and grid or pixel arithmetic, and it often survives testing because sample inputs divide evenly; it also appears in macros whose arguments happen to be integers, and the same semantics exist in Python 2, Ruby, Kotlin, Swift and SQL integer columns. Divisions where at least one operand is already floating point (`total / (double)count`, `sum / 2.0`, `(float)a / b`), deliberate integer arithmetic such as index, page, bucket or chunk calculations, Python 3 `/` (true division) and JavaScript or TypeScript `/` (always floating point) are not affected. Derived from Goldberg (1991), Section 3.2.1.
detection_methods: Search for `/` where both operands are integer-typed (`int`, `long`, `size_t`, `usize`, `i32`, `Integer`, `.size()`, `.length`, `.Count`, `len(...)`, loop counters) and the result is assigned to or combined with `double`, `float`, `f64` or `decimal`

Search for casts applied after the division (`(double)(a / b)`, `static_cast<double>(a / b)`, `float64(a / b)`, `(a / b) as f64`) and integer literal divisions such as `1 / 2`, `1 / n` and `100 / total`
Check averages, percentages, rates, ratios and unit conversions for integer operands, especially where tests use evenly divisible values
Run analysers such as clang-tidy `bugprone-integer-division`, SpotBugs `ICAST_IDIV_CAST_TO_DOUBLE` and ReSharper `PossibleLossOfFraction`
potential_mitigations: Convert an operand before dividing: `total / (double)count`, `static_cast<double>(a) / b`, `float64(a) / float64(b)`, `a as f64 / b as f64`.
Write floating literals (`2.0`, `100.0`) in mixed expressions so that the division is performed in floating point.
Where an integer quotient is intended, make it explicit with a named helper or comment so reviewers and analysers can tell it apart.
Check the divisor for zero, because switching to floating-point division turns a crash into infinity or NaN.

name: Large Integer Stored in Floating-Point Type
description: The code holds integers such as identifiers, timestamps or counters in a floating-point type, so values beyond the significand range (2^24 for float, 2^53 for double) are silently rounded to a neighbouring integer.
extended_description: A binary floating-point value has a fixed number of significand bits, 24 for float and 53 for double, so above 2^24 (16,777,216) a float cannot represent every integer and above 2^53 (about 9.007e15) a double cannot; larger values round to the nearest representable one, so increments are lost (`f + 1 == f`), distinct identifiers collide and lookups by equality fail. The most common case is JavaScript and TypeScript, where every `Number` is a double, so 64-bit database keys, snowflake-style IDs, nanosecond timestamps and 64-bit hashes decoded by `JSON.parse`, `parseInt` or `Number()` are corrupted; similar losses occur with JSON decoders that map all numbers to double (Go `encoding/json` into `interface{}` without `UseNumber`, dynamic JSON APIs in C# and Java, jq), pandas integer columns that become `float64` once they contain missing values, float counters or accumulators in C, C++ and shader code that stop increasing at 16,777,216, epoch milliseconds or microseconds stored in a float, and conversions of `long`, `int64` or `u64` to double in Java, C#, Go and Rust. Integers guaranteed to stay below 2^53 in double (2^24 in float), JavaScript `BigInt`, Python `int`, and identifiers carried as strings are not affected. Derived from Goldberg (1991), Section 2.1.
detection_methods: Search JavaScript and TypeScript for `JSON.parse`, `parseInt`, `Number(` and unary `+` applied to IDs, keys, hashes and timestamps that can exceed `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER`, and check whether the API sends them as numbers rather than strings
Search Go for `json.Unmarshal` into `interface{}` or `map[string]interface{}` without `Decoder.UseNumber()`, and pandas code where integer ID columns may contain NaN and become `float64`

Search for float or double variables used as counters, indices, identifiers or time values (`float frameCount`, `double id`, `float timeMs`), and for conversions such as `(double)longValue`, `float64(int64Value)` and `as f64` on `i64` or `u64`
Check equality comparisons, map keys, set membership and deduplication on values that have passed through a floating-point type
potential_mitigations: Keep identifiers, hashes and large counters in 64-bit integer types, `BigInt` or strings end to end, and have APIs emit 64-bit IDs as JSON strings.
Use lossless decoding options such as Go `Decoder.UseNumber()`, a big-integer JSON parser or reviver in JavaScript, and nullable integer dtypes (`Int64`) in pandas.
Store timestamps as integer epoch units (for example `int64` nanoseconds or milliseconds) and convert to floating point only for display or short relative intervals.
Add checks against `Number.MAX_SAFE_INTEGER` or 2^53 wherever a value must pass through a double.

name: Real-Valued Exponentiation With Negative Base or Undefined Cases
description: The code raises a floating-point base to a floating-point power without handling negative bases or the indeterminate cases, so it receives NaN, an exception, a complex number or a convention-dependent value where a real result was expected.
extended_description: Library power functions handle real exponents in a way that only allows a negative base when the exponent is an exact integer: `pow(-8.0, 1.0/3.0)` returns NaN rather than -2 in C, C++, Java, C#, Go, Rust and JavaScript, Python `math.pow` raises ValueError, Python `(-8) ** (1/3)` silently returns a complex number, and `numpy.power` returns NaN with a runtime warning; whether `pow(-2.0, e)` works also depends on `e` being exactly integral, so a computed exponent of 3.0000000000000004 fails. Edge cases follow conventions that may not match the domain: `pow(x, 0.0)` is 1 even for NaN x, `pow(0.0, -1.0)` is infinity, and `pow(1.0, NaN)` and `pow(1.0, inf)` are 1 in C, C++, Python and Go but NaN in Java `Math.pow` and JavaScript, while `0^0` varies between SQL engines, spreadsheets and symbolic libraries. The defect appears in cube roots of signed values (geometry, CIELAB and other colour conversions, audio shaping), gamma and tone curves applied to values that can turn negative after filtering or interpolation, generalised means, Box-Cox and similar statistical transforms, and finance formulas with negative rates or fractional periods. Integer powers via `powi`, integer `**` or repeated multiplication, bases guaranteed non-negative by clamping or validation, and dedicated `cbrt` functions are not affected. Derived from Goldberg (1991), Section 3.2.1.
detection_methods: Search for `pow(`, `powf(`, `std::pow`, `Math.pow`, `Math.Pow`, `math.pow`, `math.Pow`, Rust `powf`, `np.power` and `**` with a non-integer or computed exponent, and check whether the base can be negative or zero
Search for fractional exponents written as `1.0/3.0`, `1/3`, `1/gamma`, `1.0/n` or `0.5` where a signed root such as `cbrt` was intended
Check gamma, colour, audio, statistical transform and finance functions for bases that can become negative or zero after subtraction, filtering or interpolation
Check code that relies on particular results for `0^0`, `1^inf`, `1^NaN` or zero raised to a negative power, especially logic ported between C, Java, JavaScript, Python and SQL
potential_mitigations: Use `cbrt` (`std::cbrt`, `Math.cbrt`, Python 3.11 `math.cbrt`, `numpy.cbrt`, `f64::cbrt`) for cube roots, and `copysign(pow(fabs(x), y), x)` where an odd root of a signed value is meant.
Clamp or validate the base before fractional powers in gamma, colour and curve code, and handle the negative case explicitly.
Use integer exponentiation (`powi`, integer `**`, repeated multiplication) when the exponent is integral by design.
Define and test the required behaviour for 0^0, 1^inf, NaN inputs and zero bases with negative exponents instead of relying on library conventions, and check results with `isnan` or `np.errstate`.
common_consequences: Availability; DoS: Crash, Exit, or Restart

name: Unsafe Floating-Point Optimisation Flags Enabled in Build
description: The build enables value-changing floating-point optimisation modes such as `-ffast-math`, `-Ofast` or `/fp:fast`, so the compiler may reorder, contract or simplify arithmetic and assume NaN and infinity never occur, which silently changes results and breaks code that relies on IEEE 754 semantics.
extended_description: Under these modes the compiler may treat floating-point values as if they obeyed real-number algebra: it can reassociate sums, replace division by multiplication with a reciprocal, fuse multiply-add, drop signed zeros, assume operands are finite and, on GCC and Clang, link start-up code that switches the whole process to flush-to-zero. Code that depends on exact IEEE behaviour then fails without warning, for example compensated (Kahan or Neumaier) summation whose correction term is simplified to zero, `isnan(x)`, `std::isinf` or `x != x` tests folded to false, and results that differ between debug and release builds or between machines. The settings usually live in build files rather than source: `CMAKE_CXX_FLAGS`, `target_compile_options` or `add_compile_options` in CMakeLists.txt, `CFLAGS`/`CXXFLAGS` in a Makefile, `extra_compile_args` in setup.py or pyproject.toml, `copts` in Bazel BUILD files, meson.build, `<FloatingPointModel>Fast</FloatingPointModel>` in .vcxproj files, `--use_fast_math` for CUDA, Intel compilers whose default model is a fast one, `rustflags` in .cargo/config.toml or Rust `fadd_fast`/`fmul_fast` intrinsics, and Numba `@njit(fastmath=True)` decorators, plus in-source `#pragma GCC optimize('fast-math')` or `__attribute__((optimize('Ofast')))`. Plain `-O2`/`-O3`, `/fp:precise`, `/fp:strict` and `-ffp-contract=off` are not findings, and pure Java, C#, JavaScript, Go and CPython code is unaffected unless it loads native extensions built with these flags. A fast-math setting confined to a self-contained kernel (shaders, game physics, ML inference) that has been validated against a tolerance and contains no NaN checks, compensated arithmetic or exact comparisons is acceptable. Derived from Goldberg (1991), Section 3.2.3.
detection_methods: Search CMakeLists.txt, *.cmake, Makefile, *.mk, meson.build, BUILD and BUILD.bazel, setup.py, pyproject.toml, *.vcxproj, *.csproj, Cargo.toml and .cargo/config.toml for -ffast-math, -Ofast, -funsafe-math-optimizations, -fassociative-math, -freciprocal-math, -ffinite-math-only, -fno-signed-zeros, /fp:fast, -fp-model fast, --use_fast_math and FloatingPointModel Fast

Search source for `#pragma GCC optimize`, `__attribute__((optimize(...)))`, `#pragma float_control`, `#pragma clang fp`, Numba `fastmath=True` or `fastmath={...}` arguments, and Rust `*_fast` float intrinsics, and note which functions or files they cover

In each affected file, check for NaN or infinity tests (isnan, isinf, isfinite, `x != x`), compensated summation or error-free transformations, exact equality comparisons, and parenthesised evaluation order that the flag would void

Check whether a shared library or Python extension built with fast-math is loaded into a process that also runs precision-sensitive code, since its start-up code may enable flush-to-zero for every thread
potential_mitigations: Remove the unsafe flags from global build settings and use -O2 or -O3 with the default or `/fp:precise` model, re-enabling only a reviewed safe subset such as `-fno-math-errno` where it is needed.

Scope any remaining fast-math setting to the specific validated files or functions, for example with `set_source_files_properties` in CMake or per-function attributes, and keep NaN checks and compensated arithmetic in separately compiled units.
In Numba, pass a restricted flag set such as `fastmath={'contract', 'arcp'}` instead of `True`, and never enable `nnan` or `ninf` in functions that test for NaN or infinity.
Add regression tests that run the release build against reference results with explicit tolerances and with NaN, infinity, signed zero and subnormal inputs.

name: Algebraically Equivalent Rewrite Changes Floating-Point Result
description: The code replaces a floating-point expression with a form that is equal only in exact real arithmetic, such as `x / 10` with `x * 0.1` or a factored product with an expanded one, so results change and accuracy properties of the original form are lost.
extended_description: Decimal fractions such as 0.1 and 0.01 have no exact binary value, so multiplying by a rounded reciprocal can differ by one unit in the last place from a correctly rounded division, which matters when the result is compared for equality, rounded to cents, used as a bucket or bin boundary, hashed or printed. Factoring and expanding change which rounding errors occur: `x*y - x*z` subtracts two already rounded products and can lose most of its significant digits when y and z are close, whereas `x*(y - z)` does not, so expanding a carefully factored expression (or factoring one whose accuracy analysis assumed the other form) changes results; regrouping or reordering a sum likewise changes the answer whenever terms differ greatly in magnitude. These hand-written rewrites appear in C and C++ hot loops (`const double inv = 1.0 / n;` then `x * inv`), Java and C# unit-conversion and money code, JavaScript `amount * 0.01` in place of `amount / 100`, NumPy code reshaped for vectorisation, parallel reductions that split a sum into partial sums, and refactors that simplify `(a + b) - a` to `b` or remove the correction term of compensated summation. Multiplying by the reciprocal of a power of two (`x * 0.5` for `x / 2`, `x * 0.25`) is exact and not a finding, nor is swapping the operands of a single addition or multiplication, nor rewrites in code whose results are only used within a loose documented tolerance such as graphics or approximate ML features. Derived from Goldberg (1991), Section 3.2.3.
detection_methods: Search for multiplication by decimal literals that are not powers of two (`* 0.1`, `* 0.01`, `* 0.001`, `* 1e-3`, `* (1.0 / n)`) and precomputed reciprocal variables named like inv, recip or oneOver, and check whether an exact division was intended because the result is compared, rounded, binned or displayed
Search diffs and refactored code for factored versus expanded products (`a*b - a*c` against `a*(b - c)`, `x*x - y*y` against `(x - y)*(x + y)`) and check whether the operands can be close in value

Look for regrouped or reordered sums: terms moved across parentheses, accumulation split for parallelism (OpenMP `reduction`, Java `parallelStream().reduce`, C# `Parallel.For` partial sums, NumPy pairwise versus loop sums) where reproducible results are expected, and simplifications such as `(a + b) - a` to `b`
Check compensated summation and error-free transformation code (Kahan, Neumaier, TwoSum, FastTwoSum, Dekker split) for any term that has been algebraically simplified away
potential_mitigations: Keep the division (`x / 10.0`) where the result must be correctly rounded, and multiply by a reciprocal only when the divisor is a power of two or a documented tolerance allows it.
Choose the factored or expanded form deliberately for accuracy, record the reason in a comment, and protect it from later simplification with a unit test on inputs where the forms differ.
Use `math.fsum`, a Kahan or Neumaier summation helper, or a fixed reduction order where sums must be accurate or reproducible.
Represent money with `Decimal`, `BigDecimal` or integer minor units so that scaling by powers of ten is exact.

name: Floating-Point Environment Modified Without Restoration on All Exits
description: The code changes the floating-point rounding mode, exception trap masks or flush-to-zero settings and does not restore the previous state on every return, exception or jump path, so unrelated code later runs under an unexpected arithmetic mode.
extended_description: The floating-point control state (rounding direction, trap enables, and the flush-to-zero and denormals-are-zero bits in the x86 MXCSR register or the Arm FPCR) is held per thread and applies to everything that thread executes, so a change made for one calculation leaks into library calls, later requests handled by pooled worker threads, and callers that assume round-to-nearest with all traps masked. Typical sources are C and C++ calls to `fesetround(FE_UPWARD)`, `fesetenv`, `feenableexcept`, `_controlfp`, `_controlfp_s`, `_control87`, `_MM_SET_ROUNDING_MODE`, `_MM_SET_FLUSH_ZERO_MODE`, `_MM_SET_DENORMALS_ZERO_MODE`, `_mm_setcsr` or inline assembly writing MXCSR or FPCR, C# code that calls `_controlfp` through P/Invoke, and Python code that calls `numpy.seterr(...)` globally; interval arithmetic, directed rounding for error bounds, audio callbacks and plug-ins are frequent users. The leak happens when a function returns early, throws, breaks out of a loop or uses `longjmp` between the change and the restore, when only part of the state is saved, or when the change is made inside a library or plug-in loaded into a host process; separately, unless the file is compiled with `#pragma STDC FENV_ACCESS ON`, `-frounding-math` or `/fp:strict`, the compiler may move or constant-fold arithmetic across the mode change. Saving with `fegetenv` or `feholdexcept` and restoring with `fesetenv` or `feupdateenv` in a destructor, scope guard or `finally` block, using `with numpy.errstate(...)`, and a single documented setting made at program or thread start-up are not findings. Derived from Goldberg (1991), Sections 2.3.3 and 3.2.2.
detection_methods: Search for fesetround, fesetenv, feupdateenv, feholdexcept, feenableexcept, fedisableexcept, _controlfp, _controlfp_s, _control87, __control87_2, _MM_SET_ROUNDING_MODE, _MM_SET_FLUSH_ZERO_MODE, _MM_SET_DENORMALS_ZERO_MODE, _mm_setcsr, ldmxcsr and FPCR writes, and pair each change with its restore
For each change, follow every return, throw, break, goto and longjmp between the change and the restore, and check whether the restore runs from a destructor, scope guard or finally block
Search Python for numpy.seterr and numpy.seterrcall calls outside a `with numpy.errstate(...)` block, and for decimal.getcontext() changes to rounding or traps not made through decimal.localcontext()

Check that files changing the rounding mode are compiled with `#pragma STDC FENV_ACCESS ON`, `-frounding-math` or `/fp:strict` (look in CMakeLists.txt, Makefile or .vcxproj), so the compiler does not move operations across the change
Check thread-pool workers, audio callbacks and plug-in entry points that set flush-to-zero or trap masks to see whether the state is reset before the thread returns to the host
potential_mitigations: Save the full environment with `fegetenv` or `feholdexcept` before changing it and restore it with `fesetenv` or `feupdateenv` in an RAII guard or a cleanup path that every exit passes through.
In Python use `with numpy.errstate(...)` and `with decimal.localcontext()` instead of changing global settings.
Prefer libraries that take the rounding direction as a parameter, or compute outward bounds with `nextafter`, rather than changing the global rounding mode.
Set flush-to-zero or trap masks once per thread as a documented policy rather than toggling them around individual calls, and reset them before returning pooled or host-owned threads.
Compile files that change the environment with FENV_ACCESS enabled or the compiler's strict floating-point model.

name: Floating-Point Format Properties Estimated by Probing Loops
description: The code computes machine epsilon, the smallest positive value or the overflow threshold at run time with a halving or doubling loop instead of reading library constants, so the result depends on optimisation settings and evaluation precision and can be wrong or fail to terminate.
extended_description: A probe such as `for (e = 1.0; 1.0 + e / 2 != 1.0; e /= 2) ;` only works if every intermediate sum is rounded to the declared type: an optimiser that rewrites the test as `e / 2 != 0` turns it into a search for the smallest subnormal, x87 extended-precision registers or `FLT_EVAL_METHOD` 2 return the epsilon of the wider format, and fast-math or flush-to-zero settings move where the loop stops. Doubling loops that run until a value becomes infinite can spin forever when `-ffinite-math-only` lets the compiler assume `isinf` is always false. The pattern appears in older numerical C and Fortran-derived code (dlamch-style routines), in ported Java, C#, JavaScript and Python helpers that compute `EPS`, `TINY` or `HUGE` at start-up, and in tolerance utilities that try to detect the hardware. Using `DBL_EPSILON`, `FLT_EPSILON`, `DBL_MIN`, `DBL_TRUE_MIN`, `std::numeric_limits<T>::epsilon()`, `min()`, `denorm_min()` and `max()`, Java `Math.ulp(1.0)` and `Double.MIN_NORMAL`, JavaScript `Number.EPSILON`, Python `sys.float_info` and `numpy.finfo`, Go `math.SmallestNonzeroFloat64` or Rust `f64::EPSILON` is the fix and not a finding, though note that C# `double.Epsilon` is the smallest subnormal rather than machine epsilon, so code using it as a relative tolerance is suspect. Test code that deliberately probes a platform is out of scope. Derived from Goldberg (1991), Section 3.2.3.
detection_methods: Search for loops that repeatedly halve or double a floating-point variable and compare against 1 or 0, such as `while (1.0 + eps > 1.0)`, `while (1 + eps != 1)`, `eps *= 0.5` or `eps /= 2` inside a loop, or loops multiplying by 2 until isinf or overflow
Search for names such as eps, machEps, machine_epsilon, calc_epsilon, compute_eps, dlamch, slamch, TINY and HUGE and check whether they are assigned from a loop rather than a constant

Check the build flags for files containing such loops (-ffast-math, -ffinite-math-only, -mfpmath=387, 32-bit x86 builds without SSE2, /fp:fast) in CMakeLists.txt, Makefile, setup.py or .vcxproj, since they change the result
Check uses of C# `double.Epsilon` or `float.Epsilon` as a relative comparison tolerance, because they are the smallest subnormal values
potential_mitigations: Replace the loop with the language constant: DBL_EPSILON or std::numeric_limits<double>::epsilon() in C and C++, Math.ulp(1.0) in Java, Number.EPSILON in JavaScript, sys.float_info.epsilon or numpy.finfo(dtype).eps in Python, f64::EPSILON in Rust, and the matching minimum, maximum and denorm_min constants.
Where the spacing at a particular value is needed, use nextafter, std::nextafter, Math.ulp, math.ulp or numpy.spacing rather than scaling epsilon by hand.
If a run-time probe is genuinely required, store each intermediate in a volatile variable of the target type and compile that file without fast-math or extended-precision evaluation.

name: Floating-Point Division by Zero Assumed to Raise an Error
description: The code relies on an exception, signal or crash to catch floating-point division by zero, overflow or invalid operations, but IEEE 754 arithmetic by default returns infinity or NaN and carries on, so bad values propagate silently.
extended_description: With traps masked, which is the default in almost every environment, `1.0 / 0.0` yields infinity, `0.0 / 0.0`, `inf - inf` and `sqrt(-1.0)` yield NaN, and overflow yields infinity, with only a sticky status flag recording the event; a NaN then compares false with everything, so checks like `if (x > limit) reject` let it through. Typical faults are a Java `catch (ArithmeticException)` or C# `catch (DivideByZeroException)` around double arithmetic (those exceptions come only from integer division and, in C#, from `decimal`), a C `signal(SIGFPE, ...)` handler expected to catch float division without traps being enabled, JavaScript code expecting `x / 0` to throw, Go code that assumes float division panics like integer division, NumPy array division that only emits a RuntimeWarning, and validation that tests for null or relies on a `try` block instead of a finiteness check. Python built-in floats are a partial exception, since `1.0 / 0.0` and `math.sqrt(-1)` raise `ZeroDivisionError` and `ValueError`, but NumPy scalars and arrays, `math.inf` arithmetic and most multiplications that overflow do not raise, so code mixing them is easy to get wrong. Code that checks the divisor or validates results with `isfinite` or `isnan`, enables traps deliberately (`feenableexcept`, `numpy.errstate(divide='raise')`) or intentionally uses infinity as a sentinel is not a finding. Derived from Goldberg (1991), Section 2.3.
detection_methods: Search Java and C# for `catch (ArithmeticException` and `catch (DivideByZeroException` blocks whose try body divides double or float values, and for comments or tests asserting that floating-point division throws
Search C and C++ for SIGFPE handlers and setjmp-based recovery intended to catch floating-point faults, and check whether feenableexcept or _controlfp actually unmasks the exception

Find divisions and calls to log, sqrt, pow, acos and asin whose arguments can be zero, negative or out of domain, and check whether results are validated with isfinite, isnan, Double.isFinite, Number.isFinite, math.isfinite or numpy.isfinite before being stored, returned or compared
In NumPy code, look for numpy.seterr(all='ignore') or warnings filters that silence divide-by-zero and invalid-value RuntimeWarnings, and for results used without a finiteness check
Check validation code that only tests for null, exceptions or ranges written as `x < min || x > max`, which a NaN passes
potential_mitigations: Check the divisor explicitly, or validate results with `isfinite` before storing, returning or comparing them.
Where trapping is wanted, enable it deliberately and locally, for example `with numpy.errstate(divide='raise', invalid='raise')` or `feenableexcept` inside a scoped guard, rather than assuming it.
Write range checks so that NaN fails them, for example `if (!(x >= min && x <= max)) reject`.
Document which functions can return infinity or NaN, and test them with zero, negative, very large and NaN inputs.
